item.description:
## 一、"先有鸡还是先有蛋"的真相：这不是一个技术问题，而是一个**授权成本**问题
韩歆毅提到"用户想用但商家没有Agent，商家看到没用户就不投入"——这个僵局的表述看似经典，但真正的卡点其实藏在一个更深的地方：**每一次Agent交易，用户都在支付一笔隐形的"授权成本"**——想清楚我能容忍它出错多少、我要授权它到什么边界、如果它删了别人的普拉提课我要不要负责。
这笔成本在传统支付中几乎为零（我付钱=我确认），但在Agent时代被急剧放大。有意思的是：整场讨论的所有嘉宾——从KYA到沙箱到区块链追溯——**本质上都在做同一件事：把这笔授权成本从用户侧转移到基础设施侧**。谁能把用户的"认知负担"吸收得最彻底，谁就赢得这一轮。这也解释了为什么Jorn反复强调"如果出问题我们兜底"——万事达卡真正卖的从来不是支付通道，而是**"你不用想"的这份心安**。
## 二、令人意外的观察：Agent经济正在悄悄复刻**中世纪行会制度**，而不是互联网
大家默认Agent经济是"互联网2.0"，但仔细听这四位的规则设计，它更像是**14世纪佛罗伦萨的商人行会**——身份认证（KYA）

item.title: [Lex Clips] Crisis in psychiatry - historian of psychiatry explains | Andrew Scull and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、DSM 的"软件版本"悖论：升级了外壳，从未重写内核

Scull 讲了一个看似轻描淡写的细节：DSM5 放弃罗马数字改用阿拉伯数字，是为了模仿"Windows 10、11"那样的软件迭代。但这里藏着精神病学界很少愿意承认的黑色幽默——你可以给一个 1980 年写就的操作系统打无穷多个补丁，却没有资格称它为"新版本"。真正的重写需要更换内核，即从"症状清单"转向"底层病理学"。他们花了近二十年、超过 200 亿美元想要完成这次内核重写，最终在 2008 年前后放弃，回到 Robert Spitzer 在 1980 年搭起来的老架构继续加打补丁。

跨领域连接：这与哥白尼之前的托勒密天体系统如出一辙——不断加入本轮（epicycles）来修补预测误差，形式上越来越精细，结构上越来越接近崩溃。DSM 从 106 种膨胀到 300 多种诊断，就是精神医学的本轮。

二、令人不安的观察：DSM 之所以扎根，不是因为它"真"，而是因为它对多方"有用"

访谈里最容易被漏读的一句话是：DSM3 落地时，同时讨好了制药公司（他们需要稳定的"疾病"去开发和申报药物）、保险公司（他们需要可编码的诊断来定价赔付）、患者和家属（他们需要一个名字来命名痛苦）。也就是说，DSM 更像一个"协调博弈"的均衡点，而不是一次科学发现。

这解释了一个诡异现象：当 NIMH 的两位前任掌门人（Insel 与 Hyman）公开把 DSM5 骂为"unscientific and useless"，它仍然屹立为全球精神病学的通用语言。原因和法定货币一样——不是因为背后真有黄金，而是因为所有人同意假装它有价值；拆掉它的协调成本，远高于承认它是错的道德成本。

三、隐藏的历史回旋：监狱 → 收容所 → 监狱的两百年循环

Scull 提到 19 世纪初收容所（asylum）的最初目的，恰恰是把精神病人从监狱和乞丐窝里救出来。而两百年后，全美最大的三家"精神科住院机构"却是洛杉矶县监狱、库克县监狱和 Rikers Island。这不是偶然，而是一种流体力学式的社会现象：当社会拒绝在社区精神卫生投入时，问题会以更高的成本从别处涌出——街头、急诊、监狱。

跨领域类比：经济学家称之为外部性，但在精神病学史里它有一个更精确的名字——责任的地理转移。Scull 用了一个绝妙的比喻，"社区照护是没有豌豆的三只杯子把戏（a shell game without a pea）"——精神病学史里最深的骗局，可能不是任何治疗方案，而是这个 1960 年代关闭大型精神病院时许下的空承诺。

四、最出人意料的一点：重塑精神病学诊断的关键研究本身是学术造假

Rosenhan 的 On Being Sane in Insane Places（1973 年发表于 Science）是催生 DSM3 的震动事件之一——Scull 直接称之为"a scientific fraud"。这意味着现代精神病学的诊断体系，某种意义上建立在一个关于假患者的假研究之上。这里有一种诡异的自反性：精神病学被"自己无法区分真假患者"的证据（而证据本身是假的）逼着重写了自己的知识论。

跨领域回响：斯坦福监狱实验、Milgram 电击实验的部分数据近年都被曝出严重的方法论问题，但它们塑造的社会心理学方向已难以逆转。这揭示一个更深的机制——制度惯性可以从虚构中生长出真实。学科的地基是水泥的，即便浇筑时用的是想象。

五、被低估的第三条路径：Eisenberg 的钟摆诊断

"当我进入精神病学时，它是 brainless（无脑的）；当我离开时，它是 mindless（无心的）。" Leon Eisenberg 这句话在访谈里一闪而过，但它其实是整场对话的病理切片。精神病学过去一个世纪走的不是进步曲线，而是钟摆——从纯心理学（弗洛伊德）摆到纯神经生物学（NIMH 的"脑病模型"）。

Scull 最有力的一击是提出这是一个"category mistake"（类别错误）：大脑的可塑性意味着"社会/心理"和"生物"根本不是二选一——社会经验最终会物理性地嵌入突触结构本身。

这里的跨领域灵光：这一洞见与表观遗传学产生共振——环境不改变 DNA 序列，却改变基因表达；同样地，创伤不改变神经元，却改变突触权重。真正颠覆性的暗示是——精神病学下一次范式革命的语言，很可能不在精神病学内部诞生。发展心理学、社会流行病学、系统生物学早已在锻造那种可以同时容纳"脑"与"心"、"个体"与"社会"的语法。这才是最出人意料的"啊哈时刻"：一门学科的救赎，往往必须由它的邻居来完成。

📝 转录文本

Crisis in Psychiatry — Andrew Scull × Lex Fridman

1. 开场：精神病学是否处于危机之中？

Lex: Is it fair to characterize your view on psychiatry and mental illness is that there's a crisis in modern psychiatry? We have made some progress over the past century but mostly we still are not good at treating mental illness either via the drugs or talk therapy — meaning psychopharmacology or psychotherapy, or as you put it, the brain or the mind route.

Scull: Yeah.

Lex: So let's start at the end of our story. Let's start at where we stand before we go into the rich history that you so eloquently write about.

2. 精神病学试图处理的，是极其复杂的对象

Scull: So psychiatry is a profession that tries to deal with an enormously complicated thing: the human mind, the human emotions, the human ability to attempt to understand the world. And in particular, obviously, it focuses on people where our common-sense approach to the world seems to break down — people whose emotional life is filled with turmoil, people whose ability to relate to others is badly damaged, people who see things in the world that the rest of us simply think aren't there. They're illusions, they're hallucinations, they're delusions.

And this is a subject that has occupied some very clever minds over the years. And there's no question that in the course of at least the last three quarters of a century, there has been some limited progress in dealing with the problems that mental illness creates. Some of that is confined to the milder forms of mental distress; the more serious forms of psychosis and breakdown of emotional control — those are areas where I think, again, there's been some progress, but it's easy to overstate how much of that there's been.

3. 现代精神药理学的偶然起源

As we'll see, probably later in our conversation today, the advent of modern psychopharmacology, which occurred in the early 1950s, was a serendipitous event. It wasn't planned for. It happened almost by accident, and it did mark in some ways an advance over some of the things that psychiatry had engaged in before that. And no question, for some people that revolution — and a parallel revolution in the psychotherapeutic realm — have created some advance for patients, and we should not minimize that.

What we have available to us are symptomatic treatments, not cures. We don't have a psychiatric penicillin for any of the conditions we're going to be talking about. That doesn't mean we can't do some things that help, but the help is quite limited.

4. 医源性问题：治疗本身可能制造新问题

And it's important to understand both the ways in which we have progressed and the limits of that progress. And also to understand that when we treat something, sometimes we create new problems — what we call iatrogenic problems — things caused by the interventions that we use. That's true of some psychotherapeutic interventions and it's most certainly true of the drugs we use to treat mental illness these days.

So for example, in treating PTSD, we often get patients to confront the episode — the trauma which provoked their distress — and that is often a very, very fraught process, and for many patients it actually makes things worse; for some patients it makes them better. So that's a situation where you can see problems.

With both antipsychotics and antidepressants, the two main classes of psychotropic drugs that we use, they're at best partially effective and they don't work for a significant fraction of patients who are given them. And one of the big problems psychiatry faces is that psychiatrists don't know in advance who's going to respond well to the drugs, who's going to respond badly, for which group of patients in the middle the side effects and the main effects — if that's what we want to call them, the therapeutic effects — are finely balanced. And making those judgment calls about what to do is very, very difficult.

5. 危机的第一条线：诊断系统

Now in terms of the crisis psychiatry faces at the moment, as I see it there are a number of strands that point to this. Psychiatry's diagnostic system that is still used — I mean, the fundamental basis of psychiatric diagnosis today — was really first formulated in 1980 with the third edition of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of the profession.

Lex: DSM3.

Scull: DSM3, and then there's been DSM3R, DSM4, DSM4-TR, and now DSM5 —

Lex: finally not with a Roman numeral but with an Arabic numeral.

Scull: So they thought with DSM5, when they needed to modify it, it would be like a piece of software — you have Windows 10, Windows 11, and so on.

6. Rosenhan 事件与"打勾诊断法"的诞生

Right, now that diagnostic system came into being because psychiatrists had a very hard time agreeing with one another about what was wrong with somebody, and that became embarrassingly clear — first in the professional literature, which outsiders didn't read, and then via a very famous study that's a scientific fraud by David Rosenhan called On Being Sane in Insane Places, where he claimed to have sent in pseudo-patients to the hospital, and they all were diagnosed as schizophrenic — all but one of them diagnosed as schizophrenic, the other as somebody with bipolar disorder — and they were fake patients.

So, almost in a panic after that study appeared in Science, and because there was an abundant professional literature from the 1960s showing the same thing — that diagnosis was a very erratic process — the DSM3 task force, led by Robert Spitzer, who was then at Columbia, was explicitly set up to try to create a sort of tick-the-boxes approach to deciding which box a patient belonged in. Were you schizophrenic? Were you this type of schizophrenic or that type of schizophrenic? Were you manic-depressive or bipolar? Did you have various forms of depression?

And to construct those boxes, what they relied upon was a list of symptoms. And if you had more than a certain number — if you had more than six of 10, six or 10 or more symptoms of a certain sort — you could be diagnosed with major depression, for example.

7. 谁在为 DSM 背书：药厂、保险公司、患者家庭

So that system came into being. It was partially embedded because it appealed to drug companies who were developing drugs to treat these various disorders. It appealed to insurance companies because it gave them a stable base to look at. It appealed, as diagnosis always does, to patients and their families who are scrambling to deal with these enormous upsets in the mental life of either themselves or a family member. So it provided some sense of certainty around diagnosis.

But that was always based simply on symptoms — in the way an 18th-century doctor might diagnose dropsy or diagnose some other kind of fever, for example. Well, fever and other diseases they talked about in the 18th century are really a constellation of very different things under one label. And I think that's what is turning out to be true of the DSM labels.

8. 可靠性 ≠ 有效性

But that approach was really all that psychiatry could come up with if it wanted to make sure whether you were in Walla Walla or New York or San Francisco or Atlanta, you reached the same conclusion faced by the same patient — that you had a reliable diagnostic system. That didn't mean necessarily it was a valid diagnostic system.

If you understand the distinction between validity and reliability: reliability means you and I, faced with the same sets of facts, reach the same conclusion. But that conclusion may or may not reflect the underlying reality of things, right?

So you had this diagnostic system, and it went through various iterations. Each time it went through an iteration, the number of possible psychiatric disorders you could get grew and grew and grew. And it became difficult to believe in some of those categories, shall we say, that they were really illnesses rather than some sort of social construct.

9. NIMH 的 200 亿美元豪赌：把精神疾病当作脑病

But beyond that, psychiatrists wanted to be more like other medical doctors — to root their diagnosis in an understanding of the underlying pathology of the disorder. What was it that caused people to become schizophrenic? The sense was, if we could grasp that, we'd have a better handle on how to attack it, how to treat it.

And when DSM5 was mooted, the fifth edition in the early 2000s, NIMH — then under the leadership of Steven Hyman, who's at Harvard now, and succeeded by Thomas Insel, who ruled NIMH for about 13 years — the two of them had pushed psychiatry and psychiatric research in a very particular direction: on the one hand, towards understanding the genetics of mental illness, and on the other, to looking at what the new discipline of neuroscience could contribute to understanding things. Both of them were heavily invested in the idea that mental illness was brain disease.

And if it was brain disease, then the question was: what was making the mechanism here go awry? What was causing people's emotions or their cognitive skills or their sense of the world to become so disordered? And they invested a lot of money in that approach.

10. Insel 的忏悔：花了 200 亿美元，患者境况一点没变好

When Insel stepped down, he gave an interview actually to somebody at MIT — and he's repeated it since in a book he wrote about his experiences — where he said, "Well, you know, as I look back on my 13 years, I funded an enormous amount of scientific — really cool scientific — research. I funded geneticists and I funded neuroscientists, and they did a lot of really interesting science. And after spending $20 billion, the lot of the mentally ill has improved not one bit."

Right. Wow. Which was a pretty devastating statement, I thought.

Lex: And NIMH is National Institute of Mental Health.

Scull: National Institute of Mental Health, yes. I shouldn't resort to jargon. [laughter] But the National Institute of Mental Health had been founded in the late 1940s with the goal of doing basic research, training people in the field, advancing the care of the mentally ill, and producing obviously cures and advances. Its mission has varied widely over the years since. But starting in the 1990s — the period when the first George Bush declared the Decade of the Brain — NIMH increasingly focused on the idea that mental illness was purely a brain disease.

And there's something to that, and there's also a mistake in thinking about it that way.

11. 脑 vs 心：一个"类别错误"

Lex: This is, by the way, as we'll talk about, this distinction between seeing mental health, the maladies of the human mind, as a problem of the brain — like neurobiology, neuroscience — versus the problem of the mind, which is more in the cognitive science, psychotherapy, these — less amenable to scientific rigor. So I think what's appealing about studying the brain and neurobiology, neuroscience, is there's data —

Scull: Yes.

Lex: — it's more rigorous. You could do science.

Scull: It's the kind of thing that really appealed to medical school deans, because once NIH — and the drug companies too — were funding basic research on neurobiology and basic research on genetics, the monies flooded in, and psychiatry, which had been something of an orphan, became much more popular.

Lex: And we should say that this is something you write a lot about, that there's all these factors to consider. So there's the cultural elements, there's the political public policy elements, then there's at a certain point the drug companies and the insurance companies come in. Then there's, of course, all the human beings around somebody who is suffering with a mental health issue. So the family factors, and that's connected to the cultural stuff. It's a very, very complicated area, and oversimplification is a real problem, I think.

12. 大脑的可塑性击穿了脑/心的二分

Scull: And I think even that dichotomy you just drew between the brain and the social or the psychological, or some mix of those things — I think in some ways that's a category mistake. That's a mistaken way of looking at the world, because the brain you and I have today is not the brain we were born with. Human brains are remarkably plastic things. They develop in response to the environment. So the social and the psychological end up being embedded in our brains.

And so that rigid separation of saying we — one or the other. No, there's abundant evidence from epidemiology that social factors play an important role in the development of mental illness.

13. 简化是必要的，但也是危险的

Lex: Nevertheless, the history of psychotherapy, for example, but all of these subfields — yes — the human mind is incredibly complicated with all of these factors. So in order to say anything helpful, you have to simplify. And then Freud famously simplified it a lot towards a very particular view of the human mind. And that simplification is actually — I mean, we'll talk about it — but it's not correct to do in some deeper sense, but it also can be productive.

Scull: Yes. In fact, whenever you're trying to deal with a very complicated set of issues, you have to simplify. You have to make heuristic decisions about what you're going to neglect and what you're going to emphasize.

14. Eisenberg 的钟摆诊断：从"无脑"到"无心"

But what I'm trying to say — you asked me about the crisis in psychiatry, and the simplest way for me to encapsulate the issue and the problem as I see it, that's arisen — one of the problems is a quote by Leon Eisenberg, who had a very long career at Harvard. And Eisenberg said, towards the end of his career, he said:

"When I entered psychiatry, it was a brainless psychiatry — and when I'm leaving it, it's a mindless psychiatry."

And I think that sums up the way in which the field has, to a large degree, moved. And I think in the process, important insights have been lost, even though in some ways other things are being gained.

15. 两极摆动中丢失的洞见

Freudians tended to neglect the biological — to suggest the brain as a biological organism was not something we needed to worry about. We worried at the level of a psychological model of how our minds work. And all too often — not exclusively, because some of the psychiatrists I'm friends with are very sophisticated men and women and do grasp that you can't move in these bipolar directions; you've got to meet somewhere in the middle — but that sort of got lost, I think, in all the enthusiasm for neuroscience.

16. 神经科学的兴起：从电信号到化学汤

I mean, when antipsychotic drugs were discovered in the early 1950s, we had no clue of how they worked. And one of the things that they helped to spawn, as people began to say, "Well, why did these drugs work? What did they do?" was to begin to understand that the brain wasn't just a set of electrical signals — as had been thought in the first half of the 20th century and before — but rather there was this very interesting chemical soup running around in our brains, with neurotransmitters that helped the brain work the way it did, and perhaps explained why it went awry.

So it was one of the many factors that gave rise to neuroscience. The first neuroscience conventions were in the 1970s. They attracted a few hundred people. Now it's tens of thousands of neuroscientists. It's a huge enterprise.

17. 诊断范畴本身的动摇

So diagnosis has come under threat. The categories that we have all become familiar with, that we're told are real diseases — like bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, major depression — are beginning to falter, and we're beginning to worry about whether those diagnoses are real ways of thinking about the world and may in fact mislead us. Because if we think there's something called schizophrenia — or "the schizophrenias," as the inventor of that term put it — if we think there's something like that and we try to research where it comes from, but that's not really what's going on, obviously we're probably going to not make the progress we could be making if we had a better diagnostic system. And that's what DSM5 thought it was going to be able to do and discovered it couldn't. So it stayed basically with this symptomatic approach.

18. Lex 的 DSM 历史速写

Lex: If we can just really briefly — I would love to talk a little bit more about the DSM, but just to give history here, looking it up on Perplexity:

  • DSM1 (1952) was a 32-page pamphlet with 106 diagnoses, heavily influenced by psychodynamic concepts and etiology, using broad, often vague categories like "reactions."
  • DSM2 (1968) expanded to 185 diagnoses, still psychodynamically flavored and reliability poor, but added more attention to childhood disorders, and later removed homosexuality as a disorder in 1974.

Printing then to the revolution, as you mentioned:

  • DSM3 (1980) introduced explicit symptom-based diagnostic criteria, a multiaxial assessment system, and an officially atheoretical stance about causes, aiming to improve reliability and research utility.

Scull: Yeah.

Lex: - DSM3-R (1987) revised criteria, expanded to around 297 diagnoses. - DSM4 (1994) and DSM4-TR (2000) focused on literature-empirical revisions, added and deleted some disorders, increased coordination with ICD-10, and goes on. - And then finally in 2013, DSM5 came out, which eliminated the multiaxial system, integrated most information into a single non-axial diagnostic list and separate notations for psychological and medical factors. It reorganized chapters — e.g., neurodevelopmental, obsessive-compulsive-related, trauma and stress-related disorders — introduced new and refined entities, and so on.

But big-picture trajectory: conceptually, the DSM moved from cause-focused and psychoanalytical to symptom-based, atheoretical, and reliability-driven. Over time, there has been growth in the number and granularity of categories, closer alignment with ICD, ongoing controversy over medicalization, validity, and the balance between categorical and dimensional approaches.

Scull: Yes.

Lex: It feels like that description doesn't necessarily fully get to the core of why the DSM5 doesn't quite get the full scope of the problem.

19. 为什么 DSM5 的"病理学重写"失败了

Scull: You invest a ton of money — you invest 20 billion, more than $20 billion — in a particular approach. And at the time you're constructing this, you say, "Finally, because of all the work that's been done in genetics, we now have decoded the human genome. We have PCR, so we can chop it up and we can look at bits of it. We have a lot more understanding of the role of neurotransmission in the brain. Surely we're going to be able to recast our diagnostic system based on underlying pathology, so that we won't be worrying about symptoms anymore. We'll be looking at the actual underlying pathological changes that have taken place."

But in the event, it turned out they couldn't do that. By about 2008, they had thrown up their hands and said, "No, we're going to have to continue to refine, but rely upon the same basic approach that we developed in 1980." And when that document came out, there had been a lot of criticism — some of it from Robert Spitzer, who had been largely in control of DSM3 and DSM3R, and then his successor Alan Frances, who'd run DSM4. They both were fiercely critical about what was going on and said it was being done in the dark and it was done in secrecy and it wasn't scientific.

And when it was about to come out, Thomas Insel and Steven Hyman — the two then-existing and the preceding director of the National Institute of Mental Health — denounced the document as unscientific and useless.

So if you're talking about a crisis, that's a crisis for the field. If its diagnostic system is being dissed by leading figures like that.

20. 危机的第二条线：药物本身的困境

What else was a problem? The difficulties with the existing drug therapies particularly had become more and more manifest. And to make matters worse, partly because Big Pharma had sometimes behaved, shall we say, rather unethically with these drugs — it had hidden things that undercut their claims, it had manufactured studies, it had manipulated data — and it got caught out and it paid billions of dollars in damages for some of the tricks it had got up to. And not just in psychiatry — I mean, Vioxx, for example, the painkiller, was another huge scandal, and it was a $5 billion settlement.

But the drug companies had suffered some reputational damage. Beyond that, they didn't have any real clues. Unfortunately, neuroscience hadn't thrown up new targets for different forms of drug development. And they decided they could make more money by spending their money on research on other diseases, not mental illness.

So a crisis was: you were stuck with a set of drugs that Steve Hyman says aren't really any advance on the ones that, by accident, we found in the 50s. And there isn't new research — unless it's small startups — going on to develop new ones.

21. 危机的第三条线：公共政策与"街头精神病人"

So you have an increasing sense your diagnostic process is falling apart. Your drug treatments' limitations are becoming more manifest. And as well, for people with serious mental illness, public policy has screwed things up badly.

So if you're a person with serious mental illness, you will die on average 15 to 25 years before the rest of us. And that gap has been growing rather than diminishing. So that's not a good thing. It's not something I want to lay in entirely at the door of psychiatry, so don't get me wrong — I think a lot of this is public policy that has really abandoned treatment for the seriously mentally ill.

And you see it on the streets of our cities. You see the sidewalk psychotics. You see people who are cycling between brief periods of inpatient care, the gutter or the flophouse, and the jail, you know.

22. 监狱作为最大的"精神科住院机构"

So the three largest centers of inpatient psychiatric care, if you can call it that, in the United States today are the Los Angeles County Jail, Cook County Jail in Chicago, and Rikers Island in New York. That's shocking because, by their very nature, of course, prisons aren't equipped to deal with serious mental illness.

Lex: So some dark ways to return to the asylum era.

23. 收容所的初衷：一场关于治愈的乐观主义

Scull: Yeah. Well, you know, the asylums had acquired a very bad reputation. And I've written some about some of the reasons why that happened. But when asylums were founded, it was a period of enormous optimism — that we were going to be able to cure these people, that we would rescue them from attics and from jail cells and, providing a therapeutic environment, coaxing them to work, creating a system where they learn to control themselves — not necessarily to drive their demons out, but to keep them under some sort of wraps.

The expectation was, when the asylums came along, that they'd not only rescue people from horrendous conditions in the prisons and the jails, but they'd actively cure them. And the earliest alienists, as they called themselves then, thought that they could cure 60, 70, 80% — maybe even more — of patients, as long as they came in early.

And really, asylums were built out of that sense of optimism, that sense that so much was environmental and so much was — not exacerbating the condition by treating people like animals or treating them, you know, beating them and in other ways horrifically maltreating them — that that would create a sense of cure. And really, that underlay the construction of the asylums.

24. "社区照护"：一场没有豌豆的骗局

And now, having abandoned the asylums — which we did starting a little bit in the 1950s, but really the late 1960s onwards — that was because there was going to be something miraculous called community care. But community care is a shell game without a pea. It's like one of those confidence tricks. There were no substitute community facilities for dealing with the really seriously mentally ill.

So now we're truly in this crisis, in this essentially dark ages. And in part, I think our conversation, our journey through the history of psychiatry, is an exploration of some gigantic mistakes — but also an exploration of where lay some hope for the future. So we'll talk quite a bit about this.

item.description:
## 一、DSM 的"软件版本"悖论：升级了外壳，从未重写内核
Scull 讲了一个看似轻描淡写的细节：DSM5 放弃罗马数字改用阿拉伯数字，是为了模仿"Windows 10、11"那样的软件迭代。但这里藏着精神病学界很少愿意承认的黑色幽默——**你可以给一个 1980 年写就的操作系统打无穷多个补丁，却没有资格称它为"新版本"**。真正的重写需要更换内核，即从"症状清单"转向"底层病理学"。他们花了近二十年、超过 200 亿美元想要完成这次内核重写，最终在 2008 年前后放弃，回到 Robert Spitzer 在 1980 年搭起来的老架构继续加打补丁。
跨领域连接：这与哥白尼之前的**托勒密天体系统**如出一辙——不断加入本轮（epicycles）来修补预测误差，形式上越来越精细，结构上越来越接近崩溃。DSM 从 106 种膨胀到 300 多种诊断，就是精神医学的本轮。
## 二、令人不安的观察：DSM 之所以扎根，不是因为它"真"，而是因为它对多方"有用"

item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽视的真正断层：不是模型，而是"后训练基础设施"成了新的护城河

最容易被听众漏掉的一句话是——"we essentially spend most of the time building it as an infrastructure than just like one-off training runs"。Fal 不是训练了一个更快的 H3 Max，他们训练了一台能把任何开源视频模型 order-of-magnitude 加速、并叠加相机/光照/口型/参考等控制维度的"流水线"。这意味着视频模型的差异化正在从"权重"迁移到"控制适配层"——LLM 生态在 2023-2024 年经历过一模一样的迁移（base model → SFT → LoRA 生态）。视频 AI 正在压缩时间轴速通 LLM 走过的路，只是这次谁掌握了 post-training infrastructure，谁就是下一代的 Hugging Face + Together AI。

二、一个反直觉的观察：整个视频 AI 行业其实是"配给经济"

"Since around April the whole industry and Fal itself we've been compute constrained—we are growing as much as we are adding compute。"——这句话被轻描淡写地带过，但它的含义是：过去半年公众看到的"模型能力大战"其实是一场影子戏。真正的战争是"每颗 GPU 能挤出多少像素"。这解释了一个奇怪现象——为什么突破来自一家"推理服务公司"而不是基础模型实验室。当资源是限制条件时，优势属于最会榨取硬件的玩家，而非最能堆参数的玩家。这几乎是二战时期德国"虎式坦克"与美国"谢尔曼坦克"的历史重演：在受限环境里，可制造性和吞吐量胜过绝对性能。

三、跨领域连接：H3 Max Director 的"2 分钟记忆 + 演化系统提示"是人脑架构的第三次独立发现

模型在最近 2 分钟保留原始视频 token，在 2-60 分钟范围维持一个"gradually evolving system prompt"来记住整体结构。这几乎精确复刻了人类记忆的双通道——海马体的情景记忆（rich、短、逐渐衰减）+ 皮层的语义记忆（压缩、结构化、长期）。同样的分层出现在 Transformer 长上下文方案（KV cache + summary）里，也出现在数据库设计（hot storage + cold analytics）里。这不是模仿生物，也不是工程巧合——这是一种"柏拉图式最优"，任何需要在有限算力下维持长序列连贯性的系统都会独立收敛到它。视频模型正在给我们提供第三个数据点。

四、让我意外的产品哲学翻转：从"计划发布"到"释放能力，等待涌现"

Rahan 在周六自己的笔记本上开 Twitch 直播、levels.io 独立找上门要做无限流网站、内部另一支团队同时在做 continuous 版本——三条完全平行的爆款路径，没有一条来自产品经理的路线图。这是产品发布的范式反转：传统模式是"build → hype → launch"，Fal 的模式是"drop capability → 24 小时内部创造力爆炸 → 事后追认为产品"。这与 App Store 早期病毒式应用的诞生方式高度相似，与传统模型实验室的"trickle-down demo"完全相反。当能力密度足够高，组织结构就应该从"计划式"切换到"涌现式"——这对任何在做 AI 产品的团队都是一记警钟。

五、隐藏的市场信号：Hollywood 想要的是"动词"，不是"神明"

"Hollywood wants small point solutions rather than generating everything from scratch"——延伸视频、改光照、调镜头。专业市场从来不要"通用能力"，他们要的是"确定性的动词"。这解释了为什么 MarTech 在 2015-2020 分裂成 8000 个专业工具、企业软件被"Verb-as-a-Service"（Stripe = charge、Twilio = message）收割。视频 AI 会经历一次先分裂后再整合的完整周期：接下来 18 个月，你会看到 50+ 个"AI Extend"、"AI Relight"、"AI Recam"的垂直工具，最后再由拥有 post-training infra 的少数玩家（如 Fal）把它们收编成 platform。"AI 取代 Hollywood"的叙事在事实层面已经死了；真实故事是 AI 正在成为 Hollywood 流水线里的一层新中间件——就像 CGI 在 1990 年代做的那样。

二、Token Market Fit 与"算力配给"

There is an incredible amount of demand in the market to generate video, to generate many things at the same time. A person who is doing this for their daily job — they sit in front of a computer and do this all day long, spending thousands of dollars, lots of tokens. And since around April, the whole industry and Fal itself, we've been compute-constrained. We are growing as much as we are adding compute. There are things we do here and there, but the whole industry has been compute-constrained, and we've always been looking for efficiencies to relieve that a little bit so people can use it more.

That has been the idea behind everything we've been doing since April, and this just came at the right time because this makes everything maybe an order of magnitude more efficient — so it gives more compute for other models, or even more tokens can be generated using H3 Max.

Fal (co-founder): From just system-wide optimizations — which is what we have been doing for the past three, four years — you can maybe make the model 2x, 3x faster while producing the same quality, because at the end of the day it's the same model, same architecture, same constraints. You're just trying to optimize what you can get out of the chip. There is a roofline there, and we have been approaching that roofline more and more, especially lately, because our entire team has been focusing on how to get more video pixels out of a single chip.

This new set of post-training-related optimizations — with system/model co-design — enables us to go beyond that roofline by an order of magnitude. We felt the pressure. We had been working on it on top of open-source image models: for video models, we did one version with Ideogram, one version with Flux. So we had been experimenting with how to build post-training infrastructure — take an existing model, build kernels and systems design around it, run it very very fast for a specialized version that can beat anything else. 三、层层叠加的优化栈

a16z: Incredible. Let's dig into that. There are efficiency numbers, cost numbers, speed-up numbers — not everything means efficiency, but it all adds up to be very efficient.

Fal: Yeah.

a16z: What is stunning to me is: an order of magnitude lower cost and also much faster — I think it was like 35x speed up —

Fal: — compared to the original MiniMax endpoint.

a16z: Well, at ELO score you didn't really sacrifice quality. So maybe reveal a little more of the secret sauce — is this more the type of system work you've done? Did you have to do model architecture changes? And how does the next generation of chips, like GB200, fit into the whole story?

Fal: It's a compounding effect of multiple optimization variables we've been targeting.

1. Post-training for fewer steps. You go from the base model to a model that's post-trained to be more efficient. For diffusion models this is essentially how you go from running 50 steps to running something like 20 steps. But as soon as you go from 50 to 20, you lose quality — so you need to target the optimization: I want to improve quality first, then apply the optimization. We have checkpoints of significantly higher quality but slower versions. We run our post-training and RL pipelines so we can improve the model's quality, then apply the optimization stack on top so the end result gets you to the same or higher quality than the original — but an order of magnitude faster.

2. Kernels & systems engineering. All the work that brings your hardware utilization from 30–40% (standard in many inference workloads) to 70–80% on theoretical MFU — which is essentially impossible to reach. You're at the roofline.

3. The full pipeline, not just the model. These models are not just "you give a prompt, get a video back." There are pipelines underneath: take a prompt, use a very large LLM to expand it to a format the model was originally trained on, generate the video in latent space, decode those latents into pixels, and depending on the workload there might be an upscaling component. Every single component by default is unoptimized — there's still lots to be gained. We looked at it from the perspective of: we're going to get the maximum out of every single component. This made us go around LLMs at super high speeds — a completely different set of optimizations from an agent-decoding LLM workload where you have very high cache rates and long sessions. This is single-shot: give a prompt, get a prompt back, no caching, low batch sizes. So a completely different set of optimizations on the prompt-expansion side, on the diffusion model, on the VAE from latents to pixels — combine all of these and the effect compounds.

4. Hardware. Going from Hoppers to Blackwells, you see 2–3x improvement by itself. But from a cost standpoint it's comparable — it reduces wall-clock time but not efficiency itself. It obviously helps if you want to go significantly beyond real time — e.g., generate 5 seconds of video in less than 3 or 2 seconds — you need latest-generation hardware to unlock that.

Depending on how okay you are with losing quality, you can go down. Today these models are so cheap and so fast that I don't think people need any faster or cheaper. Fal: Controllability is key. 六、连续生成与"2 分钟记忆 + 演化系统提示"

a16z: Let's talk about how we made the model more continuous. That was very surprising to me — I've never seen that actually work on a video model before.

Fal: Going back — we've been very focused on world models: essentially action-controlled, action-driven real-time continuous streams of video. The problem until something like H3 Max was that quality was not good enough at all. It degraded a lot; it didn't remember the past. But we built the infrastructure — infrastructure that could stream video, let people control it in real time, multiplex it to multiple people with very low latency.

At the same time, our ML team was trying to take every single video model and apply optimizations and tricks: how do we make this generate — instead of a 5-second video — a 15-second, 30-second video? But you were always below the real-time factor; you never could generate 5 seconds under 5 seconds.

Once H3 Max unlocked it, the ML team said: this is insane. These are separate teams internally — a research team, an inference team, an ML team — they saw this and said, we can apply all these learnings from previous models. Instead of trying to generate a 5-second chunk, generate a 10-second video where the 5 seconds from the previous one is still attended to. We still remember it. And as the video goes up, we can extend that memory up to 2 minutes.

You need extremely clever optimizations, because attending to a 2-minute video is extremely compute-intensive — it goes up exponentially. We did lots of optimizations. We could remember back to two minutes, which is generally good enough from a memory perspective. Then, obviously, with prompt tricks you can still continuously remember finer-grained details above the 2-minute mark, and essentially stream infinitely — be capped at an hour from that perspective.

That team released the model under H3 Max Director, which is public for people to use. I think it's the only model that can generate up to 60 minutes of continuous video that is action-controlled. You can start with a prompt — say, an office setting and someone working — and then 30 seconds later, it imagines by itself. You can say "a woman walks in through the door" and it takes the prompt and reflects it immediately, which is the most fun part.

a16z: And the office is still the same office. The camera can pan back to the original person, and the original person is still there in the same state.

We limited the options, so they could pick "a banana enters the office" instead of "a moon," and it's more fun. We started adding more channels, each with a concept: a full-chaos channel, an '80s-cartoons channel. The model is extremely capable — it remembers so many concepts, has a big memory from a styles and concepts perspective. It became a very fun experience underneath.

a16z: We talked about the consumer experiences this model could unlock, and it seems like Burkay is happy with all the efficiency squeezed out of the GPUs. This is an incredibly popular workflow for VFX artists, people doing this professionally, because they want to get exactly what they put into the model.

The team has been working on an amazing lip-synchronization model — you supply the audio, supply a video or image reference, and it synchronizes the lips perfectly. a16z: And this is by describing it in the prompt, or —

a16z: And this is because the base model itself already has an understanding of the camera angle —

In the market, the biggest gap is how controllable these models are.

We started with text-to-video: put a prompt, get a video back — good, but you never could describe the perfect character. Then image-to-video: use an image-editing model to generate the first scene, the model was more fitting, but you still couldn't say "I want this new character to appear at second 3" — you'd need to put it in your first frame; you could prompt it, but never perfectly. Then we added reference-to-video: provide an initial starting frame, plus "I want these characters with these voices" — a big unlock. Now we're adding: within the scene, camera at this degree at t0, this degree at t3. We're adding lighting controls: where the light comes from. These are all compounding on top of each other, and we have the unified infrastructure to apply this to any model at this point.

十、Hollywood 的实际采用曲线，以及被忽视的"法律基础设施"

Fal: Hollywood is our fastest growing segment. There's a lot of noise about how AI might disrupt Hollywood, but Hollywood usage was non-existent a year ago, and in the past year it grew — and now it's the fastest growing segment. Amazon MGM Studios, at their conference, released their NAR tool — it's mostly backed by Fal infrastructure behind the scenes. We're seeing an incredible pull coming from Hollywood, and it's exactly what they need: small point solutions rather than generating everything from scratch. They want to be able to extend the video a little bit, change camera controls, change the lighting — and someone has to build these solutions for them.

What Hollywood needs and what creators actually need, versus what research labs are working on — there's a bit of a disconnect there. We believe we can come in and do these little post-training projects to close that gap, because we work with all the Hollywood studios and we hear from them what they need. These are exactly the things they need — small point solutions that make them more efficient, push out more video, and AI can close that gap very nicely.

a16z: Maybe say it a little differently — we've been staring at this problem for the last three years. We see companies trying to build a "movie director" video model by either pre-training or post-training on the video side. But what I'm hearing is: different people express the way they want the output to come out very differently. Consumers talk about it and write the prompt very differently from a Hollywood director — which is obvious. Professionals want to talk about camera angles, lighting. You've built a library, a collection of —

Fal: — of post-training data and toolkits that can apply these on any model you can grab the weights of, so they're adapted to a different audience — where each can express their creativity in a different fashion, controlling the model, which unlocks a lot of the capability underneath.

Fal: Half the problem was capabilities of these models — we're solving that. The other half of the problem was legal and data residency. We made a ton of progress there as well. We now have a system where people can apply with their own IP, and we unlock their own IP in the models. We're going to grow that — that's going to be a very powerful thing we do with Hollywood studios. Also, we now have Seedance US-hosted as well. We already had other Chinese models — Seedance was the missing part. Every Hollywood studio wanted us to have it US-hosted. Now that's available, so there are no obstacles in front of these Hollywood studios. Everything is ready — we believe they're going to 10x, 100x their AI usage in the coming months.

十一、结尾：Generative Media Conference 的信号变化

a16z: It's such an exciting world for movie lovers, consumers, people who consume a lot of video and creative content —

Fal: — and we have our Generative Media Conference next week. This is the second time we're doing it. Last year it was mostly consumer AI — there were maybe a couple of Hollywood executives here and there, just curious about it. And now it's dominated by studios, new AI studios that are offshoots of the bigger studios trying to do only-AI shows, but also the biggest of the Hollywood studios are there, because now they have big plans integrating AI into their workflows, into their existing systems. You can see the change in the attendance of the conference as well.

a16z: That's awesome. Well, for the audience — check out the content coming out of the Gen Media conference. It's going to be very, very exciting. And thank you so much, Burkay, for coming on to our show. It's a super exciting time for gen media. Thank you.
