item.dc:creator: All-In Podcast
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

洞察一：这不是数据中心故事，而是"财政管道倒挂"的故事

多数人以为 Meta 在路易斯安那 Richland Parish 的故事是"科技巨头带来就业"。真正的机制远比这更精妙——数据中心的经济价值并不是通过工资渗入社区，而是通过销售税一夜之间从"基础设施建设"直接跳进"教师工资单"。

请注意超级学监描述的曲线：销售税征收从常态的 5–10% 增长，飙升到 260%。而路易斯安那有一条罕见的法律——征收盈余强制流向教师。这意味着：Meta 建一栋楼，Richland 教区的老师就从年终 4,000 美元奖金跳到 50,000 美元。这不是"涓滴经济学"，这是税制的意外套利——一个 20 世纪的地方财政公式，被 21 世纪的资本密度激活了。

跨领域连接：这与 19 世纪美国铁路小镇的"土地授予"模式惊人相似。当年铁路公司获得沿线土地，用土地增值反哺基础设施建设；今天则是数据中心用销售税盈余反哺人力资本。区别在于：铁路制造了地理网络，数据中心制造了智力网络——而 Richland 教区正在无意中把两者合并成同一个财政循环。

洞察二：反数据中心叙事之所以能赢，是因为它触发了一种"看不见的丧失"

Dina 提到情报委员会怀疑对手在推波助澜。这或许是真的，但更深层的原因藏在认知不对称里：

  • 数据中心的成本是可见的——一栋丑陋的建筑、卡车、噪音、"传说中的"用水；
  • 数据中心的收益是不可见的——教师奖金、儿子搬回家、餐厅从服务 40 人变成 400 人。

人脑对"具象损失"的敏感度是"抽象收益"的 3–5 倍（前景理论）。所以即便算数上 Meta 净贡献惊人，媒体和社交叙事天然会放大瓶装脏水这类触觉记忆。

出人意料的观察：这场争论的真正战场不是"数据中心好不好"，而是"我们是否有能力让抽象收益获得触觉证据"。Sheldon 校长做对的事情——在校董会议上宣布销售税支票金额——本质上是把"抽象收益"翻译成了"具象体验"。这套翻译工作，其实是数据中心行业最缺的产品。

跨领域连接：这和疫苗接种运动的传播困境一模一样——疫苗预防的疾病是不可见的，副作用是可见的。医学界用了 50 年才学会"讲人物故事"。数据中心行业只有 3 年时间学会同一件事。

洞察三：America's Workforce Academy 是"AI 时代的技校套利"，可能比 Meta 的模型更改变社会结构

40,000 人申请、250 人毕业、90% 留存率——这个规模似乎微不足道。但注意 Dina 提到的结构性突破：培训期间就发放正式工资，而非学徒工资。

这个决定看似简单，其实颠覆了 100 年的美国职业教育经济学。传统技校的隐形门槛不是学费，而是机会成本——一个 Uber 司机、女服务员、家庭护理工不可能停下四周去无薪培训。Meta 只是把这四周的收入风险从"劳动者"移到了"资本方"。

让人意外的观察：这实际上是资本对时间的补贴——AI 公司用它们最不缺的东西（资本）购买它们最缺的东西（合格工人的时间）。而这个模式一旦成立，可能在 5 年内取代大部分社区大学的角色。

跨领域连接：这个模式与二战期间美国的"GI Bill"惊人相似——政府用资本补贴退伍军人的时间，让他们完成教育。但这次不是政府，是数据中心资本。当 Ruth Porat、Larry Fink、Mary Barra 都加入这个联盟时，你看到的其实是私营部门在悄悄搭建一个平行的、比公立教育更快的劳动力再分配系统。这可能是本世纪最重要的教育制度变革——发生在 VFW 大厅和社区大学，而不是常春藤。

一个反直觉的结论：如果 AI 真的自动化了大量白领工作，未来 10 年真正稀缺的不是模型，而是能把 40,000 申请人变成 40,000 就业者的物流系统。Meta 无意中在为自己的 AI 失业浪潮建造社会缓冲区。这既是慈善，也是最深的自我保险。

📝 转录文本

开场介绍

A trailblazing leader in government, business, and philanthropy.

A former presidential adviser to Donald Trump, Dina Powell McCormick joined Meta Platforms as president and vice chairwoman. She'll help lead the company's massive AI expansion, including data centers, investments, and global partnerships. Powell McCormick's background is exactly where Meta's new bottlenecks are.

"There is a transformation in humanity coming. Nothing can stop that now with this technology. 3.5 billion people every day are on Meta. I think we all know that the next three years could be the whole game. Women are the secret sauce. How about that?"

Please welcome Dina Powell McCormick.

一、开场寒暄与议题切入

Host: See you. Thanks for coming out.

Dina: Hey, good to see you.

Host: All right, good to see you. How are you? Dina, thank you for being here. Um, you know, we were just finishing up a conversation with Satya about how do we tell the story about the benefit of data centers and what they're doing to communities and why they're actually net economically positive. And I know you — so I'm going to get right into it because I know you actually have a video on this. Do you want to just start with your video? Would that be okay?

Dina: That'd be great. I mean, I just want to say — so psyched to be at the All-In Summit, first time to speak, and as long as this episode and panel gets way more listeners and views than Senator McCormick did when he came on, I'll be very, very happy with that. So, now we can roll the tape.

Host: No competition. Good. We'll put it on Poly Market. Let's watch the video.

二、Richland Parish 视频：一个被"机会遗忘"的教区

"Richland Parish was the place that opportunity forgot about. I've grown up here my whole life and I've seen a lot of people move away looking for work, including my son. What you were hearing a lot lately was: there's nothing here for us anymore.

We knew that having a data center would give us an industry here that we haven't had before. That's a huge investment in our community.

We started this business simply because Meta was coming. We thought we had hit it big when we got to cater for 40 people. Now we do 400 a week.

Since Meta came to town, we've hired more employees.

A multi-billion dollar capital investment like the one that Meta is making in Richland Parish — it was transformative. It's extremely exciting to attract and retain quality teachers.

So, when I first got the news about the bonus, it was jaw-dropping. My mouth was literally wide open. We're not in it for the money. We're teachers because it's in our heart. But the bonus has been extremely helpful.

With the investment that Meta has made in our community, now we can do a better job of taking care of our home.

I do feel a lot of hope for the future of my students. It gives them the opportunity they never thought that they would have. And I would say one of the biggest things is people coming back home.

You know, the future's happening here and happening now."

三、迎接来自 Richland Parish 的嘉宾

Host: You have some folks from the video here.

Dina: I do. Can — come on out. Come on out, Sheldon and Susan. We have the superintendent from that video, the superintendent in Richland Parish.

Host: Thanks for joining us. Pleasure. Hi, sir. Thanks for joining us. Hi, how are you? Come on down. Good to meet you. How are you?

Guests: Thank you for being here. Thanks for having us.

Host: You want to do an introduction?

Dina: Sure. What an honor. It's an honor for me to be here with Sheldon and Susan. We've spent a lot of time in Louisiana. It's our largest data center investment for Meta, and I've been with them in Louisiana. And what is remarkable to me is just the leadership that frankly the governor has shown. Susan is the commerce secretary for Louisiana, the economic development secretary, and Sheldon — who I'm going to let him speak for himself, but he is such an inspirational figure there. And he is the one that realized that because of our investment, the tax surplus would go straight to teachers. Maybe you can talk just a little bit about that.

四、Sheldon（学监）：销售税奇迹与教师奖金

Sheldon: Yes. So it's great to be here. I just think back to my first interaction with Meta. It was in the summer of 2024, and it was at our local community college. I just remember after the meeting getting in my car — and it's hot in Louisiana — so I turned the air on and I just sat there and I said: the game has changed. This is going to give our parish an opportunity to do something that it's never been able to do.

So, when the groundbreaking ceremony happened in December of 2024, I could immediately start to see the increase in our sales tax collections. There are six taxing entities in our parish. The Richland Parish School Board collects 51% of the taxes for the district. So I was able to see the sales tax collections go from 5%, 10%, which is normal for a school system, to about 60 or 70%. And at that time the number of workers at the data center site increased. Those collections peaked at about 260%.

We have a 1-cent and a half-cent sales tax that's dedicated to employee salaries. And so we're announcing these sales tax increases at our school-board meetings. And we're educators, so people can do the math. They start to figure out this is going to translate into a larger sales tax check, which directly goes into our salaries.

So in December of 2025, we gave out a half-cent sales tax check. That check doubled from the previous year. So it went from roughly about $4,000 to about $8,000, but we hadn't seen a full year of spiked increases in sales tax collections. That happened this past June. So our certified employees received an increase of about $40,000 in their sales tax.

Host: $40,000 check.

Sheldon: They got a $50,000 check.

Host: Wow. Wow. Wow.

Sheldon: So the check the previous year was $10,000. So if you take that December increase and the June increase, it was a net of about $45,000 for our teachers.

五、社区情绪：从"未知"到"招募热线"

Host: Did they all — 'cause the reason Dina and I were talking about this panel — and everyone hates data centers. They pull 80 in the United States. And Dina was telling me the story and I was like, we should tell this story because it is unbelievable. Did the teachers and the community have this negative sentiment about data centers before? Were they all "we hate data centers, we don't want them here"? Or was that before this wave happened and the community didn't really kind of pay much attention to it?

Sheldon: I think initially there was the unknown. We are the beginning. We're a starting point. There was no reference for us to access. We couldn't say, "Okay, well when was the last time we had a $50 billion capital investment in our schools?" So, how did we handle that? So yeah, where a few million dollars — that's huge for us. So there were anxious thoughts. I think Meta has done an excellent job of informing us and educating us, and that's going to have to continue to happen. Oftentimes this communication is not about the most informed person in the community — it's about the least informed person in the community. So we're working to make sure that we continue to get that positive message out about the good things that are happening, because there are a lot of good things that are happening in our parish.

Susan: Yeah. I think to the superintendent's point, Louisiana was a little bit late to the data center game, which has actually worked remarkably well to our benefit in that the Meta investment was the first one in the state. And because of the partnership — the way we negotiated the deal, I call it a partnership, not a negotiation, frankly, all along — the community, when we first brought the idea, even prior to you knowing, superintendent, the community wasn't apprehensive because there was a great deal of unknown. Now, keep in mind this was about 20 months ago is when we started the conversation there. So the chatter wasn't as much as it is now.

But you're talking about a community that was really starved for opportunity. As you saw in the video, we had lost population. The average wages in Richland Parish were roughly $36–$38,000 a year prior to this investment. So the data center went to a place in Louisiana — Mississippi River Delta parish — that was longing for this opportunity, and we got ahead of that. I think we got ahead of that very wisely in the way we addressed both the concerns, the impact on the community, the good impact on the community, and the natural resources and all the things we're hearing.

Host: Right. In a weird way, all of this noise is actually somewhat beneficial in the sense that you may just want to go to Dina and say, "we'll just take all your data centers" because — I mean, quite honestly —

Susan: I think our governor would actually — continuous change in the earnings potential of normal average Americans.

The governor just signed an executive order a few months ago creating a framework for us under which we will engage with large-load users. And the privilege that it gives us now is we get to be choosy. We have a sales tax exemption which is critical to be able to land an investment of this size and this scale. But now we get to really court who our partners are going to be. And the governor claims it all the time that Meta really was the prototype for us and it set a very high standard. That's now the standard we're going to follow. We are not one of those states who is saying no. We are one of those states that are saying yes.

六、正面回应：污染、水、电、噪音、美观

Jason: So maybe you could help us with — it's pretty clear the economic case for building and growing and creating jobs. Take us through the list of valid concerns communities have. One of them is pollution. I'm not sure if this is running off of gas or if it's all solar and renewables. Increased electricity cost. Water — closed loop versus non-closed loop. Noise pollution and aesthetics. These buildings are awfully ugly typically as created. Did any of those apply? Did you get any of that feedback from the community?

Host: Our journalist.

Jason: What's that?

Host: Our journalist.

Jason: No, no, no. Actually, it's not journalism. Actually, what it is is it's facts, Sacks. These are the facts of — Dina, the people, hold on, I'll finish — these are the facts that community members have valid concerns about. There are people who have had data centers put next to them that are polluting, that are creating noise, and there are valid water concerns, and there are communities where their electricity went up. So, I'm asking a serious question based on facts. I'm wondering if any of those apply to you.

Susan: Yeah, Janie [Jason], you said this was going to be easy. Um, yeah, clearly, we're all people, right? We all hear, we all have the same concerns. Again, some of it was that we got very lucky with the timing of all this because those issues were addressed before they became in the public forum of issues.

Number one, this was farmland. This was agricultural land. And early on in the conversations with the Meta team, they made a decision to use a more expensive but more efficient system that actually uses less water than was being used on that land when it was being farmed. Right? It's not a statistic you hear very often.

The second piece about the energy — clearly we're hearing it across the board — but there are two really critical components to this. Number one is that Louisiana has abundant natural gas. We have about 32,000 miles of natural gas pipelines in Louisiana today. If we don't add another mile, we have access to natural gas everywhere. But in the relationship that Meta created with Entergy, the energy provider there — from day one, before this was an executive order from the president or even the governor — Meta paid for its own generation. It paid for grid resilience. It paid for grid upgrades. It paid for storm costs. Louisiana has storm assessments when we have hurricanes. It happens every now and then. It's paying for storm costs in a state where they didn't operate right when these hurricanes hit. So, it's actually taking burdens off of the Louisiana consumer. So all those issues were issues and they were addressed with the original negotiated deal. And I will say, it's really why it's become the prototype for how we move forward with others.

七、错误信息战：为何反对声音如此响亮

Chamath: This is a question for you. You used to be the deputy national security adviser. So answer this maybe with just a bit of that hat on. I mean Jason brings up valid concerns, but then there's this data that is so clear for you but also for others. I mean you just heard from Satya. Why is this misinformation campaign winning so soundly in America? What has happened? Like what is going on?

Dina: Sure. Well, I think first, the questions that Jason raised are really legitimate questions. And I think we start with a premise that if a community doesn't want one of our data centers, they get to choose. They get to decide. But that we actually have to upfront and way more aggressively explain what our investment and partnership means. And we have a compact — a compact that Susan and Sheldon are describing.

First, not just pay for your own electricity — make sure that you're working to drive electricity costs down. The second is the water issue. It's very real in farmlands and rural communities, but there's absolutely now new technology — in fact, AI-driven technology — that makes you able to actually increase water consumption. The third is the teachers. I'll be very honest, this was not our idea. This actually happened because this law allows — or in fact mandates — that every extra dollar of tax surplus goes directly to the teachers. And the superintendent was telling me things that just are so remarkable. Used to have a hard time recruiting teachers. Now his phone is ringing off the hook throughout Louisiana. Teachers wanting to come there. And this may end up being the best school district in the entire state.

And now we have taken that learning and we're investing in teachers and first responders. And you saw of course the economic development impact for small businesses. That's our compact everywhere we go. Meta makes sure that we do those things.

But to answer your question, Chamath, I don't think that our industry has done a good job communicating — just flat out, we have to do a better job. But before you can communicate anything, you've actually got to be meaningful and have real impact. And so we've started with the premise that we want to be the best actor and the best partner possible. And now, having frankly the impact that we see in Louisiana — we're very proud of the impact we're having in Texas and Ohio — but I think we have to tell these stories more.

And I know you're alluding to — where is this information coming from? I was just with Chairman Cotton and Vice Chairman Mark Warner and the intelligence committees. They do believe they have evidence that our adversaries are trying to gin this up. I can't comment on that, but what I can tell you is: if you wanted to stop America right now, what would you do? This is exactly what you would try to do. If you were any of our adversaries, you would want us to stop building data centers in the United States so that we would not be on a path to being AI dominant in the world. This is what you would do. So whether they're doing it or not, this is definitely an approach you would take.

And I actually said to them very respectfully: these are great jobs, and the communities that want the jobs, want the teacher bonuses, want these investments should be allowed to have them. And those that don't should opt out. But we certainly don't want our companies — my company and our peers — to start thinking about building data centers [elsewhere].

Chamath: It's so easy to debunk these issues. The water one is the one that's just confounding — that narrative keeps staying alive. I think you did an amazing job.

Host: There's a clip on X of this woman with this bottle of dirty water that she trucks around, and you're just like — so good.

Host: You know what I love? I love that it's a federated republic that the founders designed, and some states are going to win, some states are going to be idiots and they're going to lose, and you guys are going to have this incredible economic advantage.

Susan: Yeah, I do want to add to Dina's point as well. Just as the teachers are calling Sheldon to consider going to his parish to teach, the minute that got announced that y'all were giving $50,000 bonuses, I can't tell you how many leaders of rural parishes in Louisiana called me and said, "Secretary, do y'all have any who are considering our parish? Please bring one here." So the global narrative is not happening in Louisiana. I frankly don't believe it's happening everywhere the way the propaganda —

Host: [Are others] calling you from across the country, like other states saying, "Is this real? How did this work?" and starting to kind of lean in and see if they can participate.

Sheldon: So, historically, one of the challenges we've had as a rural school system is that our best and our brightest — they'll do exceptionally well in school. They may even go to our local universities, but when they leave, I have a good idea in my head that they're not coming back to Richland Parish because we can't offer jobs that attract them. So they leave and they go to other states and they go to other cities. And now we're able to write our own narrative — that if you want to leave and go, you can, but you don't have to. We have opportunity here for you here in Richland Parish. You have the ability to stay here to raise your family. And I think it's changing the narrative in our parish.

Host: Well, Dina, I know you've got another video for us to watch also on how do we get more workers to come and participate in this growing economy. While we watch that, why don't we thank Susan and Sheldon for joining us. Thank you both for being here. Thank you so much. Yeah, that was great. Fantastic. Thank you so much. Appreciate you very much. Appreciate you coming out. Thank you so much.

八、America's Workforce Academy 视频

"I've always wanted to do something big. I know that this is the program that I need to be in in order to discover that.

In order for a lot of technology to advance, we need the infrastructure. Meta is blessing these guys with the opportunity to be a part of that — to help lay foundation for the future.

You can come into the program with no prior experience. After you finish your four weeks here, you'll be able to go into the workforce. I'm grateful for this opportunity. I'm excited to actually get to do the work.

To have a group of students who are taking the opportunity serious and are doing it with passion, that means everything.

Once they're able to finish our course, there's so many different paths that they can take. The more that we learn and establish this workforce, the more we can impact future generations.

I feel like it will change the world. I'm ready to work."

九、光纤技术员短缺与"美国劳动力学院"的诞生

Host: You were telling me a story about like a posting for fiber optic technician. Can you just tell that story because I think it's incredible.

Dina: Sure. So, even in our site in Louisiana, one of the issues is that we just can't find enough workers. And you really need a set of welders and pipe fitters and construction workers, electricians. But there's something that every data center site really needs: fiber technicians, the people that actually lay and cut the fiber. And we just could not find enough people.

And so we just made a curriculum and we partnered with a few people — CBRE and others. We realized that this program just didn't exist. So we decided: if you can do it for fiber technicians, why not go beyond? It's a five-week fast-track training program where you get all of your safety training. You get something called "job site ready" designation, so you can get the job. We at Meta guarantee you a job if you graduate on one of our data center sites, and you have that certification with you whether you want to stay at our site or elsewhere.

And the missing piece is that while there are, as David Sacks has said over and over again, 500,000 open jobs for these roles over the next couple of years, but there was this gap between people actually getting those jobs. And it's because it turns out: if you're a waitress or you're an Uber driver or you are a home healthcare worker, you live paycheck to paycheck. You cannot afford to take that time off unpaid. The training is weirdly very expensive. OSHA training and things like that. And what if you do that and you don't get a job?

So we launched America's Workforce Academy. We launched it, I don't know, four months ago. 40,000 Americans applied. We've graduated 250 people, and we have a 90% retention rate. So people that are getting into these contractor jobs on our data center sites — you can see they've learned a new trade, they've left behind a job that wasn't as fulfilling, and of course every company that's hiring them is just thrilled.

It's also something that's interesting, David, that you and I talked about, which is we have partners across the board in this program. We didn't put Meta in the name because we are so excited to be working with other companies that are interested in recruiting these workers as well. But we're working with the unions. Sean McGarvey, the head of the trades, NABTU, is a friend and we made a great partnership with him there. Some of those workers are on union sites, some are non-union. But an interesting voice that has emerged in this debate is the unions. The union leadership now is saying, "We want to be anti- the anti-data center backlash. These are our jobs. These are for our people." And so they actually put out even before the midterms a note saying they are only going to support candidates that support data centers.

Chamath: How much balance sheet capital does it take to get this thing off the ground, and do you see the other majors — the big eight — kind of joining forces and having this new educational track kind of become a de facto standard in America?

Dina: You know, all of us are working on this. In fact, I just talked to Ruth Porat at Google. She's done an incredible job on workforce and she's actually brought together — we're going to join this alliance. Larry Fink at BlackRock has joined the alliance. She's bringing together other companies. You know, we might compete on models and products, but we don't want to compete on people. We as an industry, I think, are doing this part well, where we're really working together, because anybody that gets trained to work on a Meta data center site can certainly go to a Google site or a Microsoft site. And so this is a place where we've really come together.

Host: How do you expand the capacity? So there's 40,000 that applied, but you picked 400 — that's 39,600 that [weren't picked].

Dina: Yeah. And we started 4 months ago and now we're literally getting calls from Mary Barra at GM: "I'd like a thousand employees." You know, once you have the curriculum and the certification and the partners to deliver it, you can do these everywhere. We're doing them in community colleges, VFW halls. In that particular program, you actually have to have a site that's kind of like a model data center so that you can show how to train the fiber technicians. But we're working with the Association of Builders and Contractors. They have thousands and thousands of places across the country where they operate.

Host: Why is it so expensive — outside of you guys basically backstopping this — to get something like job site ready and OSHA awareness? I mean, this should seem like you go online and —

Dina: I think the thing that we unlocked is that we actually pay during the training what you would get if you are already in the job. It used to be that there's a very low fee or an apprentice fee for so long that it wasn't the full payment of the job. And so we do that from the beginning. And then of course these jobs — I mean, David and I have been in Pittsburgh with some of these workers, and these are jobs. Welders make $120,000 a year in Pittsburgh. That is meaningful, great work. And I think the unlock that we're very proud of with this program is that there just wasn't a clear and fast path to getting on the job site and to having a guaranteed job.

Jason: It's great that you have these jobs because with AI progressing so quickly, these developers are going to need something to do. And so I think they can segue into electrician jobs. I'm kidding, obviously. But absolutely fantastic work on the data centers, fully supported. Great job on the Meta glasses — amazing. And this effort —

Dina: Where are your Meta glasses, Jason? I gave you [some].

Jason: They're right here on the bag. Right in my backpack. They're actually super impressive.

十、Jason 的"重磅问题"：Meta 与儿童

Jason: And this effort is truly impressive. But you said you wanted me to do a fastball or two, and you didn't want it to be —

Dina: She didn't say that. Jal —

Jason: She literally asked me for at least one fastball.

Dina: Jal fastball, uh —

Host: You did. Okay, so we'll just keep it all softball before you ask [the] question. Please, please come back.

Host: Go ahead, Jason.

Jason: No, no, no. We can just go. We'll go softballs. The boys prefer. Go ahead. Go ahead. Well, I mean, we have Meta here and you just paid the largest settlement in [history], second only to the tobacco industry. And just ahead of BP oil — two of the biggest disasters this country ever faced. And this one is particularly tough —

Host: And they wonder why they call him fake news.

Dina: I I I — numbers are wrong. I'm happy to talk about the Meta glasses if you prefer.

Jason: I'm so glad — go read your effective altruism.

Dina: I'm actually really glad you asked me about it because —

Jason: Yeah, well no, let me finish the question. You may not be — so I'm going to lean in now, so to speak. The real, I think, challenge a lot of us have with Facebook as an organization — and these are amazing, the videos are super inspiring and well produced — but you guys really did damage, significant damage, to children. You knew that these products were too addicting. And the philosophy of the company from the beginning, when Chamath was there — "hey, move fast, break things, let's go super fast."

My sincere question is: how has the culture changed inside of Facebook? And you're making a new series of potentially more addicting products with character-based AI companions, with Muse as a product. So I'm curious what's changed in the organization and what did you learn from that record-setting fine and something that you could have done a lot better on.

十一、Dina 反击：与 52 位州总检察长的历史性协议

Dina: Um, well I totally disagree with basically every single premise in your question.

Jason: Totally fine. Billion dollar settlement says otherwise.

Dina: Do I get to speak, or are you done with your 10-minute question? Okay. I totally disagree with the premise of that.

I've only been there eight months. I was on the board for a year, and I can tell you — cuz I work with these people every day — they are really, really focused on ensuring that parents are empowered, teens are supported. And I couldn't be actually more proud of the agreement that we just made.

We made it with 52 bipartisan attorneys general across the United States and the territories. We are now setting industry standards. We agreed that if your state signed on with us, children under 18 — not 16 — can only be on our platform for 2 hours a day. The app shuts off after that, and it completely shuts off at night. There are no notifications during the school day at all of any kind. And frankly, parents have way more supervision now — many, many ways that they can decide what their kids are on, how long they're on, and what they're seeing.

And I think that we're proud of that because if others in our peer group joined, this could be pretty historic and game-changing. And Jason, I'm a mom of six daughters, so this is really personal to me. I watched them grow up in this generation, and I feel that we really can actually find a way to come together.

The reason your numbers were wrong on the settlement is because we actually agreed to give an additional $5 billion and to go down to only one hour of use on our platform if YouTube, TikTok, and Snap join us. Because, as we know, people leave one set of apps and go to another. But wouldn't it be pretty amazing in America if children under 18 could only be on apps for an hour a day, shut off at night? And I just think that's —

Jason: 100% yes.

Dina: Thank you.

十二、家长控制 vs. 平台默认：一场"打地鼠"辩论

Host: Do you think it should be universal, Chamath, or do you think it should be controlled by the parent, like give the parent basic controls? What's your view?

Dina: Well, it is — meaning obviously a parent can override it, but our app actually just does turn off.

Host: Obviously a parent — it's funny. I was in Texas this weekend at the Texas–Ohio State game — you, my alma mater. And it was really funny. I had so many people come up to me and say, "You know, this turning off — it's literally happening. Turning off Instagram is hurting college football recruiting." I'm like, "What are you talking about?" [They said,] "In Texas, we put all of our kids' videos on Instagram and they get recruited."

Dina: So, it is interesting. I said, well, we live in America. That's up to you. You can decide as a parent if you want to do more. It does actually shut off and a parent has to override that.

Host: I think it's incredible. I remember just being with my kids at the dinner table and my son was trying to show me something and he had hit the limit — just turned off. And there's nothing. And I was like, this is fantastic. You're like, "leave it off."

Dina: What's that?

Host: You're like, "just leave it off. You don't care."

Chamath: The reason is, as a parent, it's whack-a-mole. Because the content is syndicated across all these platforms. And that's why what you're saying is so right. When my five kids go to school, they interact with YouTube as their primary outside-of-school mechanism because so much of the school content and educational content is there. So even if you shut off Shorts and Instagram, they pop up over here. So it is this whack-a-mole problem for parents, and it's a full-time job to manage it. And so if there is effectively like a labeling and a decision on governance by these companies, it's deeply helpful for all of us that have jobs, are trying to live a life, and raise kids normally so they don't become zombies.

Host: Zach, you're very active managing your kids' mobile phone usage.

Zach: Yeah. How many do you have? Look, I think the new defaults probably are better. I mean, just thinking about my kids' usage — yeah, it'd be nice if it turned off after an hour or two. So yeah, look, I think that's an improvement.

I do have to sort of defend Meta because I do think that there was a little bit of a ridiculous pile-on where, you know, the company's getting sued by adults who are blaming the use of this completely voluntary product. No one's forcing you to use any of these social network products, and then something goes wrong in their life that has many causes, and then they're suing Meta and winning big judgments, and then the state AGs get in on the act, and all the trial lawyers —

Host: The trial lawyers. The trial lawyers' money, I thought.

Zach: Yeah. So let's just acknowledge that there is a little bit of a shakedown going on here as well. I mean, let's face it, that is kind of how the American court system works. But look, I think that they have reached a resolution that I think is net beneficial, and I like the new defaults. And ultimately this is about parental control. Parents should choose what apps their kids use and for how long. It should not be the government doing that. It should be the parents. And we should just make it as easy as possible for the parents to do it. And in my view, the only reason to do these new defaults is because of the whack-a-mole problem.

十三、成瘾设计、RSI 与"新默认"的意义

Jason: I mean, I'm glad we're having this discussion. The issue for me has been the industry got very addicted to gamification and designing products to be addicting, and increasing time spent on app was in fact internally what Facebook was focused on. The challenge is, you can be too good at something. And I think Facebook, along with YouTube and their algorithm, were just too good at addicting people to it, whether they're adults or kids. And I will commend you — even if it was late — as an organization in doing the right thing now and then leading the other organizations to do the right thing.

Chamath: Let me build on what you were saying with the statement. Satya talked about this. I think Jensen will talk about it. Elon will talk about it. But you're going to hear this word RSI over and over over the next 18 months — recursive self-improvement — which is this idea that if you define a reward function for an AI and let it go, it's going to self-improve.

So, to your point, Jason: anything, whether it's World of Warcraft or Angry Birds or whatever app, you put it into an RSI loop and you add the reward function being time, all these apps will proliferate. Microsoft Word will keep you there for 9 hours if it can. So unless companies make a decision like you guys — to say, "here's a threshold, and beyond this threshold we're just going to turn it off" — it's going to be kind of turtles all [the way down].

Jason: Which was my point: how does it inform product decisions going forward? You got this incredible new product, Muse. You're in the mix on the bots. But again, I think the leadership and challenging the other organizations is what I will give you kudos for.

十四、Meta Glasses：从时尚到盲人退伍军人

Chamath: You know, I don't want to speculate. I want to talk about this addiction thing as it relates to the product that we all tried on backstage. We all put on a Meta glass and I'd never — I've never had the product before. What is the repeated use case of that product you think? Like what is it that gets people —

Dina: The glasses. Sorry.

Chamath: Yeah. So, I remember when Google had the goggles and then Apple had VR, and everyone's had an effort at putting something on your face and none of them have stickiness. They're all like really interesting novelty experiences, and then your usage tapers off and you kind of put it in the drawer and it's like a cool tech relic.

Host: Well, they're very stylish.

Host: Yeah, these are the Kylie Jenners.

Dina: No, actually we are so excited about this as a product. The engineers have been working on this for 10 years. You make a good point that if people don't look good in them and they're not stylish, they're not going to put them on. But billions of people wear glasses, whether they're to see or obviously sunglasses.

And we're really excited about the features. You can obviously listen to music. The only way I listen to All-In every week is wearing my Meta glasses as I'm walking or working out. They actually have the incredible speaker, and so your phone calls are perfect. And now we have a couple of features we're really excited about:

  • Conversation focus. So when Chamath is at dinner with his beautiful wife and he actually wants to hear her — if he looks at her, all the noise goes away except her voice, which is pretty cool.
  • Translation.

Host: That's great — translation as well.

Chamath: Can I do the opposite when I'm — Chamath? It's interesting, Dina.

Dina: Great people I talk to. I'd like more of that.

Chamath: Chamath is just telling me he got the new Apple AirPods 5 specifically because of wife-canceling. The opposite. Want the opposite feature.

Host: You can actually tune in. But let me tell you why you're wrong and I'm right. Okay, thanks.

Zach: By the way, with these products, you're damned if you do and damned if you don't in the sense that if you design it poorly, no one's going to want to use it. If you design it really well and it's a big success, a bunch of trial lawyers are going to say it was addictive and then you get sued for that.

Dina: So true.

Chamath: Dina, can you — sorry, I just wanted to move to AI for a second before —

Dina: No, I want to finish on this. The reason so many people are working — I mean all of our peers are working on wearables — because I do think people want to be part of the world. They actually don't want to be holding boxes walking around. They actually really want to be able to talk to their family, take a picture, take a video, listen to music, and it be hands-free. We have Oakleys that are really really cool for extreme sports. So the use cases are just everyday life.

And I think you're going to show a video. The thing that surprised us was one use case that we hadn't anticipated — blind veterans. Somebody was joking with me, they said, "How are you getting blind people to wear glasses? That doesn't make sense to me." But can we show this video?

十五、盲人退伍军人视频

"It is such an honor to be here. We're in Austin, Texas at a VFW hall where Metamates are sitting down with amazing men and women who've served our country and who lost their eyesight. They have just been telling us they feel like they're getting their independence back, and we're so proud to be giving them Meta glasses.

I took them to church. They have the scriptures on the screen in front. I've never been able to read that, but I asked Meta and it read it word for word for me.

Seeing these extraordinary servicemen and women — all we've been saying is thank you. Thank you. We don't have America without all of them. And as a big surprise, we are about to introduce them to Chris Stapleton.

Just want to come by and say thank you for all your service. We're so grateful for you."

十六、"独立生活"的时刻

Dina: Chris Stapleton's the best. He came and joined us. It was actually on 9/11, just a couple days ago. And what we learned is that a group of blind veterans from the organization that supports them came and actually worked with the Meta engineers and designed specific features. And it just turns out obviously the glasses can see for you and read to you.

One of the gentlemen I was sitting next to put the glasses on and he said, "Hey Meta, call John." And I was sitting there — I couldn't hear obviously what he was hearing — and he just started sobbing. And I said, "Is everything okay, sir?" He said, "That's the first time I've ever called my son on my own independently."

Host: Wow.

Dina: So we're seeing these kinds of use cases, of course, that we're incredibly proud of.

Host: I guess AI creates the unlock for the glass form factor. That makes a lot of sense. Is that the form factor that you think kind of gets AI in a prevalent way for most people in the world — the glasses form factor — or is there something else you think?

Dina: I'm sure there will be many products. I think what I have learned from our team is that glasses are a thing — people wear glasses, and it's something that many people — they're affordable. And people — obviously we really worked hard. Mark was very focused not just on the design but the weight of it. So takes a lot to put the technology in here and to still keep it stylish.

Host: I think you're a minority owner of Ray-Ban. No? Or of — looks like the broad partner.

Dina: Yeah. We have an exclusive with —

Host: I think that's why people should reconsider these as a product category, 'cause I've had them since Google Glass. And the battery never worked. They were too bulky. You look like a dork in them. And now the battery works, and because you can control them — you know, not with Siri, which is still kind of broken — but this actually works. And when you're with your kids and you want to take videos when you're skiing or you want to take pictures, it actually — putting a phone between you is much more intrusive. So I think this actually brings you into the real world. And the translation feature is also very slick. So when you go to Japan or you go somewhere and they're talking to you in another language, it can actually translate. Or if you see a sign, boom, just instant translation without taking your phone out. It's time for people to reconsider these specifically for those reasons.

Dina: Yeah. You've used them a long time though, so you really know.

Host: Yeah. The battery problem, the fidelity — they didn't work, and now it does. Yeah.

十七、Dario 的呼吁与 Zuckerberg 的信念

Host: Dina, just talking about Dario's essay this weekend — there was a report, but it was unverified, that Zach said something to the effect of "we need to go as fast as we can." I don't know if that was kind of misinformation.

Host: No, no, it was like a report that just hit Twitter at the same time that Dario's [essay dropped] — but just taking a step back broadly, how did you process that essay and the call for regulation, or how are you guys thinking about this?

Dina: Sure. Well, first, I really agree with a lot of what Satya said. I mean, the premise, the starting point, is that safety is paramount, and that is something that Mark talks about all the time. I watch daily how he and Alexandr Wang and Nat Friedman, who run our lab, think about it. And a whole team of people exist to think about the safety of the models. And I think that there are very legitimate questions around that.

I think the difference is that Mark just has a very different view. And I think that view is based on 20 years of a business model of empowering and connecting people, and that 3.6 billion people are on our platform every single day. 200 million small business owners operate their business every single day.

And so his belief is that the more you distribute this technology, the more people that have superintelligence and are able to reach their potential, are able to have access to education and health care that they could have never imagined before, learning that they could have never achieved before — is not only better for each of those individuals, but it's better for society as a whole. So he fundamentally just believes — when he wrote in his piece, "the future is for everyone" — that the democratization of artificial intelligence will actually lead to a more stable society. That is just a fundamental belief that he has.

And I think that the thing that he thinks about is: so then what is his role? What is our role? And I think we were extremely proud to have the very first American open-source model just a few weeks ago.

十八、收尾

Host: Well, Dina, you've got a lot on your plate. We really appreciate you taking the time to come and join us today. We covered a lot. It was awesome. Thank you for being here.

Dina: Thank you guys so much. Thank you so much.

Host: Thank you. You're welcome. That was great.

item.description:
## 洞察一：这不是数据中心故事，而是"财政管道倒挂"的故事
多数人以为 Meta 在路易斯安那 Richland Parish 的故事是"科技巨头带来就业"。真正的机制远比这更精妙——**数据中心的经济价值并不是通过工资渗入社区，而是通过销售税一夜之间从"基础设施建设"直接跳进"教师工资单"**。
请注意超级学监描述的曲线：销售税征收从常态的 5–10% 增长，飙升到 260%。而路易斯安那有一条罕见的法律——**征收盈余强制流向教师**。这意味着：Meta 建一栋楼，Richland 教区的老师就从年终 4,000 美元奖金跳到 50,000 美元。这不是"涓滴经济学"，这是**税制的意外套利**——一个 20 世纪的地方财政公式，被 21 世纪的资本密度激活了。
跨领域连接：这与 19 世纪美国铁路小镇的"土地授予"模式惊人相似。当年铁路公司获得沿线土地，用土地增值反哺基础设施建设；今天则是数据中心用**销售税盈余反哺人力资本**。区别在于：铁路制造了地理网络，数据中心制造了智力网络——而 Richland 教区正在无意中把两者合并成同一个财政循环。
## 洞察二：反数据

item.title: [YC Root Access] Building the Safety Layer for AI Agents
item.dc:creator: YC Root Access
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、能力越强 → 安全需求越大：一个反直觉的"容量悖论"

大多数人本能地相信：模型越聪明，护栏产业就越萎缩，就像发动机越可靠，修车厂就越少。但 Raindrop 揭示了一个反向增长的市场结构——他们的收入曲线不是随着模型缺陷放大，而是随着模型能力放大。

为什么？因为 Opus 4.5 让开发者敢做以前不敢做的事：--dangerously-skip-permissions 成了默认动作，agent 被接入生产日志、退款系统、处方系统。能力的上升不是消灭风险，而是把风险面从"用户皱眉"迁移到"公司破产"。

这里有个跨领域的镜像：民航业越安全，飞行模拟器和黑匣子分析公司越值钱；核电站越可靠，安全冗余供应商越赚钱。成熟基础设施背后的"影子产业"，往往在主产业不出事时才真正做大。Raindrop 押的正是这条曲线：它不靠 AI 失败盈利，它靠 AI 被信任到可以承担昂贵失败时盈利。

二、"二元分类"是 AI 时代最被低估的哲学问题

访谈中最锋利的一句话，被创始人几乎一带而过：

"hallucination is a binary classification problem... but binary classification is extremely hard. Like every choice in your life you could say is either you should do it or you should not do it."

这句话把一个工程问题瞬间拽进了决策论和伦理学的深水区。OpenAI 那篇"幻觉本质是二元分类"的论文被围观群众欢呼，但创始人指出的其实是：二元本身不难，难的是那条决策边界由谁来画、在哪里画、为谁而画。

这和法律哲学中的一个古老难题同构——H.L.A. Hart 说法律的核心问题不是"是否违法"，而是"谁定义违法"。Raindrop 把自己定位成"alignment company"其实是在悄悄接管这条边界的定义权：在企业内部，让人类的意图与 agent 的行为之间达成宪法级契约。这是一个比"监控 agent 是否犯错"深得多的定位——他们卖的不是检测器，是组织内部的价值观翻译层。

三、意想不到的观察：观察层比被观察对象更值钱，这是数字世界的"元规律"

最容易被忽略的一点是 Raindrop 的起源故事本身：他们本来在做一个"终端里的 coding agent"，然后发现自己造的工具坏掉时，比工具本身更需要一个东西——看清楚工具怎么坏的仪器。于是那个内部小工具变成了公司，客户是 Vercell、Clay、Framer 这些做 agent 的公司。

这不是一次"转型"，这是数字生态中反复出现的一种权力转移： - 采金热中最赚钱的不是矿工，是卖铲子和牛仔裤的 Levi's - 广告业繁荣时最赚钱的不是广告公司，是 Nielsen 这样的收视测量者 - Web 2.0 应用潮里，Datadog、Sentry、Segment 的市值追平甚至超越了他们所观测的应用 - 当代金融里，Bloomberg 比大多数它服务的对冲基金都值钱

规律是：当一个层级出现爆炸性扩张，为这一层提供"可见性"的元层级，会以更陡的斜率崛起。 因为爆炸性扩张必然伴随可见性缺失，而缺失产生的焦虑值高于扩张本身产生的兴奋值。

更微妙的一点——他们即将发布的 Raindrop Simulations 又把这个模式再叠了一层："在 CI 阶段模拟 agent 未来会如何失败"。这不是监控，是给未来的错误建模。这和金融业的压力测试、气候科学的耦合模型、甚至历史学家 Jared Diamond 研究"文明为何崩溃"是同一种认知动作——用当下的信号推演还没发生的坍塌。当创始人说他们能"detect the rise and fall of ancient civilizations"，这不只是玩梗，这是在暗示：agent 群落本身就是一种新兴文明形态，而 Raindrop 正在成为它的考古学家兼预言家。

真正令人震撼的推论是：如果 agent 真的开始"运行大部分经济"，那么 Raindrop 这类公司在结构上等价于新经济的央行——不是发行货币，而是发行"信任"。信任才是 agent 经济的底层流动性。

📝 转录文本

开场：Raindrop 完成 A 轮融资

[music]

Host: I'm excited today to welcome the founders of Raindrop on closing a big Series A led by CRV, bringing your total funding to $50 million, where Lightspeed did your seed round. So this was just two years after the batch. It's pretty cool.

Tell us — what do you guys do?

Founder: Yeah, really simply, we detect issues with agents in production, and now prevent those issues from getting into production in the first place.

客户与真实场景

Host: So who are some of your big customers right now?

Founder: So we have a number of really amazing AI agents that we work with — companies like Vercel, Clay, Framer, Speak, etc. And then also Fortune 500s of multiple industries.

Host: Do you have concrete examples of how these customers use you?

Founder: Yeah, there's all sorts. So one common one with customer support agents is basically a tool-call / agent-response mismatch. So let's look at something really specific: a customer support agent is trying to issue a refund, but the tool call to issue the refund fails — and the agent says, "Issued your refund." So that's a problem.

Founder: That's definitely one — right around like an agent saying it took an action and it didn't. There's, you know, capability gaps like the user asking for something the agent can't do; task failure, like the agent isn't able to complete something for some reason. And we really just have hundreds of these sort of metrics.

And what we see is that companies — the entire company — use these metrics to determine how good or bad their agent is.

反直觉：模型越强，问题越多

Host: So you guys basically are watching whenever agents go rogue — whenever you have problems like hallucination, errors with tool calls, broken loops, or any of these kinds of issues.

What is very interesting to me and counterintuitive is that as model capabilities increase, it seems like the big labs should solve this. But it's the opposite problem. You guys are seeing more demand than ever with the newest models. Why is that?

Founder: Yeah. So you can see with Hugging Face, for example, right — that as agents get better, they're calling hundreds of tools. They're reading and writing from critical data sources. They're being deployed in healthcare, the military, and finance.

And so as capabilities go up, complexity goes up, and the cost of issues goes up dramatically — and you have all these failure modes that you never anticipated.

为什么 LLM-as-a-Judge 不够用

Host: And a regular LLM-as-a-judge doesn't cut it. Why is that?

Founder: I think there's really two reasons.

The first is easy — it's cost. I think that if you were going to have an LLM look at every single trace, it would double your costs at least.

I think the second is actually a lot trickier, and something I think our company sort of exists to solve — which is that binary classification is very, very hard. And so, we were talking earlier, there's this paper from OpenAI, uh, maybe two years ago or something now, where they said, you know, hallucination is a binary classification problem — like something is either true or it's not true. And there were all these people on Twitter that were kind of like, "Wow, OpenAI solved hallucination because it's just binary." And it's like, no, actually, binary classification is extremely hard. Like every choice in your life, you could say, is either you should do it or you should not do it.

And I think that similarly, something in your agent — some behavior it's doing — is either wrong or it's right. And it's really up to the company to define what's wrong or what's right. And so we sort of think of ourselves as an alignment company: aligning humans inside of the company with their agents' behavior.

主动式问题发现，而不只是抽样

Host: So I think the cool thing that you do then is that you enable your customers to basically watch the full traces of all of their agents, rather than just doing sampling and then getting a judge to run, which is how people do it today — but it doesn't catch all the errors. And you guys basically catch all of them.

Founder: Yeah. And I think it's more than just catching errors. It's proactive issue detection.

So [clears throat] when you have LLMs as a judge, again, you can only run it on 1% of data, 10%. But also, you can only look for problems you know about ahead of time. You tell your LLM, "Look at this, you know, rate the answer on like XYZ parameter I care about."

But what Raindrop does is proactively find issues you didn't know about. Right? So if you take the OpenAI / Hugging Face problem — these agents are talking, they have all these like tons and tons of logs, and it's going unnoticed for weeks because you didn't know to look for it.

And Raindrop, by having powerful signals but also having proactive issue detection — you're finding, and our customers are finding, issues that are creating risk, creating liability, and also creating excess token costs, like across things they didn't know about.

创业转型：从 Coding Agent 到 Agent 观测

Host: What's interesting — this journey sounds pretty straightforward, but the reality is when you guys went through the batch about two years ago, you were a very different company. When I interviewed you guys, you were building basically a coding agent for the terminal — before agents were even a thing. That was not even in the spoken world in terms of how people thought about agents, but you were basically building a coding agent on the terminal.

Founder: Yeah.

Host: So tell us what happened.

Founder: Totally. Yeah, we — I mean, we've all been best friends for many years, and we were all just hacking on things that we wanted for ourselves. And very early, we found ourselves wanting what are now called coding agents — or, like, basically at the time we'd say chatbots that can do things. And this was like the earliest way we thought about agents.

And as we were building those coding agents, we ran into this issue ourselves where we had no idea why these issues were popping up or what was going wrong. And so what's now Raindrop started as an internal tool that we used for our own coding agents.

Claude Opus 4.5 与拐点

Host: Agents really had a very slow trickling since 2024 — it was not even a thing until probably 2025.

Founder: And it really started to work around Claude Code, Opus 4.5, with agentic coding starting to work.

Host: Yeah. And that's when things took off for you guys. Basically your revenue went like this.

Founder: Yeah.

Host: So tell us what happened. Is like, more coding agents created more issues for people to follow up?

Founder: It's exactly what Zan was saying before — is that the more capabilities, the more complexity, and the more ways that they go wrong.

I think what you also saw with Opus 4.5 is that the guardrails start coming off, right? The permissions start coming off. Like everyone's like, you know, "dangerously skip all permissions." Everyone's like, "Oh, maybe we should hook it up into production. Maybe it should have access to production logs."

And so it's exactly the second part of what was saying — is that the stakes get higher.

为何坚持：朋友、信念与长期视角

Host: What was actually really cool about all of you is that, as you mentioned, you are very close friends. And this was basically your second company. Your previous one was a crypto company that you sold through Coinbase. And you basically had this company kind of not making a lot of progress for a bit, until things took off last year.

What made you keep going?

Founder: Well, I think one of the biggest things is like — getting to work with each other. Honestly, like when your life is: you wake up in the morning and you walk to an office and work on the most interesting problems in the world with your best friends — you're like, life is pretty good.

Uh [clears throat] like, you're learning a lot, you're creating things that you genuinely want to use.

And I think we just had this also conviction in the future — where like, these AIs are going to do things, and eventually, you know, people are going to hook them up to production databases. Eventually, they're going to be issuing prescriptions. Like, I think it was obvious to us very early that these agents would basically run a lot of the economy. And now that they are, people are realizing that it's kind of a hair-on-fire problem.

Founder: Yes. I think that we definitely frame things a lot as just like fundamental truths. Like, our fundamental beliefs — and everything else around your fundamental beliefs as a company — can change. Like, the way, I mean, in a year our product will look entirely different. I have no idea.

But the things we know as a company are that: (1) agents will get more capable, and (2) the cost of their mistakes will increase. And so if both of those things happen, then people will pay us money to make sure those things don't happen.

新发布：Raindrop Simulations

Host: So, you guys have a pretty cool announcement — that you're solving a very hard problem that was described by Dwarkesh's post on "the rise and fall of agent civilizations," that basically describes how Hugging Face was pwned by the OpenAI agents. And you guys have this new solution that's going to solve this.

Tell us more about that.

Founder: We're going to be launching Raindrop Simulations.

So what this does is: every single change you make, any PR you make, we show you how it might go wrong before it ever hits production. So we take all the issue detection we do in production and bring that to CI.

We try to find cases where things might go wrong that you haven't even imagined. And so this is a very, very different strategy than evals, which mostly are testing things you already know about.

And this, really, today — OpenAI and Anthropic are the only ones that have access to this sort of technology. And we're bringing that to every company in the world.

Host: Pretty cool. So you guys can detect the rise and fall of ancient civilizations.

Founder: Yes.

Host: Quite literally.

Founder: I think that that is an extremely good example of something where — sure, now that you know about it, you could add an eval, right? But the reality — and this is true for most companies, if it's true for OpenAI — is that that sat in logs for weeks before anyone found it. It took, you know, crashing their internal package manager before it was detected.

招聘方向

Host: So tell us about the roles that you're hiring for.

Founder: Yeah, hiring across the board, right? This is such an important problem. Hiring across engineering — I think these are some of the most interesting engineering problems, period. Right? As Ben said earlier, we're taking some of the tools that only OpenAI and Anthropic have in-house, and just making them available to the entire world as agents proliferate.

And also — when we think about agents proliferating and getting these tools to everyone in the world, every developer in the world — that requires a huge distribution in sort of like GTM. And so we're hiring a lot for everything from marketing, sales, DevRel, etc., etc.

Host: Yeah. All right, guys. Congratulations.

Founder: Thank you.

[music]

观看原视频 →
item.description:
## 一、能力越强 → 安全需求越大：一个反直觉的"容量悖论"
大多数人本能地相信：模型越聪明，护栏产业就越萎缩，就像发动机越可靠，修车厂就越少。但 Raindrop 揭示了一个**反向增长的市场结构**——他们的收入曲线不是随着模型缺陷放大，而是随着模型能力放大。
为什么？因为 Opus 4.5 让开发者敢做以前不敢做的事：`--dangerously-skip-permissions` 成了默认动作，agent 被接入生产日志、退款系统、处方系统。**能力的上升不是消灭风险，而是把风险面从"用户皱眉"迁移到"公司破产"**。
这里有个跨领域的镜像：民航业越安全，飞行模拟器和黑匣子分析公司越值钱；核电站越可靠，安全冗余供应商越赚钱。**成熟基础设施背后的"影子产业"，往往在主产业不出事时才真正做大**。Raindrop 押的正是这条曲线：它不靠 AI 失败盈利，它靠 AI 被信任到可以承担昂贵失败时盈利。

item.title: [Lex Clips] One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest - psychiatrist analysis | Andrew Scull and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被一部电影"杀死"的疗法：叙事对经验的碾压

1975年的一部电影，让一种在1980年后被反复证明能救治重度抑郁症的治疗方式，在公众心智中沉睡了整整半个世纪。Scull几乎是无奈地承认："即便到现在，它仍然让人们对这种治疗心存犹豫。" 这里发生的不是医学争议，而是一种文化性的神经损伤——Nurse Ratched按下开关的那个镜头，不只击碎了McMurphy，也切断了后世无数抑郁症患者与一种有效疗法之间的神经通路。Lex的朋友"试遍所有办法二十年"才敢碰ECT，这不是个人的犹豫，是Louise Fletcher的表演在他大脑里投下的阴影。

而最讽刺、访谈里被一带而过的细节是：片中的精神科主任，由俄勒冈州立精神病院的真实院长本人扮演。这个机构亲手参演了对自己的控诉——历史上极其罕见的、体制自愿走上被告席、并在自己的判决书上签名的时刻。

二、跨领域连接：为什么我们吃降压药，却怕电击？

Scull说了一句非常关键、但没有充分展开的话："我们完全不知道ECT为什么起作用。它是一种纯粹经验性的治疗。" 但他自己每天吃降压药——降压药在深层也是经验性的（我们并不真正掌握每一种降压机制的完整因果链），只是"降低压力"这个词组恰好匹配了我们对身体的朴素力学直觉。而"用电流引发癫痫发作从而治愈抑郁"违反了每一个日常隐喻。

这里藏着一条可以推广到AI、疫苗、核能、加密货币的通用规律：人类接受哪些经验主义技术，不取决于它是否有效，而取决于它是否能被现有隐喻消化。ECT的失败不是医学失败，而是隐喻工程的失败——若它一开始被命名为"神经系统重启"而非"电击疗法"，历史轨迹会完全不同。这条规律对任何系统性工作者都成立：一个方案能否推行，往往不取决于它对不对，而取决于它押不押韵。

三、诊断作为一台隐形的社会分类装置

这是整段访谈里最容易被略过、却最具冲击力的模式：Henry Cotton的患者70%是女性；脑叶白质切除术60–70%是女性；ECT压倒性地施加于女性。而男性获得的是"人格障碍"、"ADHD"这类性格标签。

同样是心理痛苦，社会分给女性的是身体侵入（切、电、胰岛素休克），分给男性的是人格描述。这不是精神病学的孤立现象，而是整个西方医学的深层结构：女性的痛苦被身体化，男性的痛苦被性格化。类比一下：经前综合症 vs 中年危机、纤维肌痛 vs 职业倦怠、慢性疲劳综合征 vs 男子气概衰退——你会发现同一场深层痛苦，一旦落在不同性别身上，就会被送进完全不同的诊断—治疗流水线。

四、意外的时间尺度：40 年酝酿一本书

Scull在1981年就想写《Desperate Remedies》，2022年才出版。他不经意地透露了一种反生产力主义的创作方法论——永远同时进行至少两个项目，让概念在潜意识里长期发酵。这不是拖延，是一种智力上的湿润气候。一本关于精神病学的书需要40年，是因为它必须活过80年代的DSM革命、90年代的Prozac神话、2000年代的神经影像热潮，才能看清整个山脉的地貌。这一点对任何在做长线知识管道、笔记系统、慢速研究的人都是一个提醒：真正深刻的洞察不是被"生产"出来的，而是被"允许"发生的。

五、一条几乎没人指出的因果链

Kesey笔下的精神病院系统，其实是二战亲手创造的。Scull提到，二战美军精神伤员是一战的2–3倍——这一事实催生了VA大规模培训精神科医生。也就是说：为了照顾从战场归来的男人而建立的系统，最终变成了压迫女性、少数族裔与异见者的机器。这与社交媒体、推荐算法、公共卫生监控走过的路径是同一种剧本——"善意基础设施最终异化为控制装置"几乎是现代性的默认结局。One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest 之所以持久震撼，是因为它无意中拍下了这个剧本的第一次上演。

📝 转录文本

关于《飞越疯人院》与 ECT 的缘起

Lex: It's just to talk a little bit more about ECT and One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest. So, what can we say about that? That little cultural moment, one of the most famous moments about psychiatry. First of all, Ken Kesey wrote this book about his own experience in a mental institution.

Scull: Park, yes.

Lex: How representative is it of the system at the time?

精神病院的历史脉络：一战、二战与 VA 系统

Scull: Mental hospitals have had a very patchy and complicated history. He was working actually in a hospital for veterans. Those were largely created after the Second World War when there were very many more psychiatric casualties among the American troops than even the First World War.

You know, the interesting thing is we all by osmosis know that in the First World War there was something called shell shock that afflicted the troops and that the military initially resisted recognizing and ultimately were forced to grasp. But in World War II, American psychiatric casualties among the troops were two to three times as high as in World War I. And that's an important part of the history of psychiatry.

But the upshot of that was that post-war the VA was heavily involved in first of all paying to train psychiatrists and even psychologists. And then had in its mental hospital system a considerable involvement with psychiatric disorders.

小说与电影的差异

Kesey, well, the book is different than the film. That's the first thing to say. Obviously, the film is heavily indebted to the book, but it changes various things.

Lex: Uh if I may, just going to perplexity — the book and the 1975 film tell the same basic story of McMurphy challenging an oppressive psychiatric ward, but they differ sharply in point of view, tone, and what the story is about. The novel is weirder, more political, and more about Chief Bromden's inner world and the Combine, while the film is more naturalistic, character-driven, and turns McMurphy into the central hero.

Scull: Yes, I think that's right.

Lex: Murphy is the person that received ECT, played by Jack Nicholson.

Scull: Yes. And you have a nurse figure in Nurse Ratched — Louise Fletcher, I think, is an equally powerful performance.

Lex: It's just one of the greatest films of all time. Who happens to be — which is unfortunate for, you know, maybe some of the —

Scull: psychiatry, yes.

"Madness in the Movies" 与最伟大的疯狂电影

It's very interesting. I used to teach a class called Madness in the Movies. And I didn't just use — in fact, I used relatively few contemporary films. And among all the films from back then, the one almost everybody in the class had seen was One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest. So, 19- and 20-year-olds in 2015, if I showed them Alfred Hitchcock's Spellbound, no chance, they'd never seen that — maybe one, cuz they were a class of people interested in film, but everybody'd seen One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest.

Lex: On that tangent, really quick, what is the greatest film on madness in your view?

Scull: Oh, well.

Lex: Would it be One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest?

Scull: One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest, I think. Uh, oddly, a very different film that appeared at about the same time was I Never Promised You a Rose Garden, which is a much more sympathetic portrait of a different kind of psychiatry — a very Freudian psychiatry. Really about Frieda Fromm-Reichmann who worked at Chestnut Lodge in Maryland and treated schizophrenia with psychotherapy rather than with drugs or other forms of physical intervention. And that was a best-selling novel by a young girl who had been her patient, with some fairly serious delusions and a very complicated family background. And again, the film changed a lot of things in the novel. That's what films do.

缺失的"第三幕"：Madhouse 与好莱坞的困境

My book Madhouse at one point interested Hollywood, and one of the two principals said to me, "I really like this story. It's got a great first act and a great second act, but where's the third act?" — meaning, "Where's the happy ending?" And I had to say there wasn't any happy ending to that story. It was just rather grim.

Lex: Madhouse: A Tragic Tale of Megalomania and Modern Medicine is the book you're referring to. And that reminds me of Flowers for Algernon. That doesn't have a happy ending, and that's not about mental health necessarily, but it's about the journey of the institution in relation to the health of a patient.

Scull: Yes. Pat Barker's trilogy of novels about World War I was turned into a film — I think it was called Regeneration. And that was quite powerful. It was about World War I and the treatment of shell shock. And I thought was quite well done.

And my friend Patrick McGrath, who's a novelist, wrote a book called Asylum. Patrick grew up in the grounds of Broadmoor. Broadmoor is England's premier hospital for the criminally insane. And he was baby-sat by some of the patients. And when you read his novels, you can see how that upbringing affected his rather macabre imagination. But anyway.

电影对精神病院环境的还原

So, One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest — the poverty of the environment, the room that the patients were in, I think fairly successfully recreates that. The way in which staff very often put patients down, didn't listen to them, or poked fun at them, or even were physically abusive — although you don't see that — those were all features of mental hospitals. The general boredom of life is sort of there, but yeah, it's hard to — putting boredom on the screen will turn an audience off rather fast, so.

Lex: What about nurse and this kind of abusive element, you know?

Scull: Yeah, I think that there was an abusive element in a lot of mental hospitals, and it was almost inevitable. If you look at who had the most contact with the patients, it was the lowest-paid, least-respected ward attendants — very few even RNs — and, you know, the ratio of doctor to patient in the large state mental hospitals meant that patients hardly ever saw a physician.

一个惊人的细节：真实的院长出演电影

What's remarkable about the film — there are many remarkable things about the film, as well as its polemical edge — I think is that the chief psychiatrist that you see in the film is the real head of Oregon State Mental Hospital. He really was. That was his introduction to acting, and I thought he was pretty remarkable, actually. But obviously there's a lot of exaggeration there.

ECT 作为纪律工具，以及性别不对称

But ECT was used in the '50s and '60s as a tool of discipline in the hospitals. It was also used therapeutically, but overwhelmingly, it was used as a tool of discipline and control. And that's true to life.

Lobotomy — one of the interesting things we haven't talked about with all these treatments we've been discussing is that, almost invariably, except for the case of the syphilitic patients (for obvious reasons, men were more troubled by that condition than women), it was women that got the brunt of these experiments. So, Henry Cotton — about 70% of his patients who were treated were female. Lobotomy patients — it's hard to get overall numbers, but those of us who've looked at the records of a number of different hospitals, again and again, discover 60% or 70% of the patients are female.

ECT tends to be heavily female. That's complicated by the fact that it's used primarily, as we were discussing, in serious cases of depression and so-called treatment-resistant depression. And depression is a diagnosis that is more to be found among women than men. Not that there aren't very many men with depression, but again, the ratio is such. Men tend to get different diagnoses — personality disorders, for example, are very very common and a more male diagnosis. ADHD is more male than female, and so on. So, it's good to point that out.

电影带来的长久后果

It helped end interest in ECT except for a small handful of enthusiasts for decades — that film. And probably even now it creates hesitation in people about the treatment. So it's one that has had a very powerful and long-lasting effect, I think.

ECT 的真实临床价值

Lex: I think one of the surprising things that I recently learned is a friend of mine tried everything about 20 years ago — tried everything to — with depression, and the ECT is the last thing he tried, and it changed his life.

Scull: Yeah.

Lex: For the better.

Scull: That's not an uncommon story. Yeah.

Lex: And then I looked online and there's a lot of stories like this. And before learning of that, my — I'm embarrassed to say — knowledge of ECT was just One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest.

Scull: You know, it has a terrible history in the '40s, '50s, and '60s. The CIA funded Ewen Cameron up in Canada, and he was giving multiple ECTs a day and reducing people to — well, they couldn't walk, they couldn't talk, they couldn't feed themselves, they were incontinent — and then he built them back up, or so he claimed. Pretty many cases they were left permanently damaged. So I could recite lots of real horror stories about ECT.

But it's also — if you're honest about the thing — what you just described, that is, patients who were on the brink of suicide, who had long-running depressions, some of them had ECT and they describe it as life-saving. And as I say, when more controlled trials have been done recently, there's enough evidence now that it's hard to say this never works — this is just one of these desperate remedies we should consign to the dark ages.

我们不知道它为什么起作用

The complicating thing is: we have no clue why it works. It's a purely empirical treatment. And that itself, I think, tends to put people off.

If you have a curable form of cancer and the surgeon says, "Well, I'm going to remove it," and she does — that's that. Because we understand even a little bit — even if our knowledge of human biology is pretty primitive — we do understand a little bit that cancer is cells dividing uncontrollably and taking over and doing damage to the body and eventually killing you. And the fact that we can surgically remove it is a big deal.

There are lots of disorders. I have high blood pressure. If untreated, my blood pressure is — like a 20-year-old's, thanks to treatment. It's an ongoing thing. I take the damn pill every day and it has a few minor side effects, but for me very minor ones. And it turns what could have killed me — either a stroke or a heart attack — into a condition that's very well controlled.

So, all of these things — they're complicated. It's easy with some of these things — with lobotomy, with insulin comas, deep sleep treatments, Henry Cotton's endeavors — those you can just say, "Well, we'll throw them away." And for a long time, I think ECT would have formed part of that cast of characters.

Desperate Remedies：一本酝酿了 40 年的书

So, when I first conceived the idea of writing Desperate Remedies, the book — it was back in 1981, and I was in London on a Guggenheim fellowship at the Wellcome Institute. And I hadn't done research in detail, but I was aware there were all these things — looking about, that had happened in the 1920s and 30s — and I thought that would be a very interesting thing to study.

And luckily, I didn't do it right away, or I did it piecemeal over the years. And I ended up writing a much more comprehensive look at psychiatry — really from its origins to now. And I couldn't have written that book back then. I would have missed all the developments from 1980 onwards, which are very, very important to the overall picture.

Lex: So 40 years later, 2022.

Scull: Yes. [laughter] Yes, exactly.

Lex: Remedies: Psychiatrists' Turbulent Quest to Cure Mental Illness.

双线并进的写作方法论

Scull: I've written a lot of books, and along the way, part of the way I think I've been productive and kept interested — I always had at least two projects on the go at once. You can't simultaneously write two things, but I'd have one and I'd work on it, and if I got tired of it, I'd pick up the other one for a bit and then go back. And it also meant when I was working on one main project, I had other things percolating in my head. And I would come across things that were relevant to them and I'd make a note, and then I'd go back.

So when I finally did Desperate Remedies, I'd been thinking about those issues for 40 years. And that made a big difference, I think, to the way I approached things and to what I thought. Because — like Thomas says — you either say the same thing over and over and over again for 40 years, or you learn new things and you broaden what you know, and you think about things in a different way because you realize you haven't grasped the full complexity of what you're looking at.

为什么精神病学始终值得研究

And so — look, what I found with psychiatry is there are really a couple of fundamental things that have kept me engaged with the field.

One, it's an arena where there's tremendous human suffering, and it spreads out. And, as far as I know — and I wrote a big book called Madness and Civilization about, from the ancient Greeks and ancient China to now — in every society I've studied, they have to cope with this. It takes different forms, it's regarded in different ways, it's treated differently, but people that deviate so far from the norm of what we regard as culturally appropriate — they exist everywhere.

So, the suffering, the difficulty of studying it, and then the fact that it is such a complex and difficult subject to understand — the very fact that we have such limits to our knowledge means there's space there to examine things in a very complicated way. And so it's an intellectual puzzle that's attracted some very, very smart people — but there's a long way to go.

Lex: Yeah, we have glimpses of insights about how the mind works, but if you look at the span of human history, we're probably in the very early days of understanding this particular one.

Scull: Mhm.
