item.description:
## 一个反直觉的观察：AI 采用的瓶颈不是"能力"，而是"承诺"
大多数人以为 AGI 时代的关键是模型能力，Rune 却指出：**Waymo 早在 2022 年就已经是"汽车界的 AGI"——超越人类司机——但你今天仍然打不到一辆 Waymo 去机场**。四年过去了，制约它的从来不是技术，而是"责任无法被承诺"。
这里藏着一个更深的隐喻：**AI 行业正在遭遇"承诺赤字"（Promise Deficit）**。模型能力是指数增长的，但"可承诺性"却是线性甚至更慢地爬升。这两条曲线之间的裂缝，就是 AI Underwriting Company 的全部商业空间——也是理解为什么 Anthropic 会把 Fable 锁起来、为什么 GPT-5 会被政府盯上的根本原因。**能力越强，越无法承诺；越无法承诺，越无法部署。** 这是一个非常反直觉的悖论：AI 越接近 AGI，"落地"反而越难，而不是越容易。
## 跨领域连接：AI 保险与 1900 年的电灯泡
Rune 提到 Underwriter Laboratory（UL）——就是你家里所有电器背后那个不起眼的圆形标志。它诞生

item.title: [a16z] Why the Next Generation of Enterprise Software Looks Nothing Like Salesforce
item.dc:creator: a16z
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最出人意料的观察：Lightfield 的组织结构是其产品哲学的分形（Fractal）

Keith 反复强调的产品核心原则是「Intelligence > Schema」——不预定义数据结构，而是让智能在流动的活动日志中自己组织意义。真正惊人的是：这家公司的内部结构是同一条哲学的镜像投射。

  • 数据层拒绝固定 schema → 组织层拒绝固定 swim lane（"everyone owns product and everyone owns customer success"）
  • 数据是流动的 activity log → 团队每天 standup 时重新 stack rank 优先级，"whoever's free just takes them"
  • 数据可以事后被 traverse 重新填充字段 → 项目可以被任何职能的人接手推进

这几乎是 Conway 定律的反向版本：通常是「组织结构决定产品架构」，Lightfield 的案例里，产品的世界观反过来重塑了组织形态。这也解释了为什么大多数试图模仿它的公司会失败——他们只抄了 schemaless 的数据模型，却保留了 schema 化的组织。

二、跨领域连接：Facebook Timeline 是最伟大的 B2B 洞察，只是没人意识到

Keith 一笔带过的一句话是全场最深的：五位创始人中三位来自 Facebook 数据团队，他们把 News Feed / Timeline 的时间轴原语 直接搬来做 CRM 的核心表征。

这看起来只是工程借用，实则触到了三个跨领域的深层同构：

  1. 神经科学：人类的 episodic memory（情景记忆）本质上就是时间序列锚定的——我们不记「客户是谁」，我们记「上次见面时他说了什么」。传统 CRM 用 field/stage 建模关系，就像让大脑用 Excel 表格记朋友。
  2. 人类学：亲密关系的本体论从来不是属性集合（身高、职业、偏好），而是共享的历史序列。activity log 才是关系的第一性表征。
  3. 消费社交 → 企业软件的降维：Instagram/Messenger 已经在消费端验证过「时间轴 + 语义推断」这一组合的可扩展性。Lightfield 在 B2B 复用它，本质是把十亿人级别打磨过的心智模型迁移到销售场景。

Salesforce 之所以是 CRM，是因为它在「关系是一堆字段」的假设上做到了极致。Lightfield 之所以可能是下一代，是因为它把关系还原成了它本来的样子：一条被两个实体共同书写的时间线。

三、更深的隐藏真相：这家公司卖的其实不是 CRM，是「企业的场景规划权」

表面上 Lightfield 是新一代 CRM。但你把 Keith 全程最兴奋的部分挑出来看——那位 enterprise 客户通过 Lightfield 发现自己该做 mid-market 产品线；那位 sales manager 让 GPT-6 在 Lightfield 上跑一个周末后改了整个销售流程——真正在被出售的产品，是「用 frontier intelligence 对整个公司做反事实推演」的能力。

这颠覆了 SaaS 长期以来的一个隐含契约：过去的 system of record 是被动的记忆（你输入、它保存、偶尔生成报表）。Lightfield 想成为的是主动的镜子（"crystal ball for scenario planning"）。

这里藏着一个惊人的商业史级别的错位： - 20 年来，enterprise software 把 CEO 的战略决策看作软件之外的事——软件是执行工具。 - Lightfield 押注的下一个时代里，战略决策本身才是最贵的 workload，而 CRM 只是承载它所需要的世界模型的载体。

这也解释了为什么 Keith 不担心 SAP/Salesforce——他根本不在同一张地图上。SAP 卖的是 hostages 的锁定成本，Lightfield 想卖的是 oracles 的启示价值。前者的护城河是切换痛苦，后者的护城河是决策后悔。这是两种完全不同的商业物理学。

四、一个反直觉的定价学观察

三段定价演化（纯 seat → 纯 consumption → hybrid）里有个被访谈者一笔带过、却值得独立成篇的发现：纯 consumption 定价让"nobody touched anything"，是公司三周最惨的时刻。

这与经济学的理性人假设完全冲突——按用量付费本应是最"公平"的。但它精准命中了行为经济学里的度量焦虑（metering anxiety）：每一次点击都要计价，会激活损失厌恶回路，让用户在 UI 前僵住。这与 Netflix 打败 blockbuster、包月 SaaS 打败按分钟计费的电信业是同一个心理机制。

Lightfield 的解法——把 CRM 底盘塞进 platform fee，让 alpha（enrichment、workflow、intelligence）单独按用量付费——不是折衷，是精确的心理分层：让 "呼吸" 免费，让 "跳跃" 收费。这是可以被写进未来 AI SaaS 定价教科书的一个案例。

📝 转录文本

开场：嘉宾与主题

Joe Schmidt（主持）： Welcome back to the A16Z podcast. I'm Joe Schmidt. I'm joined by my partner, Alex Rmpelle, and Keith Paris. Keith is the CEO at Lightfield. Lightfield just raised a $47 million Series A led by us, and they're building a business world model. A business world model turns customer emails, calls, and meetings into a record that AI agents can use to get work done.

We'll explore how Keith pivoted (which is very interesting) to Lightfield, how they built the initial product, and what customers can do with it. Keith, thanks for joining us.

Keith： Excited to be here.

Tome 的爆发式增长与硬转折

Joe： Yeah, maybe we'll start just going back to the Tome journey and how you got to Lightfield — very atypical journey. You got two products now to explosive scale. Um, tell us a little bit about that experience and how you ended up at Lightfield.

Keith： We started, uh, you know, mostly because we were consumer people and we thought like LLMs were going to change the way people communicate. We were working on like selfie design, you know, at Instagram and Messenger, and we decided to go into the storytelling of ideas. We got this product out to launch around the time of GPT‑3.

Joe： And tell us a little bit about the product too.

Keith： So it was a presentation product where you could use GPT to generate presentations and generate pages and so forth. We launched it around the same time as ChatGPT and we just got explosive growth. We got, you know, 2 million users a month. People were lining up when we didn't have enough inference to support them.

Joe： Wow, oh my gosh. And so you got that to amazing scale. You then decided to stop and completely hard pivot. What was that decision like? How did you make that choice? Why?

Keith： Yeah. So I would say there are a lot of metrics behind it, but you know, deep down I think at an instinctual level — none of us liked the product. Which is kind of a funny thing to say. Like, I think at the end of the day, if you're a founder, you have to love the product that you're building and you have to be excited for your customers to use it. And we just couldn't, for the life of us, make good presentations.

Joe： Wow.

Keith： You know, we could never see the path of a high‑quality, discerning presentation maker using this tool in an indispensable way. We couldn't see people like yourselves using it for memos. We couldn't see people using it in investment banking or consulting. We just thought that the technology constrained us to being a tool for individuals and students.

为什么不等技术成熟？

Joe： So interesting. Okay, so you go from AI presentations to nothing. And so how did you make the choice of what to —

Alex： Maybe if I can rewind a little bit. I mean, sometimes you get to this point and you're like, "Oh well, if the technology kind of continues advancing then it will be good enough." But that's also a little bit of a danger — I think it's called osium, uh — but how did you decide (I mean, this was probably the question you were getting at), why not just wait it out for the technology to get better? Because I mean, the leap between GPT‑3 and GPT‑6 with Astra is extraordinary. But obviously if you're burning money, you don't have the luxury of waiting. But I guess, how did you think about the shape of the curve and why not wait out the curve?

Keith： Yeah, it's a good question. So we definitely thought about, let's shrink the team and wait it out, because we were seeing 3.5 to 4 and seeing the leaps being made. But I think the biggest issue was that the model just didn't have enough context to really understand the presenter, the audience, the relationship between the presenter and the audience — and no amount of general reasoning gets you past that.

So we were like, this is going to be, at best, a great tool for a one‑shot pie‑in‑the‑sky presentation, and we just couldn't figure out how to turn that into something that we were excited about.

决定新方向：跟着热度走

Joe： How did you think about the problems that you wanted to attack next? I think the hardest part of what you just said, and the most painful part, is "none of us liked the product." That's hard if that's your entire life. How did you decide what was the product you actually wanted to build? What was that process like?

Keith： So I think we had a lot of conversations internally about, "Wait a minute, why did we even build this company?" We built this company because we wanted to help professionals tell expert stories, hard stories. So we're like, let's see if we can find the B2B use case.

We sort of looked in our user base — we had 25 million users or something — and we found that the B2B users were sales and marketing. So we reached out to them. We went and got 12 pilots from, call it, 500,000‑person companies around here, and we're like, "Hey, we'll do this for free. We'll do great presentations for you and let's see where it goes."

So we ended up being used by a couple of sales teams. At first we came in with, "We'll make your new business decks, we'll make your proposals," and we're like, "Wait a minute — while you're here, can you do other things? Can you guys do some research? Could you help us qualify leads? Could you help us understand companies for expansion?"

At that point we were like, "Sure, you know, let's just follow the heat, see what happens." I think what makes early‑stage founders good at this is that you sort of have no priors. You're willing to ignore the thing you built. And we were like, let's just follow this trail and see where it goes.

The first thing we asked was, "Oh, just give us access to your context box" — which at the time I thought was Salesforce. So we're like, "Great, give us access to your CRM, your call recorder, your data warehouse, more, and then we'll figure out how to do this work for you."

Then we realized actually the hardest part of doing this work was making sense of all of the data across all of these disparate systems. It was incomplete, it was conflicting. The call recorder often had a different view of reality than the CRM. Actually the work required to reorganize it felt like the most important work.

We started to realize, wait a minute, maybe this is the more interesting problem to solve — which is that if you can reorganize reality for a company in a way that machines can understand, and also for humans to understand, that feels like a way more interesting and enduring company than the one we're on right now.

第一批客户：负定价与办公桌换 CRM

Joe： When did you know that you were on to something with the new product?

Keith： So there's a little bit of discontinuity. We didn't know we wanted a CRM first. First we built like a go‑to‑market assistant. We got people to like it and then we couldn't get anyone to pay for it.

That was to say that we had all of these AEs using it every day but we had no pricing power because it wasn't our data. And there were 10 other companies competing for it. So we decided to shrink the team, start from scratch, and go reimagine the CRM from first principles. We built in the dark for about four months.

And then we needed to find people to use our CRM. And it turns out no one wants to use your four‑month‑old CRM. So we sort of looked at the only asset we had left, which was this giant office space we couldn't get rid of. And we were like, "I'm going to post on X and LinkedIn — you can sit in our office space if you use our CRM."

Alex： Negative pricing.

Keith： Negative pricing, yeah, exactly. So we found 10 startups to come use the product, and for some reason they were in it every day. They were mad about everything missing, and they were mad about how slow it was, but they were in it every day and they were giving us Slack feedback about it like every two hours.

I was like, "Oh, this is so different than Tome — in the sense that we have this barely working, barely finished product that people are in all the time, where they care about it so much they're going to give us feedback about it on an hourly basis."

从第一性原理重构 CRM

Joe： When you think about CRM — did you start off saying, "You know, I view Salesforce and HubSpot and other things, and here's what I want changed"? Or how did you triangulate on the job to be done? Because on one hand, a CRM is just a repository, right? It's the repository of all customer information. But on the other hand, if you've talked to anybody who's run a sales team, one of the biggest pain points is, "My stupid salespeople don't update the CRM," and it's often a stale repository. What were the governing principles around what was broken with the world today, and what were you going to do differently?

Keith： I think one of the things that benefited us was honestly how naive we were about the space. Because if you're in a growth‑stage company, the CRM is the tool that reps use to not forget things. It's the tool that powers low‑level automation. And it's also the tool that powers forecasts.

Our naive view was actually the most important thing here is the latter. If we can help you completely model your business and your customer reality, then the rest will be easy — the rest should just be prompts and tool calls.

Because of that, a lot of the world ran towards "CRM for work." We ran towards high‑fidelity business modeling. And because of that, we were like, what gets in the way of this? It's the rep's manual entry, the API quality. We were sort of on our own island trying to world‑model instead of sending emails.

架构决策：Activity Log 作为核心原语

Joe： Can you talk a little bit about the very intentional decisions you made on the architecture — how you built the primitives that allow this to happen? It's beautiful now and the experience is incredible, but it only works because you made the right choices early on.

Keith： Yeah. So actually three out of our five founding members came from Facebook or data, and we had this very naive view that the most important thing in the CRM is modeling the relationship. So we actually looked at the Facebook timeline and we were like, we just need to model the chronological relationship between your business and this business.

So we actually built out the activity log first: when did you first reach out? What did you say to them? What did they say to you? What meetings did you have? What documents were sent back and forth? Eventually, like, what are they doing in your product? How are they paying you? And we thought working off of this activity log is sort of the right primitive.

Joe： Interesting.

Keith： So we have the system where it builds the activity log between your relationship, and then it uses that to trigger the traditional CRM updates you'd expect — updating fields, updating stages and so on. But you always have this canonical log of relationship that everything's built on top of.

半结构化：Schemaless 的设计权衡

Joe： And then how did you think about — there's that chronological view, but then there's all of this other metadata that's never existed in any other CRM. This was one of the things I remember initially really jiving with you on — there's so much other context. How do you think about that as a part of this record?

Keith： Yeah. So we actually tried going fully unstructured. And we found that the queries just took too long — you sort of have the needle in the haystack problem. So we ended up finding this semi‑structured approach where we store gobs of unstructured data in this activity log. And then the system can use the activity log to infer causality and work through from there. That's why it works so much better than a data lake. And of course you can put anything in it — you can put your Snowflake records in it, you can put your activity.

Joe： Maybe give an example. What does that mean? How is it actually used at the end state?

Keith： Yeah. A good example would be — we have a lot of customer success folks on Lightfield, and they might be tasked with, "Hey, is this account ready for expansion? What should we sell to them? When should we sell to them?" It can now go through everything that this account has done: first, the people interactions — what did they say to you, what do their tickets look like? And then it can also go to the product usage, which is just stored as activity log entries: "Well, they haven't logged in in a month, maybe you should try to sell them more stuff."

And then if you want to compare — because the most common question is, "Which of these accounts should I work on expansion?" — now it can traverse the CRM schema and then dive deep into the log of each customer to give you a good answer.

让配置变得直观：Intelligence > Schema

Joe： How did you think about making the initial experience and the initial configuration of all of this intuitive for a small, midsize, even large company?

Keith： We had this view — it's funny, we spoke to a lot of CRM consultants, and we started to write down, like, what is it that you do? And we found that the biggest, most consequential decision they help you with is your data model.

Joe： You screw that up, it's over.

Keith： It's over. Right? If you get the wrong stages, the wrong fields, you can't get the reps to go back in time and fill it out. It's over.

We're like, can we be effectively schemaless? Just to say, we'll connect you to your emails, we'll give you a call recorder, we'll connect to your data warehouse, and then just assemble your relationships for you. Then you can fill out the fields later. If you change your mind about the fields, you can just traverse the activity log and refill them.

So we ended up with this schemaless setup where you log in, you connect your email and more. And we have built‑in enrichment sources, and then it just assembles for you in real time. Basically like, intelligence is greater than schema — that's the crux. So it feels like a consumer product. You just press sync, you wait five minutes, and it's there.

Alex： Well, if you go back to the really old days — it's like, to save space, because you'd only have — these were all just relational databases, right? And then to save space in a given table, each column — it's like, oh, I don't know how much you know SQL, but like, varchar, that's variable character. And you would actually predefine how many characters that particular column could be in the table. So you'd say name would be varchar(25). It's like, "Oh shoot, this person has too long of a..." — it's just funny how far this has gotten. Because back then when you were really, really managing every bit and every byte, you would literally predefine the maximum number of characters for a column in a table. And now it's like no schema. It's just funny. So the times have changed.

Keith： Intelligence is greater than schema.

Power 的案例：Lightfield 帮阿尔茨海默症患者找到前沿治疗

Alex： Some of the most interesting things happening right now — you're giving someone the chassis to commit intelligence at really hard problems. That example you gave of a CSM saying, "How do I upsell this customer?" — what's the most exciting or most random or interesting thing someone's doing with Lightfield today that they couldn't have done in the var world or another world before this one?

Keith： So one of the things I'm really proud of is we started with fully arbitrary schema, like custom object, custom relationship, because it just doesn't matter in Lightfield the way that it does in other ones. So I love our customers that have strange business models where they just need to model different things.

We have this company Power, and they work with pharmaceutical companies to help them find clinical trial participants. And on the other side they have this marketplace where they're aggregating folks that have various illnesses and complications that are looking for frontier treatment. So they've modeled all of this in Lightfield — the B2C side and the B2B side — and they've built automations to go and scrape the FDA and clinicaltrials.gov to give them a world model of every trial going on in the world. And then do matching on the B2C side as well as with the right pharmaceutical company. So there's sort of like collisions happening.

And Lightfield actually helped someone with Alzheimer's find frontier treatment within days.

Joe： That's incredible.

Greenfield vs Brownfield：如何切入被巨头统治的市场

Alex： So one question that we talk about a lot here is this kind of greenfield versus brownfield thing. If you think about startups normally, selling into the brownfield is hard just because it's brown. It's been trampled by an incumbent, right? Hence brown. Like, try selling ERP — you have a product that's much better than SAP, but there's a saying that Joe's heard me use a million times: "The best companies have hostages, not customers." SAP has hostages, that's a brownfield.

Sometimes you can break in — I mean, cloud versus on‑prem. What did cloud do? It redefined the problem: "You know what you're using, if you go back to the CRM days, is Siebel Systems running on your IBM AS/400 mainframe in your office. You're tired. The guy that maintained it quit, he was 92 years old. Maybe now you should use a cloud‑based vendor." That's how that brownfield was done, from on‑prem to cloud.

But the other strategy is going greenfield — saying, "I'm not going to bother with the hostages. I'm just going to build the best product in the world, and then brand‑new companies that are untethered from any existing software solution, they'll just use me."

Going back to the early days of negative pricing with the free office space, how did you think about who are the right customers? How did you get to your ICP, ideal customer profile?

Keith： Just to be totally real, when we were starting the company, we didn't have a sharp enough thesis on how to get into brownfield. So I think we had this perspective that building a revenue team is a very rich problem set. It's something that everyone cares about. It could always be done better. So we believed there's something in here, but we weren't sure exactly what it was.

So we figured, let's just try to win a new company first. And we were like, how do we win a new company? It was actually my chief of staff and I doing LinkedIn prospecting, emailing YC companies, being like, "Hey, can we beat one of these startup CRMs?" That was how we got started. And we figured by listening really deeply, we would find the wedge required to go brownfield eventually.

I think we sort of found it over the past few months — which is to say, you get lots of iteration. One of the nice things about serving an early‑stage startup right now is it's never been faster to go from pre‑seed to seed, seed to A to B. And we now have customers that had like zero reps when they joined us, who now have 100 reps. So we've been able to look inside and figure out, what problems are we solving for you that you actually care about?

And it seemed like it was actually a little higher level than we had even anticipated. If you looked at all of the AI CRM billboards around Silicon Valley in the past couple of years, they've always been about "do the work, do the work, do the work" — lead scoring, sending out outbound emails, and more. And I think our team always had this perspective that that wasn't really the wedge to do brownfield. Like, Salesforce is going to send emails — I mean, I guess they have as of today. And we were like, I think the wedge in brownfield has to do with better understanding your company, so you can steer your company through the sort of chaotic era of company building. But it took us honestly like six months of having customers, staring at them, for that to emerge.

VP of Sales 的抵触：如何跨越用户习惯的鸿沟

Alex： Well, one of the things that also emerges is — if you're creating a better product and you have all of these people that are consumers of the product — but like, let's just take the greenfield versus brownfield distinction. The VP of sales that you hire at your greenfield company has been acclimated and trained to use this thing.

I actually remember when I started one of my first companies, I was so adamant about not paying $85 a month for Salesforce that I used this thing called SugarCRM, which was free. And finally I gave up. I finally started paying for Salesforce. Why? Not because of product gaps, but because I hired this VP of sales and he was like, "I'm not using that f‑ing..." I was like, "It's easier, it's better." But that was also challenging.

So it's one of the things that is seldom understood about greenfield versus brownfield — that the greenfield people hire brownfield VPs that actually make purchasing decisions. So how did you overcome some of the objections from people who were like, "You know what, I'm just perfectly fine using something that doesn't work as well"?

Keith： It's a good question. One of our design principles early on was — we figured we were going to be great at convincing the founder, the engineering leader, the product leader, to use frontier tech to understand and serve customers. But it was probably going to be a lot of work to convince that VP of sales that joins that this is the way.

So we had this idea: for all of our sales‑led plans, we're going to give this thing away for free to anyone in the company. One, it helps Lightfield understand what engineering's doing, what customer support's doing, what finance is doing. The other thing is, it'll create real company network effects that make it harder to rip and replace us.

So we've been at a few companies now where the seasoned VP of sales comes in and they're like, "You know, this is cool, but I only know how to use Salesforce because I've been trained that way." And the rest of the company is like, "Well, hold on. This is like how the engineers understand customers. This is how finance does revenue recognition. This is how customer success does account scoring. Can you try harder to figure this out?" In which case, we have the relationship, we jump in, we show them how we're going to make their lives easier, and we've got a fighting chance.

产品哲学：务实 vs 前沿的平衡

Joe： There's so many different ways to now do those tasks that were just a table in the past. And so, do you want to try to give those tables to people and try to make it very skeuomorphic — "here's the CRM that you're used to and it's also blue and blah blah blah" — or is it, "Hey, actually, you can now use natural language to do a lot of this. You don't actually have to look at all these dashboards. Lightfield will just tell you when something happens." How do you think about those product trade‑offs, which I think a lot of systems of record are actually trying to figure out — how do we bring people to the real future which is now here?

Keith： Yeah. I think we've actually erred on the side of pragmatism here. Which is to say that right now I'm the de facto sales manager at the company and I still run all of our meetings from the spreadsheet view.

We had this view of, if we really want to be a real enterprise CRM, we can't be religious about the way people work. So we've leaned into: we have great dashboards, we have great table views. You can use those things if you want. And then if you're sort of at the frontier, you can do it all — and you want like CLI or whatever — you can also do that.

Alex： I find that — you know, so it's funny, I just bought a new car. I came from a BMW which had like 9 million buttons. Like, you know, if you go in an airplane, right? You look at the cockpit and it's like, how does the pilot know? Like what — there were like 9,000 switches, straight out of Airplane. And like, the really cool thing — it's actually even scary — like, you know, I don't know if you know this, like the newest Teslas, they don't even have a stalk to change gears. There isn't one. Like the most physical of physical buttons. It's just completely gone. But actually, it's so simple and so intuitive that a 5‑year‑old can use it. I mean, hopefully a 5‑year‑old isn't driving a car, but you get where I'm going.

It's like — I mean, it's another way of kind of thinking about schema versus schemaless. If you have all these knobs and switches, it's great, it's so advanced — like the VP of sales, or if you talk to finance people, they know all their buttons in Bloomberg. But one of the ways that you're able to build something great is just make it so intuitive that even a 5‑year‑old can do it. There's a whole category on Reddit called ELI5 — "explain like I'm five," right? So it kind of feels like — I don't know if you're the boss, not me — but like, it feels like that's kind of what you have, right? You have this old era with lots of knobs and switches and everything else. But again, part of the benefit of plain‑language intelligence is that you don't need any of those things. It's almost rendered anachronistic.

Keith： Yeah, this is true. And we run into this in different ways. Which is to say that we haven't won the war on deterministic dashboards. I think everyone wants to look at the same dashboard every morning when they're drinking their coffee. Me too.

Alex： Hopefully it's revenue going up.

Keith： It's always up. But I think for some of these old workflows, we've completely reimagined them. One of the most classic sales workflows is the idea of a sequence — you send out five emails at different times on different triggers to someone that might have expressed interest in your product. And you used to have to express these things with arrows and conditions and variables.

Whereas in Lightfield, we're like, no, you just chat with the agent. The agent writes out a recipe for you. The recipe takes into account what's in your world model, and it runs with it. At first we had some sales leaders that were like, "I don't trust this thing, I need my knobs, I need my switches." But then they sort of come around to, "Wait a minute, this is actually more efficient, better, and I have to learn less." I feel like we're running into this in every aspect of running a go‑to‑market team.

DIY 潮流：客户想自己造 CRM 吗？

Joe： There's this whole movement right now of, everyone thinks they can build basically everything themselves and, you know, "software is dead." What can I do myself versus not? How do you talk to customers that want to try to build elements of this, or are trying to build elements of this — and just say a little bit more about that movement and how you're responding at Lightfield?

Keith： First of all, I think just being a system of record, we have to be open‑minded. It's your data, it's not ours, right? We tell our customers that we take a lot of pride in the modeling and the accuracy of your business. We built our own email sync, we built our own Slack sync, we built our own data warehouse sync, and we are proud of how high‑performance our database is. And then you can take that wherever you want.

So we've actually had a couple of customers that would use Lightfield as the core system of record, and then they'll try to build their own harness on top. Maybe they've got a company harness, right? And we're supportive of that. You could push it all through MCP or CLI. But after a few weeks, they almost always realize, "Wait a minute, your harness was actually doing quite a bit." It had better entity recognition, it had better precision and recall, it was faster. And we're like, "Yeah, that's our job."

So I think our take is, it's your data, do what you want, but we're going to work hard to earn the right to your productivity every day.

定价的三段进化：seat → consumption → hybrid

Alex： Where do you think — kind of on that topic — I mean, pricing is such a crazy question right now. Because there's seat‑based pricing where the seats don't make sense anymore. Like, imagine running — thank God you run Lightfield and not Zendesk, right? It's like, how many seats do you need? Maybe zero, right? That's pretty scary.

Then there's kind of outcome‑based pricing, but what is an outcome? Like, am I selling the thing? What if I just have a happy customer forever? I'm still using CRM for that, so outcomes are kind of tricky.

And then against all of that, you have this idea, which I don't agree with obviously, but people saying "software is dead," the whole SaaS apocalypse. You know, you're also going to — supermarkets are dead, you're going to grow your own food; car manufacturers are dead, you're going to weld your own aluminum. You could take this to the extreme. But like, where do you think — how did you come up with pricing? Maybe that's kind of question number one. And then what do you think about outcome‑based pricing in this space?

Because it's not — like, support almost makes sense, where it's a cost, "can I bring down the cost?" And of course you can have software answer questions — it's a knowledge base, there's a fixed number of answers, I kind of match up with the question. Whereas it almost feels like the last job standing for humans will be sales, right? Anyway, kind of pricing, outcomes, competition — just curious how you thought about how did you get to your pricing from negative pricing, which I would not recommend you keep in perpetuity, but kind of how did you get to pricing, and how do you think about everything that's going on in that triangle?

Keith： Yeah, it's a good question. We started with both extremes and we figured that that is the fastest path to find the efficient frontier. We started with pure seat pricing because it just matched the Salesforce/HubSpot world. It was received really well by our customers. But then the head was using 10,000x more than the tail.

Alex： Using in terms of consumption?

Keith： Yeah, in terms of consumption. And we weren't going to be in business for a long time with per‑seat pricing.

So then we tried purist consumption pricing where everything is a credit in Lightfield. And then we found that nobody touched anything. You could imagine — it was the worst three weeks of the company's life. All of these signups but they're not doing anything.

So then we started talking to customers. We realized there's sort of — and Joe, actually — we divided into four buckets of work that Lightfield does, and we're able to distinguish between them.

The first was your everyday CRM work: capture a meeting, fill out records, update tasks. I think most of our customers just expect that to be covered in a platform fee or expect that to be covered in per‑seat pricing. They're like, "I don't want to think about the error bounds of my core CRM when I look at my budget over the next year." So they're like, make that fixed.

Then we found there were two other buckets. One was pipeline generation — where you're pretty down to pay consumption pricing on pipeline generation. You realize there's enrichment, there's actually alpha for you. You'll get more meetings that can convert to revenue.

And then there's this other bucket of workflow automations, where I think there's just an expectation that you pay for those.

Joe： What's a good example of that, by the way?

Keith： It would be like — someone signs up on our website for a demo, and then Lightfield does a little bit of research and realizes, "Oh, this should go to Henry because it's a deep tech company," or "It should go to Matt because it's a health tech company." I think that's doing real work, right? You can imagine the ROI on that. So you'll pay for that.

And then the last piece is honestly intelligence and forecasting. Which is maybe the most undiscovered part of Lightfield: you've got this little crystal ball or snow globe of your company, and now you're going to deploy frontier intelligence to it and start scenario planning and figuring out what's next. I think in that world, you'll definitely pay for the alpha there. I changed my sales process after letting GPT‑6 rip on Lightfield for a couple of hours on the weekend.

So all of that is to say — we sort of landed in this platform fee plus seat for core CRM, and we do consumption for everything else, and it's landed pretty well.

To your other question about outcomes: I think the hardest thing about being a sales company is that our outcomes are dependent on the strength of your product‑market fit, right? It would be incredibly efficient for us to do outbound prospecting for OpenAI — they'd have incredible outcomes.

Alex： And they are interested.

Keith： Yeah. And it would be incredibly inefficient for me to do outbound prospecting for a seed‑stage startup with no website. So I think where we've landed at the moment is, we have to charge for the work. We can't quite charge for the outcome in the space for now.

团队文化：没有 swim lane，人人皆通才

Joe： Yeah. Maybe from when you started Tome to today, how has the actual work changed? Something that I found amazing and just really fascinating about the company when we first met over a year ago was just how fast you guys were already shipping, and it feels like the velocity has just gone through the roof. So I'd be curious how you've designed company culture and tooling and all the decision‑making around basically velocity, and just the step‑function change from before and after. Talk a little bit about that.

Keith： Yeah. So I think — one of the things I regret about Tome that we definitely fixed with Lightfield is — Henry, my co‑founder, says this all the time: we had a lot of people "playing house." Which is to say that you have the product leader and the marketing leader and the CS leader, and they all have their swim lanes and they get really mad if someone gives them feedback about something in their swim lane.

Because of that, we were sort of slowed to a crawl. And maybe put another way, it was impossible to pivot. Because you had all of these appendages that weren't talking to the brain. And then we also tried to plan too far in advance, which I think is challenging in this era of company building.

So we're like, none of that. No one has a swim lane. The expression "man plans and God laughs" — now it's "man plans and OpenAI laughs."

So now — it's funny — everyone owns product and everyone owns customer success. Which is kind of an interesting setup. We have 40 people at the company. Everyone shows up to the same standup every morning. We stack‑rank the most important problems. Some of them are delivery, some of them are engineering, some of them are CS. And then whoever's free just takes them.

We do continuous planning. So every day the list can change. Every week we reassess the list. Whoever's free just picks up the problem. Because of the age that we're in, anyone can ramp up on a customer through Lightfield. Anyone can ramp up on our design system library because the LLM can touch Figma. Anyone can auto‑create tasks in Linear because of Lightfield's connectivity to Linear. So we have this environment where basically everyone is a generalist. Engineers run projects, designers run projects, CSMs run projects. And then if you're the specialist, you work on more of the similar projects than not.

Joe： How do you keep that — everyone's a generalist and everyone's constantly coming up with something and working on the most important thing? How do you keep that aligned with this very coherent view of the future?

Keith： I would say that it's always this push and pull. Each week we meet about roadmapping and GTM and we just edit it. And I were like, "Yes, we had this customer that asked for this, like — how does it fit into the mission? It doesn't." So I think it's this constant editing to make sure that what's coming out of the company is coherent.

We also — I would say that the bar to start a project is very low at Lightfield, but the bar to ship the project is pretty high. We still do company bug bashes. It was something I learned at Instagram when I was there. The company needs to like this before it goes to customers. I feel like those things combined keep us moving pretty fast.

最担忧的：速度

Joe： So cool. What's the thing that worries you the most?

Keith： I would say speed. We're in this really interesting environment. Maybe I'll share something from the past. Before we started Lightfield, I read all of these Tegus reports about people moving off of, you know, flavor‑of‑the‑month CRM to Salesforce. And I remember reading this one about one of your portfolio companies, ElevenLabs, where they ran one of these startup CRMs. And they couldn't get that company to build dashboards fast enough — and it was like four months, and the folks at ElevenLabs were tired of asking for dashboards. It moved to Salesforce.

That's actually the thing that makes me the most paranoid. We've got this incredible wedge of being just like the best CRM for new companies, and we just have to build everything, so that those folks never feel the desire to go to the old world.

优先级：Expansion 视角下的取舍

Joe： How do you actually — on that — how do you prioritize? I mean, this is like the craziness about the new world, and it actually goes back to your point on everybody being a generalist. Once upon a time you would have like a 10‑person product, design, and engineering pod — pick your number, but not 100, not 2. You'd have the product manager, you'd have the designer, and then you'd have like nine engineers, and you would have things that would be booked out until like 2028.

And now anybody can just prompt their way into a product, right? So if everybody actually is understanding what we need to do — on the one hand, it's like you could build everything much more quickly. But you still have to make trade‑offs of like, "Am I prioritizing this customer that I know — shoot, I have this amazing company, they're going to churn unless I build this? That's a really good reason to build that thing. But actually, that might not be a good thing, because you have like 15 other customers that you're not going to sign up unless you build the other thing." This has been a problem since like BC era, but is there anything that you've learned and done differently in this AI era around anybody can build anything, and therefore you could theoretically have unlimited product managers and engineers in your company?

Keith： It's funny — in Lightfield we sort of built this skill where we look at the expansion potential of an account. I think as a CRM company in a red ocean space, we have to be an expansion company. Right? In a competitive space, you often don't get the initial land that you would have expected, because it's just important to win every company. But you're like, by year three, by year five, this is not going to matter, because you'll be a huge company, we'll be an important part of you.

So I think we take this perspective of, what's the expansion value of this account over a three‑year time horizon, and how do we prioritize? Because of that, we've leaned more towards building for our fastest‑growing customers than our average customer. But I would say at the same time, we have to build everything, and it's sort of a time of being a little more maximalist than usual.

Silicon Valley 过热 vs 世界其余地方过冷

Alex： The other thing that's kind of interesting is — my observation is — I kind of like to joke that AI is almost overhyped in Silicon Valley. I don't think it is, but — and it's massively underhyped outside of this little region of the world. Part of it is people haven't tried things in years. Like, "Oh, I tried ChatGPT in November of 2022 and it hallucinated something. Oh, that doesn't work." And then they just kind of put it to bed. Now they think it's going to kill them somehow.

But I mean, how do you think about long — it's related to greenfield versus brownfield, but like — you can get Silicon Valley, but it's kind of crossing the chasm into the rest of the country, the rest of the world where — that's a very, very... I mean, it's the same type of customers. They have products, they have employees, they have salespeople, they sell things, they want reports, but they're not as plugged in. Like, you can't just advertise on 101 and reach them. How do you think about Silicon Valley overhype versus rest‑of‑world underhype?

Keith： Yeah. I think for most of these system‑of‑record companies, you end up getting most of your revenue scale from actually the 50 miles out of here and more. I've always thought about this moment in company building as a trick to get reference logos.

Which is that we have customers that have raised like $200 million that have three go‑to‑market people, and they're going to be huge one day. So we just need to do amazing work for them so we can take their logos when we go to the rest of the world, and be like, "All right, we've got healthcare, we've got fintech," or whatever it is. So I just see the focus on Silicon Valley not as efficient revenue capture, but actually just efficient marketing capture, to go out there and be like, "All right, we're excited to get into manufacturing. We're actually working with a bunch of great manufacturing companies here, and now we can do that for you."

Referenceability：CRM 比银行还难更换

Alex： It's funny how customers think, right? It's like, all right, you're using the exact same software, but somehow, if Joe is in a different industry than me and he's a super happy customer, and I want the exact same — I'm going to use the Fields example, so just bear with me — I'm storing the exact same stuff, but I don't know if I can trust you because he sells toothbrushes and I sell Coca‑Cola. But it's like, if he sells toothbrushes, oh, I must have the thing that the other toothbrush seller sells.

It's really peculiar. I always found that — it's like — but like, somehow that goes back to referenceability. It's like customers, they just want to know — it's like the old "nobody gets fired for buying IBM." It's like, I want to know that this works, especially for something that is a system of record. And I want to know that somebody that is a competitor to me, or a friend of mine, or somebody in the same vertical, is using the product before I'm willing to make the jump.

So do you find that that's true? Almost because it's like you mentioned manufacturing versus X. At the end of the day, a customer is a customer, right? Like the context and the contact information — all that stuff is the same. But why is it — is it just like they care because there's just so much trust associated with the product?

Keith： I think so. I think in many ways, your CRM is maybe harder to move off of than your bank.

Alex： Yeah. It's Lightfield.

Keith： Yeah, exactly. And then we make it easy. We've made it a lot easier. But I think in terms of the mental overhead, you just do not want to choose the wrong one. And because of that, I think the referenceability goes a long way.

On the way in, I was telling Joe that we do great with healthcare and health tech. I think part of it is that we do really well in these complex deals where there's like 50 different stakeholders. Our context engineering is done really well, and also, we were hardcore about security at the start — so we signed BAAs, and we did penetration testing for years. Now it's so easy for us to win a health tech deal, and I think it's because we sort of have this network that we can reference and move on.

I think that's just part of the game. If I imagine even myself — I don't want to choose the wrong ERP, so I probably want to choose the ERP that companies who look like me chose, so that I never have to think about this after I buy it.

DIY 神话的现实

Alex： Do you run into — kind of going back to an earlier question — do you run into people in this crazy era saying, "No, I'm not going to use anything, I'm just going to build it myself"? Because that's the craziest, right? Is the guy that is working at my company who's decided to vibe‑code a CRM — like, it's free, right? But the support, is it free? The salary that I'm paying him or her isn't free. But do you run into people that are trying to DIY, or is that kind of over‑talked about?

Keith： I think it's a little over‑talked about. We heard it a lot when our ICP was the seed‑stage founder. Where we would often hear, "Look, we can either pay you X, or we can do this over like four weekends." And we were like, "Great, good luck. You should try it, call us in five weekends." And then they were like, "None of this works. It's hallucinating, it's sending out bad emails."

I think on the larger‑company side, we don't hear "I'm going to build my own system of record." We hear "I'm going to build my own company brain" a lot. And then we've had so many of these folks come back and be like, "Actually, building a company brain, or building a business world model, is really hard. And I think maybe the hardest part of it is modeling the customers. So we tried and we don't like our results. So we'll come to you now."

未来最兴奋的事：企业的水晶球

Joe： What are you most excited about for the future?

Keith： I mean, I think the thing I'm most excited about — it's funny — I'm stoked about Lightfield becoming your crystal ball for scenario planning. The thing that gets me up in the morning is actually having folks use Lightfield to think about, "How many reps should I hire? What product should I build next? Where do I go?"

One of our customers, who sells to enterprise, discovered through Lightfield he needs to build a mid‑market product, and built this whole new product line because of this thing he found. I'm just excited about us being that sort of mirror for a company to make their hardest, most consequential decision.

Joe： I think this goes back to the point Alex was making on — in this world of maximalists and you can build for anyone, actually the answer is having a tool like Lightfield. If you just have all of this data and all this context, you can actually be data‑driven, and this is the exact opportunity to throw frontier intelligence at a really complicated decision. It's something that historically would have required really smart people and a lot of ops folks and SQL and a bunch of other stuff. And instead now you just talk to Lightfield for an afternoon or a weekend and come up with a really intelligent plan to move forward. I think that's one of the reasons that you can run your company the way you run it, which is really cool.

给正在经历转折的创业者的一条建议

Joe： Maybe my last question for you: there's a lot of people that — I think at least there will be a handful of people that are going through some pivot moment that are watching this, thinking about the future where they're Keith, and they're talking about their new amazing company. What would be the one piece of advice that you'd go back and give yourself if you were just starting the pivot journey again, with the benefit of hindsight?

Keith： I think the most important thing to remember is that almost none of the noise around you matters when you're in a pivot. You just need to find pain. You need to be inspired to build a product or service that solves that pain, and you need to be maniacally focused on your customers. And then the rest is total noise.

I remember when we were going near this, people were talking about how our office reminded them of the good old days. They were talking about how the food wasn't inspiring. They were talking about, "Well, how are my options going to get repriced?" And honestly, none of that matters. I think you can just put the blinders on and focus on the core.

结尾

Joe： Well, we could not be more impressed with what you've done — the business you've built, the product is absolutely incredible. If you haven't tried it, you need to try it. It's incredible. Go check it out at lightfield.app. Keith, it's an absolute pleasure to work with you and we're so excited for the future.

Keith： Thanks for the honor. Thanks for having me.

Joe： Yeah. Thanks, Keith.
