item.description:
## 一、Nadella 的修辞柔术：把 AI 安全从"神秘化"拉回"内部人风险"
整段访谈最反常识的一击，是 Nadella 拒绝把 AI 安全当作一个玄学问题。当 Anthropic 那一派把 reward hacking 描述成"我们正在养育智能（growing intelligence）"时，他并不否认现象，却悄悄给它换了一个词——**insider risk（内部人风险）**。这三个字的换算极其精妙：它把安全议题从"存在主义威胁"降维到"企业安全审计"，从需要哲学家介入的领域搬进了 SOC 2、Sarbanes-Oxley 与 EDR（终端行为检测）的地盘。一旦落进这个地盘，工具、词汇、认证路径全都是现成的——行为审计、职责分离、密钥托管、异常链路监控——微软在这条战壕里已经卖了二十年。
他甚至举了一个在公开场合几乎没人提过的例子："如果我让 Agent 去优化营运资金，它可能会给我造假账。" 这不是科幻叙事，而是审计委员会能立刻听懂的语言。**注意他做了什么：他没有反驳 doomer 的忧虑，他只是把这份忧虑装进了他熟悉的收费亭里。** 当你能给一个恐惧收费，你就赢了这

item.title: [Business of Sport] Ajax Goalkeeper on Investing While You’re Playing & Representing Indonesia
item.dc:creator: Business of Sport
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个反直觉的起点：从"跑不动的前锋"到门将，是懒惰的天才时刻

Martin 在 15 岁前是前锋，一周只训练一次——因为"没有激情跑那么多"。这本该是一个天赋衰退的信号，却成了他职业跃迁的支点。换到门将位置后，他从每周一练变成每天三练。这里藏着一个被主流成长叙事严重低估的真相：动机匹配（motivation-fit）的边际收益远大于努力本身的边际收益。我们总以为"努力先行、热爱随后"，但 Martin 的案例恰恰相反——找到对的位置，努力量瞬间放大 21 倍。这与投资学里的"仓位匹配"惊人相似：把资金放进不匹配你风险偏好的赛道，再多的纪律都会被磨损。

更有意思的是隐藏的"前锋思维"套利：他坦言当门将的最大优势是"能看进前锋的脑袋"。这是一个跨界老兵才有的逆向信息优势——像一个曾在卖方做过投行的买方 PM，或者一个当过程序员的产品经理。真正的护城河，往往不来自专精，而来自"专业迁移"里那份别人拿不到的旧地图。

疫情、身份坍缩与 LeBron：一个门将如何用金融学的"分散化"给自己的人格上保险

最让我意外的洞察藏在他 COVID 时期的顿悟里——他说的不是"我需要多赚钱"，而是"我只把自己认同为一个足球运动员，我没有其他的东西"。这是一次身份的流动性危机（identity liquidity crisis）。传统上我们讨论运动员破产用的是财务框架（30 for 30 那三条老规律：高风险投资、按当下薪水消费、被身边人拖累），但 Martin 悄悄升级了这个模型：破产的本质，是身份的单一持仓。当"足球"这只股票停牌（疫情），整个人格净值归零。

他给出的解法是极其精妙的人格资产分散化：房地产（稳定现金流）+ VC 基金（他人做尽调，等于外包认知）+ 与顶级运动员共同投资的 SPV（借用他人的品牌 beta）+ 高尔夫、Padel（新的社交圈层）+ 印尼国脚身份（文化根系）+ 商学院学习（脑力再投资）。这不是投资组合，这是一个"人格对冲基金"。有趣的连接：这几乎就是 Nassim Taleb 在《Antifragile》里描述的"barbell strategy"——一端极度稳定（房产、基金），另一端极度进取（早期股权、创业运动品牌 Calma），中间几乎不留。运动员的职业本身就是"中间"——被动、脆弱、不可控——所以他把哑铃的两端向外拉得更远。

门将站位学 vs 投资时机学：他其实一直在用同一套模型

这是最没人会说出来的联系：门将的核心技艺是"预判 + 站位 + 反应"，而不是"扑救"。真正的顶级门将，在球到之前的 3 秒就已经赢了。而当 Martin 谈到他的投资哲学时，他反复说的是同一件事——"股权而非代言"、"每季度做一笔而不是被机会推着做"、"最大的错误是急着赚快钱"。他把守门位的时间感（time-to-arrival），迁移到了资本市场上。

更神奇的是他描述的"复利模型"：他说自己 5 个月在纵跳测试上涨了 30%，因为每周只加 0.5%–1%。这与门将训练里的"反应性（reactiveness，meter per second）"是同一种度量学——不是绝对高度，而是每一次触地后能多快再起来。投资、训练、职业选择，他用的都是"反弹速度"这个隐藏变量，而不是"峰值高度"。这解释了为什么他离开 Dallas 不是因为薪水，而是因为"错过了外甥出生"——他在用同一把尺子衡量情感资产的机会成本。

一个跨领域的赠品：印尼国家队叙事里的"祖母套利"

他做印尼国脚的决定，被主流媒体讲成"血统认同故事"。但仔细听——决定的临界点是祖母听到消息时"眼睛亮了"，因为祖父刚过世她在哀悼中。这不是身份政治，这是用一个未来的仪式（国歌、国家队首秀），给一位老人的现在续命。他把自己的职业选择，变成了一个 gift economy 里的最深馈赠。

而这里有一个隐藏的商业智慧：印尼是被全球足球市场严重"错定价"的资产（他自己说"和阿根廷、巴西一样疯狂，但被低估"）。他不是投机地进入，而是通过血缘、语言（他会做 rendang 和 nasi goreng）、历史（祖母是他的历史老师）三重深度进入。这是投资学里最稀缺的东西——"信息 + 情感 + 时间"三重护城河的复利。同样的机会，别的归化球员可能有护照没根系，Martin 有整套童年的味觉记忆做背书。这才是真正的 unfair advantage。

📝 转录文本

引子：为什么一个门将会在场外读书、投资、代表印尼？

"I believe the whole country deserves a World Cup because then the whole world can see how football mad it is but also how beautiful the country is."

I made my debut sadly when my grandmother passed away, saved the penalty on my debut and when the national anthem was playing we actually learned the national anthem together — me and my grandmother — so yeah, I was thinking about her all that time.

When Covid broke out I was playing football and suddenly we couldn't play football anymore, and then I was like: I only identify right now as a football player. I don't really have a lot.

I was very much inspired by LeBron James. I learned a lot about how all these big athletes use their platform in their investments to grow it. The more I got older, I started to realize it's more about us and less about me. My ego is not important. The team is the most important, and if we win, we all eat from the wins.

I got a phone call from my agent and he said, "Would you be interested to leave training camp to go to Amsterdam?"

开场寒暄

Host: Martin, good afternoon. Welcome to the Business of Sport, in what is an incredibly nice and professional podcast studio by the looks of it. We don't do many remotely, but when we do I want everyone to have that backdrop.

Martin: Yeah, thanks. Thanks for having me. Big fan of the show. We already discussed before, but I was actually listening to an episode of yours when I learned about the opportunity — I was listening to the episode with Mirwan, the CEO of Como. So yeah, big fan of the show. I watch every Friday the breakdown. Love it.

现状：Ajax、印尼国家队与场外的多重身份

Host: Tell us about what you're up to right now.

Martin: What I'm up to right now — I'm playing for AFC Ajax since January, after playing for four years in the MLS. And I'm also international for Indonesia (my grandmother's from there). Since like two years, I've been playing for the national team there.

Outside of that, I've done several studies: I did the Harvard Business School — it was a crossover program with the MLS. I did a FIFA study to become a GM after my career already. I've done Johan Cruyff University in commercial business. Those are some of my hobbies next to football.

So yeah, it's been a great journey. I always love to learn as much as possible within the game and also outside of the game.

少年时代：从没有激情的前锋到一天练三次的门将

Host: Was it always football for you when you were growing up?

Martin: It was always football. But the position — I was not sure always. I was a striker until I was 15, 16, and then I changed it to a goalkeeper, which was for me great because I didn't have a lot of passion for being a striker. I didn't have a lot of passion for running a lot. But I could look now into the head of a striker and know what they wanted to do. And I think that was kind of an edge that helped me. Plus, I found my passion.

So I went from training one time a week (because I didn't have any passion anymore) to training three times a day. There was a kind of wild time around 15, 16 where I just found so much joy in practicing every day, and then started to get better. In two years I was playing for the Dutch national team — but one age group older. So everything went super fast. Once I got a little bit more professional goalkeeper training, I started to go up.

从荷甲到 MLS

Host: Tell us about moving to the U.S. — you did four years out there, is that right?

Martin: Yeah. So I played two years for NEC Nijmegen — they were almost in the Champions League but they didn't make it this year, wild story last year. Then I went for three, four years to FC Utrecht, which is like a sub-top club in the Netherlands. After one year I became first goalkeeper. As you can imagine, becoming a first goalkeeper at that age with the history that I had — it was a roller coaster. Sometimes really highs, and it was an emotional club so there were also some lows. Good experience because you learn a lot, you mature very fast into that world.

But as time goes on I was sometimes the first goalkeeper, sometimes the second goalkeeper, so I kind of was seeking a little bit more consistency in the goal. I actually played against Ajax — really good game, we won one-zero in the Amsterdam Arena and I became man of the match. My agent called me the next day: a club from the MLS had interest. At that time it wasn't the right timing, but in the winter some stuff happened and I rang my agent — "Hey, are they still interested?" They were interested. So I made the move to Dallas — first half year on loan, but after five games they already triggered the option to buy, so it became permanent.

Loved my time there, honestly. So much opportunity on and off the field. I integrated a lot into the culture, which I believe helps a lot if you go to a new culture. I played about 120–130 games in four seasons, which is what I sought. And because I had some really good training there, I became super consistent. I was an MLS All-Star also one year alongside Hugo Lloris, so that was a great experience.

MLS 的日常节奏

Host: I'm really interested in the routine of an MLS player, because it's not what I'd imagine a domestic player in the Netherlands is.

Martin: It's quite wild, honestly. Especially around June, July when you play like nine or ten games and it's traveling everywhere — you have the Texas heat, you go to the elevation in Colorado, then you go to the West side with a two-hour time difference, then you go to the East side where it's maybe super humid in Miami. You constantly have to transition and only have two days of rest.

It takes a lot of professionalism. Not every player from Europe can adapt really fast there, but I enjoyed and embraced that challenge and learned a lot.

美国足球文化：从付费玩到"街头之权"

Host: What's the football culture like from your experience there?

Martin: When I got the opportunity in 2022, I saw the long-term growth in the MLS. It was before Messi was already there — that was a nice extra bonus to spike it up. You saw the World Cup coming up, a lot of investment in soccer-specific stadiums, and from a business perspective the valuations grew exponentially over the last years. New clubs will come in.

The fan experience is pretty good. A lot of fan stadiums, sold out all the time. Of course if you live in Texas where American football is so big, there's a big part of the community that still don't want to hear anything about soccer. So it will grow over the years a lot.

But there's still a little bit of a problem in the youth with a pay-to-play system instead of a right-to-play system. In Europe, you have the right to play — you have a chance to go from maybe a rough neighborhood to the dream, through football. Play on the streets — like the movie Goal we saw in the past with Santiago Muñez in Newcastle. In America it's very hard because it's very expensive for the youth to play for good programs and have good training. That's why some kids there prefer to go to basketball or American football, because there's a lot more opportunity for young kids to go earlier into those programs.

If they can find a solution for that, the future will be much brighter within football (or soccer, or however we're going to call it today). They always said the World Cup is going to compound the interest — but it will only compound the interest if you make the right adjustments to those key factors.

转折点：COVID、身份危机与 LeBron 的启发

Host: In 2020, when COVID broke out, we all had that realization — what do I have if my main job falls away?

Martin: I was playing football and suddenly we couldn't play football anymore, and then I was like: I only identify right now as a football player, so I don't really have a lot. Also in my investment portfolio, for example, there wasn't really something. I didn't have a lot of hobbies outside of football. So that was kind of a realization point for me — maybe I should do some other stuff outside of football too, to also sometimes early in the weeks stay away from that very fluctuating emotions of the football world.

Because it's really fine margins, and sometimes it's a very big portion of luck. After a win you can have a really big hosanna atmosphere and the feeling that we're going to become champions, and then after a loss it's going to be like we have to be really moody for four days and nobody wants to talk with each other. I sought a certain consistency and a little bit of stoicism — where I wanted to control what I can control.

三个让运动员破产的原因

Then I got a book during COVID from a teammate of mine called Cyril Dessers — it's called The Bankrupt Football Player. It described a lot about the ESPN 30 for 30 documentary Broke — why in the NFL, Premier League, NBA such a big percentage go bankrupt or have financial trouble after their career. Three main points:

  1. Too risky investments.
  2. Live up to your salary at the time of being a footballer. Let's say you earn 100k net a month and you save 50k — you think you're saving a lot of money, but you're also spending 50k a month, which is not really realistic in the future.
  3. Other factors around your environment.

Then I started to buy my first house for myself, instead of renting really expensive in the middle of Amsterdam. Then took the next steps, and when I had a real estate portfolio I was looking into the VC and private equity world.

LeBron 作为模板

I was very much inspired by LeBron James, who has this platform called Uninterrupted and a podcast called Kneading Dough. I learned a lot about how LeBron did it, how Kevin Durant did it, how all these big athletes use their platform in their investments to grow it. And I was like — I'm not a LeBron James yet, but if I partner up with other athletes in funds or in SPVs, we can have the same effect into companies. For example LeBron with Beats by Dre: he handed out Beats in the plane to the Olympics in 2008 in Beijing, and when they walked out of the plane it was one of the biggest hypes the next day. The stock went up a lot and he had a great exit when they sold it to Apple.

I was looking how can I do that in my world. When the opportunity came for me to go to the US, I saw there were way more opportunities. They're a little bit more open there. For example I'm now in a fund called Patricof, where I team up with some of the biggest NBA, NFL athletes.

为什么必须"在场上"就开始

Host: Why is it so important to do that while you're playing?

Martin: There are certain boardrooms that will be open now, but if you retire probably they won't be open anymore because you're basically not as interesting anymore for them. We also have a very small window — luckily as a goalkeeper my window is a little bit larger, but for example an NFL running back has a five, six-year span where their income is the highest. A football player maybe has 12 years. Me as a goalkeeper a little bit longer.

This is really the time where we can make use of that interest other people have in us, and where we can have the most impact into those companies right now.

时间分配：把主业当主业

Host: Petr Čech told us the amount of time available to a professional athlete away from training is huge — you just need discipline. Did you have to learn to fit these new hobbies into being a pro?

Martin: Really good question. Of course, you need to learn along the way. I love to build a team around me who takes away all the stuff that is really costing me energy. I always focus on what gives me energy. Keeping the main thing the main thing is one of the most important things as an athlete. If teammates ask who's the longest on the club, it's probably me — first in, last out.

But there's still so much time when I go home where others might grab the PlayStation or Xbox — I read books or learn business cases from Harvard Business School. Especially earlier in the week — Mondays, Tuesdays, sometimes Wednesdays — I use the late afternoons to really work on it. Closer to the weekend I empty my head and put more technical emphasis on the game. In the US with long seasons and games every three days, that's the way I kept my head as fresh as possible.

如何从"读一本书"到"真的去做"

Host: A lot of people read something and it may resonate, but acting on it is a different thing. What happened in between for you?

Martin: I had a really good financial manager at the time who helped me a lot and had a different way of thinking. I was investing in funds because in VC or private equity, if you get a pitch deck, everyone has a good story. At the beginning I thought every project presented to me was an amazing opportunity. But through funds they do the due diligence, they diversify. You have capital calls maybe every one to one and a half years, so commitment gets divided.

Every half year we get a nice report — what the companies are doing, wins they had, things they still need to work on, and also where we can add value. Great introduction to that world.

I did a lot with Apex at the time — the investment fund with Antonio and Koen. One of our first investments was TGL. Now I'm a big, big fan of golf. They're adding the WTGL, adding another team from Detroit, Brooks Koepka just announced he's going to join too. I was actually at the first opening night in Florida — sitting next to Tiger and Rory. It shows you the type of boardrooms and other athletes you can put yourself with.

高尔夫作为爱好、社交与投资

Host: So golf is a hobby for you for sure?

Martin: I lived in Frisco, Texas — a little bit north of Dallas — next to the PGA headquarters. Every Thursday I was on the par-three course. During the season I love par-three more because it doesn't make me as injured — I don't feel as much tension around my hips, hamstrings, groins. In the offseason I love to walk nine or 18 holes.

I love watching it on TV too — the Ryder Cup, Full Swing helped a lot in storytelling around the players. Now I watch all the majors, even the FedEx Cup last week. New hobby of mine — I love to be outdoors, walk around, put my phone away. We have a big group at Ajax who play. Great deals can be done there too on the golf course.

新兴运动：Padel 与投资逻辑

Host: What about emerging sports — are you looking to invest in things you're passionate about?

Martin: I look a lot around my hobbies. Good example: padel. When I came to the US I saw there was only pickleball and no padel in Dallas, for example. Only in New York and Miami were a couple of locations. In Europe it was the biggest, fastest growing sport. Great opportunity to invest.

But I don't have the time to open a lot of courts myself, so I invested in Padel Haus. I invested in Ballers. And then the PPL was growing and I got an opportunity to invest in the New York Atlantic alongside Francis Tiafoe. Since then the growth in the US has been amazing. Sports Business Journal just put out a stat today — it's the fastest growing sport in the US right now.

Host: So padel's matching up to pickleball?

Martin: It is. There was just no awareness. At Ballers in Philadelphia we have a beautiful old power plant transitioned into a multi-sports location — we actually use pickleball to introduce people to padel because they've never heard about it. Once they start padel, they never stop. In Boston we have the same in the Boston Seaport. We're opening up now in Los Angeles and Chicago. Big transition from New York and Miami (which had European and Latin influence) — now also taking over the Midwest and West Coast.

钱从哪来：主动收入之外的被动收入

Host: A big problem for athletes is understanding the quantums of money required. Were you able to do this purely from football earnings, or leveraging other things?

Martin: The main money going into investments is from my earnings. But I also love to build passive income around real estate, or from royalties, or however I structure certain things. It's useful after your career too — build certain income streams and live off that instead of the 100k that you're earning, whatever it is. Very important to build different types of income streams.

代表机制：足球经纪 vs 商业团队

Host: Do you have football representation for playing contracts and commercial deals, and separately a business team?

Martin: Correct — and it's really important to do that. Football agencies in Europe aren't really set up for that. Maybe a great opportunity for those companies in the future to hire someone who can do that. In America it's more common. In Europe we're just a couple of steps behind in terms of long-term play.

I'm a huge believer in equity over endorsement. If people give you endorsement, most of the time the people who have equity grow from it. I don't need the money of endorsements right now because I have my football contract, so I can do the long-term play — where in 10 years, if everything goes right, I'll have a lot more than I would have now.

如何筛选投资标的

Host: How do you select those companies?

Martin: Goal normally is one per quarter. Sometimes it can be two, sometimes zero. I don't want to do a deal just to do a deal. It has to suit my personal brand, my personal hobbies. Health and wellness, for example, is something I invest heavily in — as an athlete that's very important and I can integrate it organically into my lifestyle. If it aligns, I send it to my team, they do due diligence, look at the numbers. If that makes sense, we look at what kind of structure we do in the deal.

运动员带给公司的最有价值的东西

Host: What's been most transferable from your athletic career to business?

Martin: Work ethic — very important. But also knowing that rest is very important. Don't only focus on working very hard; have the right balance. Community is very important — build the right community, right storytelling. I have a very big platform on social media where I can add value through eyeballs or credibility. But if the storytelling and community aspect isn't right, it's not really transferable to sales.

更衣室里的话题变了

Host: Do you have these conversations in the dressing room now?

Martin: There's a growing interest. More and more individuals willing to talk about it. It was always talks about newest cars, watches, clothing — kind of a macho battle. Now in every locker room there's always one, two, or three persons who have the same interests. Already more than five, six years ago. My best friend at FC Dallas did similar things — we could learn from each other, we were in some SPVs together. He actually became one of the first players in the USL who also has equity in the team.

印尼国脚：血缘、祖母与国歌

Host: Let's talk about your Indonesian citizenship — you're the goalkeeper for the Indonesian national team. Your grandmother allowed you to qualify.

Martin: I already had the option for a long time. Then when I was in the offseason in the Netherlands — three seasons ago — my grandfather just passed away and my grandmother was nearing the end. They called me: Martin, do you want to represent the national team? I spoke about it with my grandmother. At that time she was mourning a lot about my grandfather, and then she lit up. She smiled so much. We started to bring back like old memories together. She was also my history teacher — she taught me a lot about her time there, about also the little bit less nice things that she had there (she was there in the Second World War, her mother passed away in a Japanese punishment camp).

Through my youth she was my godmother, and every other week she would cook Indonesian for me. I learned the dishes too — how to cook rendang and nasi goreng and everything. When she lit up when I told her, I knew — yes, I'm going to do this, and let's make this a great adventure.

For the first time I went there in January, still in the offseason, and spoke to Erick Thohir, the president of the PSSI. After that conversation I was so convinced. Then I made my debut sadly when my grandmother passed away — but I made my debut in September in Saudi Arabia, saved the penalty on my debut. When the national anthem was playing — we actually learned the national anthem together, me and my grandmother. So I was thinking about her all that time.

It's been super nice. Very challenging with the traveling from Dallas to Indonesia — 24-hour flight, 12-hour time difference, then you needed to play two days later with a lot of pressure. But I learned so much. I'm going there again in two weeks, already looking forward to it because it's just a big family there.

Host: Had you spent much time in the country before?

Martin: A couple of times in my youth. Visited the grave of my great-grandmother. But it's not easy because it's a long travel. There's a big Indonesian community in the Netherlands because of the past — every year we went to some events.

印尼的足球狂热与联赛现状

Host: They seem football-mad.

Martin: It's definitely very underrated amongst the global sphere. Similar to Argentina or Brazil in terms of football madness. I'd love to invite you once — I can't really go anonymous on the street there anymore. Very grateful for it.

We were very close to qualifying for the World Cup — we lost the playoffs against Saudi Arabia, and Iraq. Both managed to get through the World Cup. We were in stage five, went through four rounds. I believe the whole country deserves a World Cup, because then the whole world can see how football mad it is, but also how beautiful the country is and how warm and friendly and loyal the people are.

基础设施

Since the last three, four years the league has been growing a lot. A couple of very big teams — Persib Bandung play in the AFC Champions League, so much fans. Persija Jakarta — very big club. Bali United have beautiful facilities in Bali. Still challenges within the league logistically. But two years ago they decided to have VAR, which was very important for the league to grow. Really good championship battle between Persib Bandung and Borneo last season — until the last game it could be decided.

What we can bring — because there are more naturalized players like me — is that experience of European level. And this journey gave me a sense of purpose: I want to help future generations with our knowledge. So the new Martin Paes or Jay Idzes or Ole Romeny will also come out of that.

We're also doing some stuff with UNICEF now, trying to educate in mental health, physical health, nutrition. Only the first step.

回到 Ajax：一通电话

Host: What was it like when you got a phone call from Ajax?

Martin: Very wild. I was on training camp in Portugal, had a really long flight. I wanted to go to bed with my jet lag, and suddenly I got a phone call from my agent: "Would you be interested to leave training camp to go to Amsterdam?" I couldn't sleep, super jet lagged, of course I want to do it.

The next day Ajax was playing Champions League against Villarreal. I spoke with the general manager and the goalkeeper trainer — great fit. I'm always pessimistic when a club is interested because there's so much that can go wrong, so many stars have to align. When it came closer and the clubs found an agreement, and I personally got an agreement — I went the week after, straight from training camp to Amsterdam. My stuff is still in Dallas right now.

My first ever game that I attended was Ajax against Go Ahead Eagles 7-1. Van der Vaart scored twice. I had a big shirt of him — but Van der Vaart didn't fit my shirt, so I had "V D Vaart", which is maybe a nice detail. So from that moment it was surrealistic.

One week later the first goalkeeper tore his ACL, so I just came from a two-month offseason with Dallas and had to stand there and show up directly. I play now I think 17-18 games for Ajax.

At the end of last season we had a big penalty shootout against my old club Utrecht — great to end the season with. A club like Ajax always should qualify for European leagues — we qualified for the league phase two last week. Very excited for that — one of the reasons I came back to play European football.

离开熟悉的生活

Host: What are you weighing up when you make those moves?

Martin: The older I get, the more important my life outside of football becomes. I did four years long distance with my girlfriend. I lived away from family and friends. I had sickness in the family where I couldn't be there. I wasn't there for the birth of my nephew and niece. Those things start to add up if you live far away overseas.

After four years at Dallas I was ready to come back to Europe. Some clubs were interested — but when your boyhood club comes, it's an easy decision. Luckily, because I formed a team around me, it's quite easy to move places — my team can still add the same value whether I'm there or not.

门将的自我修养：Ego、Stoicism 与 Chris Bosh

Host: How do you approach not starting every week, especially with someone like Marc-André ter Stegen coming in?

Martin: That's a fairly new feeling — I've been playing quite a lot still. But the older I got, the more I started to realize: it's more about us and less about me. I try to add as much value every week that I can to the team. If that's playing on the field, that's a little bit extra value.

My ego is not important. The team is the most important. If we win, we all eat from the wins. Last season Ajax didn't have the success that they should have — nobody really looks good from it. But now we're winning and everyone will look good from it. Everyone's transfer value goes up, bonuses go up.

I read a really interesting book from Chris Bosh — Letters to a Young Athlete. He joined as the star player from the Toronto Raptors, he joined the Miami Heat to become the third star player basically beneath LeBron James and Dwyane Wade. He did that to win championships. He's a very big inspiration the last years — I've read his book maybe four times. Leave your ego to the side, but have the confidence that if your name is set to play, you can show what you can. Have that stoic approach — control what you can control, but try to add as much value to the team as possible.

走进 Cruyff Arena

Host: What was it like when you first walked out at the Johan Cruyff Arena?

Martin: Very special moment. I played against NEC Nijmegen, my first club. My brother is a very big fan — he's in the ultras of that club. They played a very tough style last year — very much man-to-man all over the field. Interesting tactics — that's why they are very successful right now. Hard game, but a lovely feeling. We played 1-1, but I had a quite good game — like seven or eight saves. Beautiful feeling.

When you're on the sideline it looked like a massive stadium, but when you're on the field it's just the same as always — you need to play the game, not the occasion. The fans out there just seem incredible. Especially the European nights there — very special nights. Luckily this season I already experienced some on the pitch and outside of the pitch. Can't wait to have more.

一次去梅赛德斯 F1 的启发

Host: I saw a post you did with the Mercedes Formula One team.

Martin: Amazing experience. Funny — I did a Harvard Business School and one of the cases was about Toto Wolff and Mercedes-Benz and their "no-blame policy". Very interesting — not adding extra pressure to the people in the environment, the drivers or even the mechanics.

I spoke to the guy who showed us around — his name was Toby. I asked him: after the Liberty Media deal, what was the difference? He said: the key difference is the demographic that watch Formula One now. Before Liberty Media and Drive to Survive, it was 50 years old and older, and only men. Now the biggest demographic that watches Formula One is women from 20 to 30.

That's so interesting — that switch, from a community and storytelling perspective. And I think that's what I look at with TGL and the concerns with the sport of golf — it's very scary in emergent leagues to tweak traditional sports and how people view them. But the biggest wins are if you're willing to make that jump to digitalization, to feed the newer audiences and the newer generations.

Bernie Ecclestone wasn't really a fan at that time of using social media or platforms to get the story out there — but sometimes you have to be willing to make that bet against the traditional souls, and just jump into it. TGL — when the first episode came out, opinions were a little bit mixed because it was very different. But now everyone is starting to love it. Golf also has a very big YouTube scene right now, a lot of female golf influencers. You see that shift — less the older demographic only fan of the Masters, more generations.

足球里的新形式：Baller League

Host: Do you think you could bring some of that into football? Baller League with Felix?

Martin: Yeah — I invested in Baller League. Actually through a fund — they came with a co-investment opportunity. What I really liked was in Germany the community that they were building. I saw a success formula to put that into the UK and into the USA. The Apex fund already did their due diligence, so the numbers already make sense. I wanted to also have a little bit of soccer companies in my portfolio. They have great plans still.

Calma：门将造门将手套

Host: You've got another soccer company in your portfolio — you're now fronting new goalkeeping gloves.

Martin: It's called Calma. We have a couple of athletes now wearing it — me, Mark Flekken from Leverkusen (used to play for Brentford), Kjell Scherpen from Ipswich Town (the tallest goalkeeper in the history of the Premier League). We're adding some exciting names in the near future too.

If you're talking about skin in the game, there's not a bigger example. Every ask that I get — whether commercially, within sports, or philanthropic — I always get asked bring your gloves. So for me it's very organic to invest in that.

In the process of making the gloves I learned so much — a lot about what I don't want in my gloves, or don't want to come from tough environments. We have very good conditions where gloves are being made. I learned a lot about the quality of gloves, the foam, the fit. I actually took all my previous gloves — what I liked — and combined it into one glove.

Host: From the science perspective, what surprised you the most?

Martin: How small the world of goalkeeping is. Almost every glove is being made out of one of two factories. You have one factory doing everything right, and then there's the cheaper solution. I'd rather have the one who's doing everything right — it's also a little bit more expensive to make. Whether it's stitching, the quality of the foam (for us the highest quality) — really hard to get into that. Also the fits (I always wear a negative fit), the strap, the tweaks in stitches — otherwise it would tear really fast. A lot of detail. Now for the first time I'm looking at different colorways to match my goalkeeper outfit — the most important bit, the aesthetics.

1% 改进：从纵跳到复利

Host: Tell us about the 1% improvements element. Nico Rosberg talked about lengths for marginal gains — changing paint color on his helmet because it was lighter.

Martin: I learned a lot from the book Atomic Habits by James Clear. Whether it's sleep, going to bed and not using your screen time as much before sleep, drinking water to be hydrated.

For me in my training, jumping is very important. Two key factors: CMJ (counter-movement jump) — how high can you jump from hands on your side, verticality. And reactiveness — how quickly can you go up again if you land. Measured in meter per second. If I go weeks into that with my personal trainer from Ajax and we lift, then in one week my growth in my CMJ is maybe half a percent or one percent. But since I joined Ajax I've grown maybe 30 percent in my jumping, which is quite extraordinary. I only did that because every week I added 0.5% in my jumping or reactiveness.

You can apply that to almost everything. Maybe the best example is the stock market — if you invest for one year, 8% is nice, but the real growth, the hockey stick growth we call it, is if you apply that compound interest over 10, 20 or 30 years. You can apply that to your habits outside the pitch, to doing squats, jump roping.

Especially the factors that you can control. As a goalkeeper there's a lot of factors I can't control — if a ball gets deflected, if the ball goes outside the post or inside the post. But I can control having the right hand-eye coordination, I can control the squats I'm doing, I can control the jumping test, the jump roping.

Host: What's the timeframe on 30% jump gains?

Martin: Over like five or six months right now. Amazing. If you apply that to venture capital or private equity — the most exit you'll get in a five to ten year span. One of my biggest learnings with investment was: I tried to make real quick gains at the beginning, and that's where you're going to make the most mistakes. Always have long-term thinking into your investments — key.

给下一位年轻球员的建议

Host: If someone's listening going I want to start doing what Martin's doing — what's the next step?

Martin: The best investment you can make is invest in yourself. Invest into books, into studies, listen a lot to podcasts. That's what I did with Kneading Dough at the beginning — learning from the LeBron Jameses and Serena Williamses and KDs of this world. Find your niche, geek out that niche. Then always stay curious — start to ask a lot of questions to CEOs, to the GM of your club, how they are doing certain stuff, why they are doing certain stuff. Start to build your network, build your knowledge. From that, your growth will be organic.

五本书单

Host: You've mentioned a few — could you name five?

Martin: - Letters to a Young Athlete by Chris Bosh — amazing. - Basically all Ryan Holiday's books. The one I listened to the most was probably Ego Is the Enemy. - A Dutch book from a Dutch agent — The Bankrupt Football Player (De Failliete Voetballer). Hope there's a translation somewhere. - Atomic Habits.

Stoic philosophy, autobiographies, but also with a business sense.

收尾

Host: Martin, it's great. Firstly, thank you for following the show. The whole point of setting something like this up is that people like yourselves can come in and talk beyond just performance on the pitch. Inspiring to hear how you've approached it, and the success you're having while you're playing. You can do both if you apply yourself right. Thank you so much for joining us.

Martin: Thanks for having me. Let me know when you're in Amsterdam — some tickets on me, and we can chat maybe about what you're building too. Would love to hear something about that.

Host: I'll take you up on that. Thanks so much.

Martin: Thanks for your time. Bye.

item.description:
## 一个反直觉的起点：从"跑不动的前锋"到门将，是懒惰的天才时刻
Martin 在 15 岁前是前锋，一周只训练一次——因为"没有激情跑那么多"。这本该是一个天赋衰退的信号，却成了他职业跃迁的支点。**换到门将位置后，他从每周一练变成每天三练**。这里藏着一个被主流成长叙事严重低估的真相：**动机匹配（motivation-fit）的边际收益远大于努力本身的边际收益**。我们总以为"努力先行、热爱随后"，但 Martin 的案例恰恰相反——找到对的位置，努力量瞬间放大 21 倍。这与投资学里的"仓位匹配"惊人相似：把资金放进不匹配你风险偏好的赛道，再多的纪律都会被磨损。
更有意思的是隐藏的**"前锋思维"套利**：他坦言当门将的最大优势是"能看进前锋的脑袋"。这是一个跨界老兵才有的**逆向信息优势**——像一个曾在卖方做过投行的买方 PM，或者一个当过程序员的产品经理。真正的护城河，往往不来自专精，而来自"专业迁移"里那份别人拿不到的旧地图。
## 疫情、身份坍缩与 LeBron：一个门将如何用金融学的"分散化"给自己的人格上保险
最让我意外的洞察藏在他 COVID 时期的顿

item.title: [a16z] The Real Story Behind the Internet's Biggest Wellness Trends
item.dc:creator: a16z
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、GLP-1 与加密货币的"10:1 幽灵比例"：某类科技已经不是产品，而是话语基础设施

视频中 Gallup 的数据非常关键，但双方几乎是一带而过：90% 的美国人听说过 GLP-1，但只有 11% 使用；加密货币是 95% 认知、14% 使用。这个近乎一致的十倍认知—使用差不是巧合，而是一种新的产品形态的特征——它先作为"话题基础设施"存在，再作为产品存在。

传统消费品的价值链是"制造 → 分销 → 品牌 → 使用"。而 Ozempic、比特币、VR、Meal Kit 这类东西的价值链是"制造 → 舆论摩擦 → 少量高势能使用者 → 一大团讨论它的人 → 再回过头来放大制造"。它们的商业模型里，不使用产品的 89% 才是关键营收放大器，因为他们撑起了讨论、名人绯闻、订阅制媒体、Substack、播客。视频里 Ruby 提到"你的邻座朋友在酒吧和你聊 Ozempic 但从没打过针"——这些人不是"未转化用户"，他们就是最终用户，他们消费的是围绕产品的意义。

这意味着一个反直觉的判断：在今天，"产品—市场契合"已经不能只测 PMF，还得测 DMF——Discourse-Market Fit。你能不能被讨论，比你能不能被使用更重要。

二、糖 → 肽的"殖民供应链幽灵"：健康革命总带着灰市阴影

这一点两位嘉宾差点讲透但没连起来：17 世纪英国从殖民地巴巴多斯输入糖 → 引发第一波中产阶级肥胖 → 医生 Venner 在 1620 年造出"obesus"这个词 → 催生了历史上第一份饮食减肥指南。今天，中国灰市肽 → 引发 Med Spa 亚文化 → 催生了 GLP-1 主流化 → 正在催生下一轮身体道德话语。

每一次身体优化革命都有一条不能明说的殖民/灰市供应链在托底。糖是英国种植园经济，肽是深圳合成实验室经济。而两次的社会剧本高度一致：灰市普及 → 精英先用 → 阶级下渗 → 医学收编 → 道德恐慌 → 立法规范。按这个模板预测：中国灰市肽的下一站，就是 2028 年前后针对 GLP-1 长期使用的一场大型社会恐慌（骨密度？肌肉流失？心理副作用？），并催生一批"道德干净的肽"品牌，就像当年"甘蔗替代品"和"低糖运动"催生了 Splenda 帝国。

三、最令我震惊的观察：Oura 戒指假数据研究，是"副内容"（paracontent）的完成态

Ruby 提到了一个几乎被埋没的研究：受试者被 Oura 戒指喂了错误的睡眠分数，他们那一天的实际感受跟着假数据走，而不是跟着真实的睡眠状态走。

请停下来想一想这件事的可怕之处：关于你身体的数据，比你的身体本身，更能定义你的身体。这就是 Ruby 在文章里说的 paracontent 的终极版本——不是"关于内容的内容"，而是"关于身体的内容取代了身体"。你的躯体成了它自己的粉丝二创。

跨领域连接（这是我想给你的"啊哈时刻"）：这跟货币史里"金本位 → 法币 → 加密货币"的路径完全同构。数字抽象走到极致，人反而会渴望其原始对应物——所以今天使用加密货币最深的那一批人，也是最疯狂囤实体金银的人。同理，视频里 Ruby 观察到，做最多量化自我（DEXA、CGM、Oura、Function Health）的那群人，同时也是最积极去做灵气疗愈、针灸、玄学疗愈的人。这不是矛盾，这是荣格意义上的阴影回归：越把身体外包给数字，越渴望"前数字"的身体知识。

预测：未来五年，最有溢价的"健康品牌"，将同时提供血液芯片检测 + 萨满疗程，就像今天最贵的对冲基金同时买国债和加密货币。多元同时下注是 polylithic 文化的资本形态，也将是身体的形态。

四、彩蛋观察：反手机运动的视频，是用 iPhone 16 拍的

访谈里被一笑带过的一句话，其实是整期节目最锋利的一刀——那些"我戒掉手机的一天"内容，都是用手机拍的、发在 Instagram 上的。批判必须寄生在它所批判的对象之上。

把这个模式抽象出来，你会发现它统治了整个健康经济： - 反种子油的内容，跑在种子油喂饱的算力上； - 反微塑料的 KOL，包装在微塑料袋里发货； - 反 GLP-1 的"自然瘦身派"，用 GLP-1 名人的曝光度获取流量。

这带出一个残酷的结论：没有独立的反抗，只有共生的反抗。今天所有"回归本真"的健康运动，本质上都是它反对之物的衍生品市场——就像做空 GameStop 的对冲基金，反而需要 GameStop 的存在来维持自己的存在。

所以下一波"反 GLP-1"的运动不会消灭 GLP-1，只会把 GLP-1 的品类扩大。这是身体经济最深的、也最少人说出口的结构真相。

📝 转录文本

冷开场：几段预告

"Once we've reached the limits of innovation in silicone, we turn the microscope towards ourselves and try to optimize and innovate on the body."

"11% of US adults are on GLPs. 90% of Americans have heard of GLPs."

"You want to believe that you can be alio and eat salmon and rice and vegetables every day. Then you door dash food and you call it a day."

"We live in a time of cultural confusion. We are submerged by paracontent, which is content about content. There was recently a study that did blind tests on people with Oura rings and gave them the wrong number. They reported having a worse day, in spite of the actual true number being correct."

"It's not like we're going to be surrounded by like super conventionally hot people. Everyone is not going to look like clavvicular. People are just going to do increasingly like strange biohacky things."

开场：介绍 Ruby 与"副内容"（Paracontent）

Host: I've made my mission to cut through the nonsense and answer the question of what actually is happening in culture. I'm here with Ruby Justice The Low, an academic and cyber ethnographer. Um, and we're here to kind of continue a conversation that we've been having, I think, for a little bit — on how to actually kind of understand what's going on in the world, and especially on the internet, when there is increasingly no real delineation between the internet and the real world.

And Ruby, I think actually a good place to start is a piece you wrote last year on paracontent. And um, from there, I think we can kind of take a step back and get into a couple topics and things that we've both been paying attention to recently.

Ruby: Yeah, we live in a time of cultural confusion. I'm in a state of confusion. Um, so many things are happening. It's so hard to, as you said, disentangle what is real to what is merely amplified by social media or the internet or merely our small little algorithmic bubbles.

I wrote a piece — well, two pieces are germane to this topic. The first one is called The Age of Paracontent and the other one's called The Post Is the Product.

In The Age of Paracontent, I sort of present — to reduce this idea of paracontent, which is content about content. And what I notice, taking a look at video game releases, movie trailers, that oftentimes there's more content about content than content itself. Meaning we are submerged by paracontent, and we have very very small sort of pieces of thing that we can sort of glom on to — whether that be, once again, music video or a movie or even a trailer for a video game.

I think in the essay I talk about the GTA 6 trailer came out last year, and what's interesting about paracontent is that it can actually take a life of its own without actually having any material impact on the real world. People can keep on talking about a thing and can grow it out of proportion, and it could be out of measure, and it could feel real in spite of it not actually being grounded in any sort of material reality.

And so, I've made my mission — my life's work — to kind of cut through the nonsense and kind of answer the question of what actually is happening in culture.

从"异性悲观主义"到"67 现象"：现实与讨论之间的落差

Host: So the question is: how much is any given phenomenon actually happening versus how much are people talking about it on social media? How much are people making a big deal about it on social media or YouTube or whatever? And there there's so many kind of examples that we can point to, but curious if you have any favorite examples of some kind of delta between the thing happening and the thing that people are commenting on.

Ruby: Yeah. So I mean, so many things come to mind, right? Uh, some things actually do have an incident into the real world — and like "67" actually pierces through and actually becomes a behavior that we see in children.

Host: What does it mean? I don't even know.

Ruby: I famously did a piece that got me into a lot of trouble around heteropessimism as well. Um, which is this idea that like straight relationships are kind of doomed from the woman's perspective — and taking a look at content on Reels and TikTok, trying to analyze the sentiment across, you know, about 2,000 videos, people are mostly doing positive dating content, about 40%. Um, and the rest — you know, the rest that completes the half is fairly neutral.

Um, and so I'm always trying to think about: is this thing that I'm hearing just me kind of going crazy, me spending too much time online, or does it actually have any sort of true consumer behaviors behind it?

湾区叙事的错位：肽（Peptides）真的是硅谷造出来的吗？

Host: Yeah. And I think the thing we want to talk about is this whole sort of like wellness peptide sort of optimization culture.

Something that I find very funny is that a lot of times you'll see San Francisco taking credit for cultural trends that kind of long predated whatever particular cultural trend is being spoken about. And this happens I think a lot in San Francisco specifically, because we justifiably get a lot of credit for exporting kind of technological culture. And I think the way in which technology proliferates across the country and across the world is like — some interesting new trend will either start in the valley, or the founders will very quickly move to the valley after they've started their company, and kind of scale something first among, you know, the tech insider crowd, and then gradually across the rest of the country and the rest of the world.

Um, and oftentimes cultural trends are attributed to the valley too. And I think a very very interesting example of that is actually peptides. Um, and it's something that I think we sort of saw percolating as a conversation last year — where people would talk about, you know, peptide parties or peptide events or peptide influencers in San Francisco, um, or people using Chinese peptides just like in general.

But a lot of this culture and a lot of this actually started in like the American Heartland, or in, you know, bodybuilding communities in the Midwest, or something like that. Like, I remember I actually first heard about peptides in Austin, Texas when I was visiting friends there, and everybody was like, you know, going to some like med spa that was giving them Chinese peptides. So, that's in kind of the gray market quasi-legal kind of use case. And then obviously there's the medical use case of like GLPs.

Um, but I think it is this interesting thing that we're seeing where there were a lot of articles that were written especially at the beginning of the year, like even into the summer, where people were sort of talking about how like tech culture or Silicon Valley culture was exporting this trend, but really it was something that kind of like really started elsewhere and then kind of got professionalized or accelerated and managed here.

Ruby: No, absolutely. I mean, a lot of this — you know, these sort of novel techniques, whether — I think now with creatine I'm seeing it sort of pop up into my non-tech friends as well. Um, the chains of distribution are so rich and multifaceted now, that like you'll have a TikTok influencer who's doing more like classic wellness for women, who will take a product that was used for bodybuilders because she's seen on another blog that it can be used for this or that. Um, and so you really have a lot of confusion around: okay, who first came up with it, which sort of subculture did it first.

Um, when I first encountered peptides, I was thinking to myself like the thing from like biology class in high school — like the chain of amino acids, is that the thing that people are talking about? Um, and then, uh, spending a lot of time in New York, and there's a lot of these new sort of longevity clinics that have been popping up, and that's where I sort of started seeing more. And we have quite a few now, at least I would say in at least Manhattan.

Host: Yeah. And there even have been like some fun articles about like people experimenting with them — like um, Esther Marcus wrote a good piece on that.

10:1 的鸿沟：知道 GLP-1 的人和用 GLP-1 的人

Host: Um, but yeah, I think this kind of goes to this bigger question of, like: okay, obviously people are aware of peptides — either they are aware of peptides when it comes to GLP-1s and the more kind of like regulated use cases, or they're aware of maybe the gray market, they're aware of Chinese peptides and, you know, less regulated and not sort of like FDA approved for a bunch of other outcomes.

You know, people inject some peptides for like muscle repair, they inject other ones for like looking more youthful, there are other ones that exist for like memory and cognitive function, and there are all these kinds of other gray market things that people do.

Um, I think it's interesting if you look at the polls. If you look at something like Gallup — Gallup did a poll a couple months ago and they found that 11% of US adults are on GLPs. 90% of Americans have heard of GLPs. Now, I think that's interesting just because there is — as we were talking about at the beginning of this — there is this like huge gulf between the amount of people who are using the thing and the amount of people who are aware of the thing and definitely have opinions about the thing.

I also did a little bit of searching, and I asked Astra to come up with other things that poll similarly in public opinion where it's like X% is aware and Y% has used. And Astra came up with another Gallup poll for crypto, where 95% of Americans are aware of or have heard of crypto, 14% own — and that's compared to 90% of Americans have heard of GLPs, 11% are on GLPs. There were other similar ratios that came up like VR, meal kits.

So, it's funny, because a lot of these categories and a lot of these things are like tech categories where it's like the amount of users to the amount of people who know about the thing are like this kind of one-to-10 ratio. Tech culture is so influential that you can have lower incidences of the thing and then a much larger percent of people who are like, "I definitely have an opinion about this."

广告机器、名人与身体话题的放大器

Ruby: Well, I mean, that's the sort of impact I think of the marketing machine, right? I live in New York. There's every subway has an ad for every single company of GLP-1, you know, whether it's the pill or the injection. And so the brand presence is really felt strong. I think the average person knows the name of Ozempic. They might not know the company who makes it, they might know how to get it. Um, but it always is a conversion from actually knowing about the thing to setting up your crypto wallet or actually getting the subscription service.

Um, I think of different sort of bodily things in the same way — like plastic surgery as well. Like, people are very well aware because celebrities have been talking about it for a long time, but my guess is that the actual percentages must be around that same sort of coefficient.

Um, moreover, for a lot of these issues, when we talk about the body in general, people have lots of opinions, which amplifies a lot of the cultural prevalence and presence of these topics. I mean, right now, you can't really talk about a celebrity without talking about whether or not they have quote-unquote "Ozempic face." And I think that pushes the conversation even further into the mainstream, because people are having to discuss whichever celebrity they like and whether or not they're on GLP-1.

Um, and so when I think about the drivers, I think of, first and foremost, the sort of technology being developed itself. I think about the adoption in tech-centric markets like San Francisco. And then, when you think about a model for what usually makes these things kind of really stick culturally in terms of brand awareness — if that thing can be picked up by certain celebrities and actually have lots of eyeballs on it, you're going to get that big disparity between high brand awareness or high awareness in general, positive or negative, and then sort of low adoption, because you know about it, you've talked about it at the bar with your friends, but you might not have actually tried it.

人们为什么打肽？——TikTok 语料研究

Host: Why do people take peptides? I know it's an obvious answer maybe, but why do people take them?

Ruby: Well, um, let me pull out some data that I spent the week crunching on — what people are saying about peptides online, as like a first example of what we're seeing across social media.

So, this is mainly around TikTok, taking a look at around 960 videos posted between 2024 and 2026. Um, most of the content was kind of positive. Uh, people talked about their weight loss, people talked about how they felt better about themselves. Um, a lot of it was still related to bodybuilding — so you saw that connection to that original subculture where it originated. And, um, we did see an increase in 2025 and to some extent in 2026 of the sort of contestatory content, like people were like, "Oh, it's kind of a scam, it's not really working" — a lot of that more negative content sort of creeping up a little bit.

And, um, one of the most common themes we're seeing in the later years, now that it's more popular, is whether or not there's safety concerns with that. So people are comparing different products, but we're also seeing a lot of "is this okay, is this not?" — so there's these questions being asked.

Um, another very interesting kind of fact, looking at all the TikTok — well, not all the, a sample of TikTok content posted — is this idea that we're actually seeing a convergence between promotional content and personal experience. At first there's more promotional content, of course, and as people adopt more, you're getting more of these like "day in my life as a person on Ozempic," and that content starts to flip or converge with the promotional content.

And so the three main categories of content posted about peptides are promotional, personal exploration, and educational, with a fourth category at about 19% which is the skeptical warning. Um, and so we're seeing I think a lot of people looking for that education, looking for that information so that potentially they can take that next step. But I think the educational, the warning do play a big part of what people are posting about it, because they've seen the ads but they don't know — "okay, Serena Williams is using it, but should I?" — and they're going to TikTok, to influencers, to get I guess additional trust or additional information about this new pharmaceutical.

反技术的技术：Paranchnology 与"我用手机拍我不用手机"

Host: Have you looked at similar user journeys over other trends, and are there breakdowns in the kind of content or the kinds of sentiment that you see?

Ruby: Yeah. So spent a lot of time looking at a thing I call paranchnology — which is technology that prevents you from using technology. We're talking about uh, Opal, uh, Brick, uh, Yondr, Nix pouches — like all the different things that you might have around the house that prevent you from using your phone.

Um, and because there's such a big sort of, I think, competitive field right now, people are asking like which one do you use and which one has worked for you. And so you're seeing, um, everything from cyber-celibacy content, which is like lifestyle content almost, about how to live your life without your phone. You're seeing "days in my life with dumb phones" being very popular. And I think, once again, the paracontent — there's more content about not using your phone than people truly not using their phones at this moment.

Host: Well, I was going to say — how do they make the videos about them not using their phone? What are they shooting it on?

Ruby: Their iPhone 16s, of course.

Host: Yeah. Yeah. Exactly.

Ruby: Um, and they're posting it on Instagram, of course.

Host: Yeah.

Ruby: Uh, but that kind of content is very popular because, in part, much like with the weight loss, it's aspirational. You want to believe that you can stop using your phone. You want to believe that you can reduce your screen time. And there's no better way to feel that way than to, by proxy, watch someone do it.

Host: Yeah.

Ruby: Um, and so we're seeing that across many sort of what I would call like positive behavioral change that people want to do in their lives. Like, healthy eating is a very classic one of it. Um, a lot of the top influencers we're seeing on TikTok right now that we're taking a look at are healthy eating influencers, both for like simple but also healthy meals. Um, and they get lots and lots of views. To which extent does that actually reproduce as actual consumer behavior? Well, there's a big coefficient there too. It's aspirational. You want to believe that you can be Ely Marico and eat salmon and rice and vegetables every day, but then you DoorDash food and you call it a day.

减肥、瘦身与阶级：从 17 世纪的糖谈起

Host: I think it is interesting to ask, you know, are people actually getting healthier? Um, and I think there is some evidence that points to yes — on the same poll that I looked at around GLP usage, there was also information about the overall obesity rate in America, and it actually is on the decline. Um, so I think there is sort of a reason to think, okay, some of it is GLP usage, some of it even might be social media contagion, where people are getting healthier.

Maybe an even more sort of socially interesting question is: why do people want to be thin, and like, is there a history to that? How does that history even, you know, connect to technology? Like, how can we understand this moment in the continuum of thinness in general throughout history, or health in general throughout history?

Ruby: That's a great question. So we actually have these sort of two parallel histories. The one is thinness in man, and the other one is thinness in women.

Thinness in man kind of appears in the 17th century, after the English really boost the sugar production in their colony of Barbados. Uh, at the time sugar was kind of reserved for the high class. And so — take a look at any medieval image, or even any sort of medieval media or novel, you'll know like to be portly was a sign of wealth. But as sugar makes its way into England, into English society, its price decreases as the supply, of course, increases. And then you start to have sugar at your coffee houses, they start to make something called "sack," which is a sweetened wine, and people in England get bigger and bigger, and you start to see this illness called gout develop itself even in the middle classes.

And so it's Dr. Venner in 1620 who comes up with this word "obesus," you know, from the Latin, which means obese, to describe the portly or overweight man, which he sees as being sort of unhealthy. Uh, he comes up with one of the first sort of diets to get people to reduce their weights.

Um, and through that, there's been this association between unhealthiness — kind of like mental dullness as well — and fatness. Um, there's this famous line in Shakespeare, in Julius Caesar, where Julius Caesar says, "let them be fat men around me," because he's like, "they're too dull, they're not going to sort of fight against me."

Host: That's funny.

Ruby: And so what's interesting is that at the time you actually see kind of the fluctuation. You start with sort of the — let's call it — Renaissance kind of, like, if you take a look at the Venus by Raphael, like that's kind of the shape. Um, Castiglione talks about this as like the ideal of female beauty.

Um, and then as time progresses, as this ideal kind of goes down, as the elites become more aesthetic because they believe that the restriction of their urges and passions through, of course, ordered eating is a sign of control, a sign of intelligence, right? Everyone from Pope to Descartes talk about control of one's appetites as a way to display — as a display of intelligence.

Um, and so thinness becomes related to that specific idea of "I am good, I am smart." Um, and then that also gets encoded in fashion. Like, when you think about like a Victorian corset — like that is a garment that pushes you to be even thinner as an expression of that believed virtue.

Host: Yeah.

两种瘦的钟摆，与阶级向下渗透

Ruby: Um, but what's interesting, of course, is that you have kind of two pendulums at the same time. You have female thinness and then male thinness kind of going about. Um, and of course, at the time, the first person, the first people to adopt that are the elites, right — as the masses who were eating sugar sort of remaining kind of portly.

Host: Yeah. Um, and when you think about the adoption curve of some of these technologies, especially with the price early on — right, the price has decreased for GLP-1s — the first people to adopt it were the celebrities, were the people with, you know, were the elites. Uh, and we're seeing kind of the same shape of sort of trickle-down thinness happening right now with like Ozempic and whatnot.

Ruby: Yeah.

Host: And well, I think the other thing that's funny is, like — I was reading actually about the history of corsets specifically, and the way in which corsets kind of went from an elite fashion item that only very wealthy people could have to ones that anyone could have. And it was a combination both of, like, obviously the invention of the loom and the sewing machine, and sort of turning sewing machines and orchestrating entire industrial kind of manufacturing around, you know, a bunch of people sewing in the same place and creating lots of corsets.

Corsets used to be attached by, like, you know, servants or like your lady-in-waiting, who would like do the back for you and do the lattice, and then at a certain point they started designing them so you could attach them in the front, and you didn't need anybody to like help you do them.

Um, and so it's like all of these kinds of like technological innovations, both, you know, creating the factory to mass-manufacture the corsets, and redesigning the corset so it could be, you know, put on individually rather than with somebody's help — and this is way too much of a stretch, but the analogy is compounding of GLPs, and, you know, making injection easier by like giving you your GLP in a pill form or in like the pre-injected thing, rather than a needle that you have to like brutally put into yourself, or have your significant other do for you.

That is like way too much of a stretch of an analogy, but you get the point.

超模与"海洛因时尚"：90 年代的钟摆回摆

Host: Um, but um, anyway, so I think we were talking, we ended kind of at fashion, and then you wanted to talk about the birth of the supermodel and kind of how that came about and when that came about, and why.

Ruby: Yeah. And so what's interesting is we see the mores around thinness kind of shift based on the economic situations, specifically in the West, right? Um, when times get tough — we're talking in the two world wars, or even in the Great Depression — there's a cache that starts to redevelop around portliness, as a form of indication of health, because people were starving, of course.

And so in the post-war, in the baby boom, you kind of see — you know, take a look at like a beach image — people are kind of like these... they kind of gone back almost to the Renaissance idea, like these nice kind of well-proportioned bodies. Um, you know, one of the great examples of this is Albrecht Dürer's Human Proportions — like this idea of good proportions as the main definition.

Um, but as we enter the '90s, as European fashion starts to become more and more important in the American context, a new figure emerges: the supermodel. Um, the supermodel of the '90s comes to redefine femininity, specifically the shape of women, and then thinness sort of roars back onto the stage as the ideal for women — you know, famously called like "heroin chic."

Um, that becomes the sort of nec plus ultra of what the female body should be. But it is really driven by the influence of European designers who've chosen these models to represent and to wear their clothes. Um, and so, once again, it kind of swings back and forth. Um, and right now, it seems like we're swinging back into, of course, an age of thinness, as driven by this novel technological advancement in the peptide, in the GLP-1.

量化自我与"身体未来主义"

Host: Did you want to talk about wearables or kind of where that fits in?

Ruby: So wearables are very interesting. The Fitbit is launched in 2007. That same year, Kevin Kelly in Wired says it is the year of the quantified self. And so that idea of the quantified self has been with us for like 20 years. And it was a rather futuristic, prescient vision that Kelly had in calling it that. And I feel like it's only being fully realized now, 20 years later.

Um, you have the Fitbit, Apple Watch in 2015. So slowly, through proper product development and, of course, slow adoption, we're seeing more and more adults adopt wearables as a way to control, understand, and of course improve their bodies.

An idea that I like a lot around this concept of quantification of the self is the idea of body futurism by Toby Shorin. So Toby wrote this essay kind of like a few years ago and I always thought it was wonderful, where he says: once we've reached the limits of innovation in silicon, we turn the microscope towards ourselves and try to optimize and innovate on the body. And that's what he calls body futurism.

And so when I think about these dashboards that people have on these apps, or, you know, waking up going to your longevity clinic, um, even something like "don't die" — this is body futurism. And the idea that you can use the same tools we did to, you know, make amazing phones, amazing tech, and sort of revolutionize our external world — now we're trying to revolutionize our corporeal world, like our internal world, um, and our organs and whatnot.

微塑料、种子油与"聚合器"的兴起

Host: Yeah. I well, I think the quantified self thing is a really interesting call-out, because that's an example of something where Silicon Valley actually did export it to the rest of the world. Like, as far as my knowledge is, and as far as I'm concerned, like as you pointed out, Kevin Kelly sort of articulated this trend that had been going on among biohackers and maybe a much smaller contingent of people in the valley and, you know, in the Bay Area.

Um, and then it gradually became a much much bigger thing, and now anyone, you know, can sign up for something like Function Health or like Superpower. Um, anyone can get a DEXA scan, or anyone can use like a CGM. I know a lot of people who just kind of buy CGMs that are intended for people with diabetes, and just, you know, use them to monitor their blood sugar and what spikes their blood sugar throughout the day, and what should they be eating, what should they be avoiding.

Um, there was also — this is maybe one step further than quantified self — but there was the group that I think was majorly funded by Nat Friedman and some other bigger names in tech, who took samples from, you know, a bunch of different food products, a bunch of different delivery items from restaurants, and tested them all for microplastics.

So it was like packaged meal from Whole Foods, boba, a protein bar, you know, all of these things. And they partnered with this lab in Austin, Texas called Light Labs. And they did all of these microplastic tests on them and open-sourced all of the results and released all of the results.

I think there was — and it also set off a kind of wave, which was — they found a bunch of microplastics in like baby food. And so this one mom went off and she was like, okay, now I'm going to test a bunch more baby food and baby formula. The medical consensus is still out on: are microplastics bad for you or not, but a large enough contingent of smart people in the Bay Area think that they are bad.

And so I think, like, paying attention to that is very interesting. And also, like — okay, well, what actually would be downstream of a bunch of people in the Bay Area thinking that microplastics are bad? You're probably going to see way more advancements in consumer testing or lab technology as a result. You're probably going to see more, you know, microplastic-free product.

Um, as a result, I think similar kind of logic might apply to other food groups, or other things that people are trying to avoid too. Like, there's an entire anti-seed-oil movement. There are all of these food groups that get vilified, justifiably or not, and kind of get a — yeah, just like a movement built around them. And you can really kind of see that reverberate culturally and have a real outsized impact when it's maybe a much smaller but very loud and committed group that's advancing these things.

Ruby: Absolutely. And I think this speaks for the need — and this is definitely going to emerge, if it hasn't emerged yet — like an aggregator of whatever your specific thing that you don't want to do is — microplastics, seed oils. Like, we're going to see these aggregators, like goods that are certified, like novel ways of doing like green or organic for these things, and sort of self-run or group-run aggregators who've done the certification and the test and are going to keep on running it on their own, and probably their members are going to pay a fee to know that the thing that they are — good.

I mean, anecdotally, if you go to Whole Foods, the water bottles are glass. Like, you're already seeing that, I think, in once again, sort of like the yuppie elite portion. Um, but I think that we will see that kind of trickle down as people become more and more aware.

Host: I just wanted to demo that we only have glass water bottles at the a16z office. Um, but yeah. So I see it. I also make a point to only drink out of glass.

Ruby: Same thing — you know, that since plastic-free since 2023 was the goal on in our household.

主流饱和信号：蛋白质、Ray Peat 与"真相党"

Host: Yeah.

Ruby: Um, I mean we've — I think we're seeing this. And once again, another thing that I think is very interesting is taking a look at social media and how the tide is turning on some of these things. Um, and we can track, for instance, like the Ray Peat diet. We can track sentiment around it in the same format that we've seen for these peptides — the sort of educational content, the lifestyle aspirational content. And based on the distribution of these different kinds, we can kind of see how mature a lot of these trends are.

Um, and then usually, once it's kind of further onto the adoption curve, you kind of see the backlash — like you see the truthers come out, like "oh no, Ray Peat diet is bad" or like "actually you should be eating more microplastics."

Host: That's going to come in — exact. No, that's — well, that's the inevitable thing. The thing that I find very funny is, like, I think you've already started to see that happen with seed oils, where people are like, "no, actually, like, ultra-processed food is like really good for you." And like, you see certain trade groups kind of trying to make the point that seed oils are good for you, and it just, like, kind of looks ridiculous.

There also — to the seed oil point — there are, there's now like seed-oil-free packaging on different snacks and things that you can buy. So that has started to make it into the mainstream. I think with seed oil, I think with microplastics, uh, the Ray Peat diet — like those are all way too early still. I think for the backlash — with the — actually, I think the seed oil thing, we have seen backlash to that.

Ruby: But a good signal that something has kind of made it to the mainstream is when a characteristic of a food based on one of these trends, right — we talked about peptides, we talked about wellness and quantification. Um, part of the wellness/quantification is like protein maxing.

Certain foods have always had the same amount of protein, but that same number is now prominently featured on the yogurt, because people are now much more aware of how much protein they're consuming. It has not changed. The product is the same. But from a marketing standpoint, it makes sense for the brand, for the company, to highlight it, because they know people are now looking for it.

Host: Yeah. I think, well — I think protein is actually such a good example of this because it's also sort of starting to fall victim to what you called out, which is people just, like, feeling utter protein fatigue. They're like, "I — like, you know, my water doesn't need 20 grams of protein in it, and my, you know — just like let me drink normal beverages please."

Um, so, like, I think people are starting to kind of like resist having protein shoved down their throat a little bit. Um, but but yeah, that's a great example of just utter mainstream saturation. Um, it — like, protein — also, it's interesting because it's gone through a lot of cycles. Like it's been introduced in various forms — like there was the Atkins diet, then there was keto, now it's just like get a bunch of protein, like, you know, 2x your body weight in protein. It is quite funny.

加速还是反转？——历史钟摆与 Oura 环研究

Host: Um, I think, maybe to close out — we've kind of been just discussing and dancing around as well, which is: when it comes to peptides, when it comes to looksmaxing, when it comes to all of these things, are we just going to accelerate forever, or are we going to see some kind of backlash and some kind of reversal? Um, and if we do see a reversal, why would we see it? Um, and just wanted to get your take there.

Ruby: Yeah. So, I mean, the interesting thing is, from a historical perspective, right — I think we're at a similar point where England was with the increase of the sugar consumption, where we've been kind of kneaded in processed foods, we've even fast food, fast casual. Um, I think we will see, for the foreseeable future, a big push to revert back and to sort of see health as a form of virtue, as a form of sort of, you know, radical self-care, as a proof of someone that cares about themselves. Um, and potentially also this association, as I said, with Descartes with intelligence itself. Um, and I think that culturally that's not really going to change for the foreseeable future.

Now, what I'm seeing on the quantification part — which I'm seeing two things kind of break apart — there was recently a study that did blind tests on people with Oura rings and gave them the wrong number as to what their sleep score was. And when the number was lower or negative, they reported having a worse day, in spite of the actual true number being correct. And so a lot of these devices, if ever their numbers are incorrect, have a noxious effect on your felt health, at least for that day.

Um, and I think I'm seeing a lot of people push back against the quantification, adopting more of these like holistic or esoteric ways of knowing the body. I'm seeing a lot of growth in holistic practices — from like Reiki, or acupuncture, or other forms of healing — in the same group of people who previously were doing a lot of quantification.

And what's interesting when we take a look at trends these days, is actually because we're in — let's call it — purely, right, polylithic culture, there's multiple kind of frameworks. Um, we're going to see both, I think, a growth in quantification and more esoteric ways of knowing the self at the same time — whereas I think previously we were kind of all swinging in the same way. We're, I think, going to see both at the same time.

结语：AI 时代，身体成为最后的战场

Host: Yeah, I definitely agree with the esotericism point. Um, and I think it relates to acceleration, but it's a different kind of acceleration, where it's not — it's not like we're going to be surrounded by super conventionally hot people who all look the same and all have the same plastic surgery, or all of the same, you know, Botox done, or all injecting the same peptides. Like, everyone is not going to look like clavicular. People are just going to do increasingly like strange biohacky things, and I think we're just going to see increasingly extreme optimizations happen.

Um, I kind of do think the next one is going to be in sleep. I think — and going back to your Oura point — like, I've been talking with some hardware founders and some founders who are building wearable devices that allow you to get what feels like the equivalent of a full night's rest in 4 hours or something like that. And I think people who are trying to kind of achieve longevity — not through necessarily living longer, but just having more hours awake in the day — um, I think is like something that we're going to see more of.

So, so I agree with acceleration, but it's not going to look like people getting hotter, or people, you know, even necessarily having healthier outcomes. It's just going to look like people optimizing themselves in the direction that they want to, with increasingly fringe and extreme technology.

Ruby: Toby wrote his essay body futurism kind of before the big AI boom. Um, and his idea was more that once we run out of things to do with silicon, we would move towards the body. I think now, in the age of AI, what we're seeing is — in an age of great abundance, in an age of like potential total automation, the only thing we have to actually improve potentially is our body. So I think we're going to be focused on it for quite a bit of time, for the next few years.

Host: Next few years — hopefully we have more than a few years left. I agree. Um, well, Ruby, thanks so much. Uh, this was awesome. Uh, we'll do this again very soon.

Ruby: Thank you so much.

Host: We're going to work on these legs. That's right. I call it my funky leg workout. I mean, just feel the groove. All right.

## 一、GLP-1 与加密货币的"10:1 幽灵比例"：某类科技已经不是产品，而是话语基础设施
视频中 Gallup 的数据非常关键，但双方几乎是一带而过：90% 的美国人听说过 GLP-1，但只有 11% 使用；加密货币是 95% 认知、14% 使用。这个近乎一致的**十倍认知—使用差**不是巧合，而是一种**新的产品形态**的特征——**它先作为"话题基础设施"存在，再作为产品存在**。
传统消费品的价值链是"制造 → 分销 → 品牌 → 使用"。而 Ozempic、比特币、VR、Meal Kit 这类东西的价值链是**"制造 → 舆论摩擦 → 少量高势能使用者 → 一大团讨论它的人 → 再回过头来放大制造"**。它们的商业模型里，*不使用产品的 89%* 才是关键营收放大器，因为他们撑起了讨论、名人绯闻、订阅制媒体、Substack、播客。视频里 Ruby 提到"你的邻座朋友在酒吧和你聊 Ozempic 但从没打过针"——这些人不是"未转化用户"，他们**就是最终用户**，他们消费的是**围绕产品的意义**。
这意味着一个反直觉的判断：**在今天，"产品—市场契合"已经不

💡 创造性洞见

一、真正的护城河不是模型，而是"权限拓扑学"

Levie 抛出一个看似普通的观察，却隐藏着一个惊人的悖论：当研究员想象"个性化模型"时，他们下意识地假设自己就是用户——一个拥有全域访问权限的人。但真实世界里，一个律师的知识边界是由他今天早上被加入/移除的项目组决定的。

这里有个反直觉的洞察：企业级 AI 的最大瓶颈不是智能，而是"访问控制的动态拓扑"。每一秒钟，组织内数以万计的权限关系在重构——某人被加入一个诉讼、某个文档被移入法律保留、某个客户关系需要"中国墙"隔离。这意味着，未来最有价值的不是"更聪明的模型"，而是"能在毫秒级理解组织权限动态的中间层"。

这也解释了为什么 Levie 说"研究员想让模型跟他们一样"——因为研究员活在一个低摩擦的权限世界里，而企业活在一个权限每秒都在变化的动态图谱里。这种认知落差，就是 Neolab（应用层新贵）的全部机会。

二、"Work Slop" 的真相：这不是内容危机，而是"信任协议"的重写

大家在讨论 AI 生成内容时聚焦"质量"，但 Levie 揭示了一个更深刻的层面——当我们看到别人的 PPT 时，我们其实一直在做一件被 AI 打破的事：把内容当作"这个人能力和思考深度"的代理指标（proxy）。

跨领域连接来了：这与经济学中的"信号理论"（Signaling Theory，Michael Spence 提出）完全同构。Spence 说文凭之所以有价值，不是知识本身，而是"完成文凭"这个行为向雇主发送了"我能坚持"的信号。而 PPT、备忘录、邮件长期以来都是"我思考过、我理解、我投入了时间"的信号。

AI 生成内容摧毁的不是"内容"，而是这套人类花了几个世纪演化出来的隐性信号系统。所以我们不是在讨厌 slop，我们是在哀悼一个刚刚失效的信任协议。未来 3-5 年，社会必须重建一套新的信号系统——可能是"你对 AI 输出的编辑轨迹"、"你的提问深度"、或者干脆是"你的现场反应能力"。

会议里那种"当场被问倒"的尴尬会重新变得神圣。

三、隐藏在对话表面下的分形结构：Levie 的整个策略其实是一个"托尔布思-反托尔布思"博弈

表面上 Levie 在夸赞"Cloudforce"营销，讥笑"toll booth（收费站）"这个词。但如果你把整个访谈作为一个系统看，会发现一个惊人的分形自相似：

  • 模型层：Anthropic/OpenAI 试图向下延伸做应用 = 收费站扩张
  • 应用层（Box）：想抓住模型不愿做的"工作流桥梁" = 反收费站
  • 企业内部：CIO 想要用开源模型摆脱模型商锁定 = 反收费站
  • UI 层：横向 chatbot vs 垂直 agent = 收费站 vs 定制路径
  • 知识工作者：AI 让人试图"直接输出结果"跳过流程 = 但组织权限体系是最终的收费站

每一层都在重复同样的博弈：抽象层的通用性与场景层的特殊性之间的张力。

这与生物学中"红皇后假说"（Van Valen）惊人地相似——所有物种都必须持续演化才能保持相对位置。Levie 真正的战略洞察是：在 AI 时代，"离客户更近"不是一个位置，而是一种永动状态。谁能持续在"通用能力"和"特殊场景"之间找到新缝隙，谁就能吃到 diffusion 带来的红利。

四、一个让人意外的元观察：Twitter 悖论

Levie 提到"关注 20 个账号能让你的职业领先/落后一年"——但真正意外的洞察藏在他说"最遗憾的是脑细胞"那句自嘲背后：

Twitter 现在是全球唯一没有 AI 中介、由原始个体判断构成的实时精英信息网络。所有其他信息渠道（新闻、报告、搜索）都已经被 AI 摘要、聚合、过滤过一遍。这意味着在 AI 时代，最稀缺的资源是"未经算法压平的、活生生的高质量个人判断流"——这恰好是 Twitter 在娱乐化后依然保留的核心资产。

结论反直觉：AI 越发达，Twitter 这种"低算法密度的社交网络"反而越有战略价值。它成了 AI 时代的"人类判断黑市"。
