The idea was: enterprises would be moving from on-premises systems to the cloud, and they would need a better way to store, share, collaborate, and manage all of this unstructured data — their corporate documents, financial documents, marketing assets, research materials — in the cloud securely.

第一次 AI 冬天 (2015–2018)

We had been flirting with AI products and experiences really since 2015. If you remember, the first rise of — at least in modern times — the AI winter happened in like the 2015 to 2018 period. Which is like, we think it's going to happen now, and then it didn't.

That was a period where these very early AI models were showing us signs: okay, if you looked at an image and you could classify the image, well, that's pretty useful if you're in an enterprise — because now maybe you take all of your image data and label it, or maybe you'd OCR something and pull out the text. That's enormously helpful.

The problem was: insanely expensive, and you had to have a model for every single use case — required a hyper-trained model for each workflow. So we shelved it.

ChatGPT 时刻

Few years later, started paying attention to the GPTs. We had some hackathons where people were like, "Oh, we could do type-ahead in one of our note-taking products." Those were early versions. We did some early work in text detection and classification which helped with security use cases.

Then obviously ChatGPT moment hits, and that was the big head-exploding moment. If for no other reason than they figured out a form factor that opened up everybody's mind to: oh, these could be interactive systems that you just ask a question, get an answer back, of increasing complexity and length.

We looked at that very quickly, jumped all in. We did the whole company pivot — like everything was exactly academically what you should do. We had a team carved out, we put the best people on the team, we met every day, looked at the updates, and slowly but surely built out what today is our AI stack and basically the Box Agent.

Box 的核心用例

For us, the use case is very straightforward. We sit on hundreds of billions of files. Every single one of those files contains critical information for an enterprise — contracts, research files, marketing assets, loan documents.

The problem is they rarely know what's actually inside of it. Unless you literally look at the document and search and find it, you just don't know what's inside.

So now agents can go and basically be farmed out to answer questions about that data. They can pre-process it and extract metadata from those documents and turn it into structured data. You can use agents to automate steps and workflows. So we've built a platform that basically lets you deploy agents against all of that unstructured data.

For most of the world, code is a utility. It's just trying to accomplish something, automate something, put an interface up so somebody presses a button and moves to the next step.

内容作为"信号"

At least the way society functions and the way our brains work at the moment — maybe this changes — when you get a presentation from somebody, there's still this association: I'm trying to decide if I can trust that person to execute on that thing, deliver that result, or understand that topic.

Right now we're going through this evolution: What is the person's role? What is the content a proxy for? Is it a proxy for how much that person knows? Is it a proxy for what we think they can execute on? We're in this very messy period.

六、Harnesses（工具编排层）

Let's talk about harnesses. How does the Box —

Aaron: Great transition to harnesses.

Speaking of calculators, let's talk about harnesses.

Aaron: This is back to the neolab / applied layer. There's a bunch of things we know about our file system, permission structures, our search engine that — by all means, we would love all the labs to train on our understanding of this because it would only make external agents as good as possible. We always talk to labs, "Hey, we'll give you as much data as you want about how the system works."

But let's just say that aside — we have a lot of depth of understanding of: what do people do in Box? How do they search Box? How do they decide, when they look through 10 files, which is the one to pick? What is their internal calculus or heuristic on figuring out the most relevant document to look at?

We know all of that, and we've built an agentic harness that attempts to understand that set of domain understanding about our system. It has access to our search system, our file system, a bunch of mechanisms for pulling out just the text of a document, just pulling out chunks, doing embeddings on the fly.

Effectively, it's a harness for asking questions of a large data set. In my Box account I have — I don't even know the latest number — but on the order of tens of millions of files. It's like everything that has ever accumulated over 20 years. But I can now ask any question of all that data set using the Box Agent. It does multiple searches in one, re-ranks it, quickly pulls out the most relevant information, and in some cases reads the full document.

We compare that against: well, what if we just gave Claude our API, or gave OpenAI our API? And we see meaningfully better results on accuracy and latency, because we know exactly how to tune it for our workflows.

Evals

What evals matter the most to you?

Aaron: I have a couple funny personal ones I keep track of, of my own use cases. But we have hundreds of different tests we do on every single model. We actually have two evals at the moment:

  1. Complex Work Eval — a set of domain-specific work in life sciences, financial services, public sector, tech, etc. Given these five documents and this set of problems, what would your answers be? We test every single model against those with our agent.

  2. Holdback Eval — our Box instance and how Box employees use their data. Then we eval every model again on that.

We keep track of all incremental progress — we see when things move by half a point in terms of model improvement. Then we roll out default models based on different cost and accuracy thresholds. And we let customers choose any model they want from effectively our model garden.

模型比赛：Race Perspective

What's your current view of the race — where all the horses are in terms of model performance on your use case?

Aaron: They more or less closely correlate to code, with one exception: in some of our use cases, Gemini is disproportionately better than what you'd see from coding. It might be better tool use — given the Gemini ecosystem and what they need to build for. It solves a strong set of general knowledge work use cases as well.

But mostly correlating to code. So Fable 5.1 was clearly state-of-the-art and the best model we've seen. There's obviously rumors about other models, so we'll see how the race continues. When you look at GDPval, Mercor has their APEX eval — these will all generally follow the coding models. It's neck-and-neck on Grok, Muse, the Fable class, GPT-5.6, whatever they're building next. It's a total race right now.

客户选择

Do your customers typically express a preference on which model, or do they just use your default?

Aaron: By volume they use our default, because it's easy and works extremely well. But by volume of tokens, most goes through our workflow agents or data extraction. That's where customers actually do evals — saying, "Okay, I want to really make sure that at this cost profile I can get 98% accuracy on data extraction." That's a place where we have an FTE that goes in and helps understand your data environment, tests against five different models, and then you're basically at the mercy of the eval.

七、开源模型的采用

What are you seeing in terms of the adoption of open-weight models in your customer base?

Aaron: Higher than people think, lower than what enterprises actually want, and much, much, much, much lower than what it'll be in five years. Some mix of that would be the message.

Is it primarily cost driving that decision?

Aaron: I have to probably attribute 30-plus percent to just the sexiness of "I want to try GLM."

Yeah, I've heard CIOs of Fortune 500 companies say, "We're playing with open source here" — and I look at that and I'm like, well, Gemini or Muse would have been just fine at that particular cost profile you're trying to do. Or probably even 5.6 Luna, or Terra, or whichever had the crazy discounting they just did — it probably would have been totally fine. But you want to be able to be like, "Okay, I'm a little hedged." It's cool — we're at that phase still.

Over time, it stands to reason you'll see meaningful different costs, because you'll be able to peel off workloads that only make sense at grinding down to the cost of inference — in which case open weights will have the economic advantage.

Right now there's this challenge — sometimes it's more token-inefficient, sometimes randomly (I've heard stories) it'll just speak Chinese mid-chain, so you're like, "Okay, well, that'll be weird for a bank." So funny. We need to work on some of those things. But long-term, you're going to peel off those workloads.

Decagon 的悖论

One of the more interesting posts on this that I totally subscribe to is Jesse at Decagon. Did you read that post about this paradox — we're going to see closed just continue to go exponential, but what's going to happen is each use case that matures you can peel off to open source. Once you have stability in that use case, it starts to make sense to veer it toward an open-weights model, assuming one of two things is true: (1) it's actually literally cheaper, or (2) having some post-training gets you X% more performance.

You will be in a reality where — this is going to be very confusing probably for the press more than people in the Valley — the revenue of Anthropic, OpenAI, etc. are off the charts, but somehow open weights is also growing exponentially. You're like, "How is Open Router so fast? The pie is growing so fast."

There's an interesting duality — not even just "rising tide lifts all boats." It's: no, we either use Fable or 5.6 for orchestration and then farm out all these long-tail tasks to a cheaper model. Or the opposite: you have an orchestration agent that by default does the cheaper stuff, but occasionally sees something too hard and pops it out to one of these heavier models. You might have blended 50% spend on each, but 10 times the amount of tokens on the open-weights model. Everybody's winning, but there's an interplay between why they're winning.

八、记忆、个性化与持续学习

I'm curious how you think about memory and customization or personalization, and where that's going to go. It seems today the dominant architecture is still RAG-based — you get fancy on the RAG, but it's still context lookup, where the weights themselves aren't fundamentally changing. If I listen to my friends at the labs, like continual learning — this idea that the model's weights should adapt as it gets to know you.

We had Engram on the podcast. I don't know if you know Dan —

Aaron: I just got introduced to him. I listened to the podcast. I would have loved to have been the fourth person in the room.

They're working with customers to help bake in some of the context into the weights themselves. What direction do you think this is going to go?

Aaron: You're catching me at a time right before I'm actually doing my call with Dan, so I wish I could have talked to him first and then I'd have a way more eloquent answer.

I'm extremely fascinated by the approach. I have no reason for not wanting it to work and exist. We live in a world at Box where we see the high degree of complexity on permissions and access controls and data that tends to be the rub on a lot of these types of approaches.

权限的复杂性

I'm going to put Engram aside — I'm sure they've thought this through — so I'll talk more generic philosophically.

Sometimes you talk to a researcher who imagines the world working the way they work: "I'm a researcher, I have access to everything, and if I had a model that was trained just on my world, this would be amazing."

And then you're like, "Let me introduce you to a lawyer." The lawyer has this tiny little access point of just the five projects they're working on, because somebody one door over is working on the competitive project to another company in the space that they can't have any overlap with. There can't be a single document that passes between those two walls — they have to be hard barriers.

Sure, you could still train a model just for that one user, but what happens if every single day they get added or removed from something that adds important context to what they need to understand?

I think there will probably be breakthroughs in continual learning that resolve this. This is why previously it was just — there was no way you could pull this off 5 years ago because it would be insanely expensive, impossible to wrap your head around how those access controls are supposed to work. But obviously, as the cost curve goes down, as open weights get cheaper, smaller, faster, better, this becomes super interesting.

什么进 Context vs. 什么进 Weights？

One thing on the podcast that I found very fascinating — I just need a T-chart, honestly — is: what is the decision point of what goes in context and what goes in the weights? You have to be a little thoughtful about where the massive performance gain by baking in the weights is. There's probably some incredible calculation of when the rate of change of the data is not so fast, but the upside of the weights dramatically changes the accuracy of the model — you'd have to land on some rubric like that.

If you could wave a magic wand, it almost seems like — I think Karpathy has said this in some prior interviews — if you could almost remove all the memorized information from the models and just have it encapsulate the specific reasoning capabilities, like the ethos of how we do things at Sequoia, and then you have all the actual content in a lookup system. That almost feels like, if you could wave a magic wand, what the system would look like.

Aaron: That's super interesting. The question will be: how much are enterprises different at that level, versus is it actually their literal IP that is what makes them different? How many different types of styles of execution are there in the world, versus, "No, it's just the depth of knowledge about that particular legal case and how I apply it to this other project I'm working on" — that's where so much of the value sits.

Wait till my Zoom call with Dan, and then I'll really know the answer. But I'm a fan — because no matter what, at a firm level, there's probably ways to take this approach.

I'm a big fan of what Trajectory or Applied Compute doing, or Prime Intellect — because there's no question that if you're Eli Lilly, you want a model for how you do drug discovery, and that probably does need to go farther, deeper, or more specific than what you're getting off the shelf. There's not a lot of church-and-state problems for drug discovery workflows — they probably want as much information available to as many people as possible.

It's going to be domain-specific. You're going to have different outcomes based on which vertical or type of use case, and where the firewalls need to be in that process.

九、Box Labs 的研究领域

You hinted at the beginning that there's a Box Labs. What type of work is Box Labs doing?

Aaron: It's the equivalent of Box Labs — I don't know if we've used capital L yet — but basically it's our applied AI team.

What research areas are most interesting to your team right now?

Aaron: The biggest areas — of the continuum of engineers, there's some cluster that's more on the research bent. Of that cluster, the things we spend time on are still at the applied layer, but a lot around: how do you take agents and make them another 10 points of accuracy improvement given X problem? How do you build a map of the problem set with a given set of data to best execute on that task?

We spend a lot of time on that style of work. We have a team working on how you do effectively, at the agent level, at the harness level, some form of auto-research on hill-climbing on accuracy of answering questions or sets of problems given a set of client data.

If you're a bank, you have a bunch of loan documents coming in — these are 100-page documents — whether you're getting 70% accuracy with an off-the-shelf model or 97% is obviously a world of difference in whether you can actually automate that process. Somehow you have to hill-climb from the base model to the 97%, and there's a lot of work going into the system to pull that off.

两件必须做的事

If you're in our contemporary group — you built a SaaS platform and have some set of data and workflow your customers operate in — there's effectively two things you just have to do. Anybody attempting to do one over the other is going to lose:

1. Build an agent that is insanely great at your product. That agent has to be provably 10 or 20 points better than an off-the-shelf agent at using your system — not because it's hobbled the other side, but you're so eval-maxed and tuned to your particular workflow that you can improve your system.

You probably, because you understand your domain (unless you're totally asleep at the wheel), have use cases that no one has thought to build products around, because you talk to customers every day and see what they run into. You're like, "Oh, we could just have our agent go do that for you."

I've had at least a dozen — I probably talk to a couple hundred customers a year in variety capacities — at least two dozen times where the customer has a use case that is a breakthrough moment for me.

Example?

Aaron: Unfortunately, since you put me on the spot, I don't know if my example will pay off the level of excitement I just had. But — a customer had this idea of wanting an agent in the background trying to figure out when documents met their governance policies. Like, does something need to go into some archive, or into some legal hold?

Oh, cool.

Aaron: See — exactly, that was exactly the voice I was worried about. No, no — I meant cool sincerely.

Aaron: Okay, I believe you. Listen, you do enterprise, so I think it was at least half-serious.

Imagine you're an enterprise. You have a head of compliance and head of governance. They can only be overseeing the whole enterprise — they've never been able to be everywhere at once. Now imagine they could sit next to the employee and basically say, "Oh, you're about to go do something that breaks our governance policy." What if there was an ongoing agent that automatically was just like, "Nah, that's going to break your governance policy"? Instead of the user having to predict or understand this stuff.

If you have an agent within your product, you're going to identify sooner and better than the rest of the market — and do things that maybe would be impossible to do off-platform.

2. Go headless. You literally have to make sure your APIs are exposed to Claude, ChatGPT, and all the different platforms. Either a direct way into deterministic APIs so those agents can use your APIs to make calls via MCP or whatever, or at least make your agent be headless and be exposed in those systems.

The only reason maybe this is a hard debate is you have to make sure as a system of record that you can find a way where commercially it makes sense on the other side and is valuable and interesting.

为什么很多人错了

The reason a lot of people got that wrong, that weren't in these companies, was underestimating the amount of new use cases that are total upside — complete whitespace opportunities for these systems of record.

In the Salesforce example, I use Salesforce today probably by an order of magnitude more than I ever have — because I MCP into it via Claude or ChatGPT. I'm always asking questions about the data inside of our CRM system.

And do you think that means the systems of record become more toll booth businesses to make sure they're capturing the opportunity?

Aaron: I don't love that term, because no one's had a good experience at a toll booth.

I love "toll booth."

Aaron: Yeah, exactly. You love it more than governance agents. So I would say — because they have a depth of purpose of organizing the workflow, managing the data, securing the data, providing guardrails — then you just need to have some kind of volume-oriented business model on that other side.

If you're solving real problems for customers, it'll just make money. This is so cheesy, but I've told LinkedIn product managers I'd probably pay 10x more for LinkedIn if I could just MCP into it. If I had a way of always understanding, "Okay, this CIO is doing this thing and I need to reach out." Whatever — take my money.

These systems actually have a tremendous amount of value based on the data that they have, and customers will absolutely find some way to reward you for that value creation if you're doing a good job.

十一、产品 UI 的未来

Super interesting. Maybe related — let's talk about product UI. Big generic chatbot / chat box agent — is that going to be the dominant UI for how people are using AI in the future, especially at the application layer?

Aaron: This is why I think the applied layer has so much room to run. The universal chat system that you ask a question, get an answer back, or it does work in the background — obviously that's going to be a mainstay. That UI will always exist. The horizontal products will have it, the vertical products will have it, everybody will have it. Just like your product has a search box — obviously it does.

That's always going to be here for one-off asks of an agent, or go find this thing, or answer this question, or produce something for me on demand.

But most of the enterprise is made up of processes and workflows that are just happening behind the scenes. Sometimes with computers running things, sometimes with other people, sometimes they should be happening with people but you could never afford to have them happen with people so they just didn't happen.

That's a slightly different metaphor than a chatbot. I want agents in the background to do things for me — read every contract, look at every log, triage every security incident. Instead of me chatting, maybe I'll chat as a means of doing catch-up. I want a dashboard. I want a workflow. I want a queue. I want a task list.

横向 vs. 垂直

The challenge becomes: does the horizontal product take on every one of those components and manifest every one of those experiences? In which case, you'll start to be like, "Man, that thing is really heavy — this is no longer this simple, easy, delightful thing anymore."

Then the vertical players actually understand the process and can manifest all the right buttons and tabs and the names of the things for that particular workflow.

As you have agents doing more work in the background, more async work, that leans more toward the applied companies that can understand those workflows and processes.

You'll have these in every field. Certainly, we already know how they're going to look in legal with Harvey, Lor, etc. We're seeing them start to emerge in security. We've seen them emerge in the long-running coding agents with Cognition and Factory.

Ultimately, in five years from now, I would bet 90% of all tokens in the enterprise are things that a user never kicked off, and they just see a result. They see a task show up and they have to review it — it's just happening.

十二、AI Diffusion 与代码之外的世界

Let's talk about AI diffusion. Coding agents — it was like, boom, January 1st 2026 happened, and the fastest diffusion of anything into the economy we've ever seen has happened. The diffusion of the rest of the AI magic into the rest of our jobs seems like it's been a lot slower. What are your thoughts, and where do you think we're going to see faster diffusion?

Aaron: You always have to compare and contrast coding versus everything else to really understand the dissimilarity.

为什么编程如此适合 AI

In coding — and this is back to the utility point on slop — the utility of code is almost 100% represented by the amount of text you can generate. Obviously an insane amount of value went into the text — knowledge, expertise, meetings, everything — but ultimately the text is the thing that produces the program that is actually the thing you're trying to do.

If you had the world's greatest programmer, and they never had to sleep, never had to eat, they could intuit what to build and just sit on a computer all day long — your value creation would be 100% correlated with how many hours they could sit at that computer and type code. Lines of code — ideally, good code — is the thing most correlated to whether you produced software that people wanted.

So it's all text. The models are hyper-trained on these. Everybody in AI labs treats coding as a competitive benchmark to constantly try and exceed. They get to do their own evals on it every single day because they are the ones coding the models themselves.

It's the most technical audience of all time. When they deploy an agentic system and run into a bug or a problem — like some MCP server comes back with "connection invalid" — they fix it. They know how to triage the problem. They don't call IT. They just, "Oh yeah, no, I didn't open up that port. Sorry, I'll go fix it."

So that's like five things. And maybe the sixth — it's a very high-paying vertical. It's automatically valuable if you could get 10% or 20% productivity gain, let alone 5x productivity gain.

与其他领域对比：法律 vs. 销售

Take those five or six things that coding has as beneficial properties to automation, then compare that to every other form of knowledge work. You'd probably have a histogram — I don't know if anybody's published this, maybe you can — of similarity to coding, and what are the domains that start to look less and less like coding as you scale out.

Legal is kind of interesting, because there's a lot of value creation to somebody sitting at a computer reviewing legal documents, writing legal documents, processing large amounts of information. Okay, so that's blowing up.

Then you go down the list. Let's take something like a sales rep. So much farther down the list in terms of likeness. The sales rep's value creation is basically convincing an external customer to buy software or technology, or a Caterpillar truck, from them.

Let's say we brought the world's best automation to them. First of all, they'd have to figure out how to technically wire it up. They'd have to make sure they give it all their data. But no matter what, they're rate-limited and constrained by: Did the customer respond to them? Do they want to meet? Can they meet next Tuesday, or can they meet today? Does the customer have budget?

That's maybe the entire continuum right there — of knowledge work (this isn't even touching working with Adam). One end: somebody rate-limited by so many external factors. The other end: somebody who could sit at a computer all day long and just type text. That's your ability to basically automate things.

GitHub 与数据可访问性

For the real world, we have to bring intelligence to these workflows in ways that somewhat feel like the shape of their workflow, somewhat feel like the shape of their work, and then find a way to deliver the change management, deliver the implementation, get data into a format and environment that actually works with these systems.

Asterisk: one of the other big things is if you go to most engineers in 2026 — maybe like minus two months ago, given the latest phenomenon — but the code's in GitHub. You just connect to GitHub. Remember, there's this period when you launched a coding agent, there was no sign up or register — it was just, "Give us your GitHub."

That doesn't exist in knowledge work. There's no "give us your GitHub" for knowledge work. There's like, "Give us your Box"—

Well, Box customers have a much easier time with all this. Unfortunately, we're only $1.3 billion in revenue run rate — that means there's a lot of people not using Box. What are they using? Their data is in on-premises systems, legacy file shares, legacy infrastructure, enterprise environments that don't talk to agents particularly well.

Think about that distinction between implementing coding agents versus everything else.

访问控制的差异

Even something you'll fall asleep about — access controls in the enterprise are totally different. In coding, you get access to basically most of the stuff ever relevant for your job. In knowledge work, you're like, "Hey Sally, can you open up that file share for me? Can you open up that project because I didn't get access to it?" How do you make sure the agent has access to those sets of things?

All of that work has to get done. Two things to prepare for:

  1. Silicon Valley has to prepare for diffusion taking a lot longer than they think — or than I'll say we — but really they, because I know how long it'll take.

  2. The good news is this is all correlated to the applied layer value creation. The companies that will have the patience, the full domain expertise, and just the sheer work ethic — because it's not like the floodgates open, you have to go pound pavement and get out there — that will be the applied layer.

This represents a trillion dollars of applied-layer AI value: how do you go get the technology to the lawyer, or to the sales rep, or to the life sciences researcher, or to the person who runs the customer support team? That's all opportunity right now that exists.

Because our customers can't possibly entrust us with their data security and compliance if we don't take that seriously. So we're always going to have a little bit of a discount on the productivity because of where we are in the stack and what we do as a business.

Jealous of being able to be fresh in that.

另一面：竞争的密度

On the other hand — for every great idea, it's instantly five competitors. We didn't have that problem. We had a good couple years where we could just grind on our product and experience. It wasn't like every three days you were like, "Oh, Sequoia funded this thing, Benchmark funded this thing." We weren't going nuts with that.

Now we had our own version of that — so at the time I probably was going nuts, but in retrospect it wasn't worthy of going nuts. Now it's like, "Oh man, this is a real race in every one of these markets."

Totally.

决胜的关键

I'm probably pretty consensus on this: in a world where AI builds things so much faster, then probably the shift moves to whoever can actually get it to the customer is in the best position.

It's fun talking to founders that are pilled on that. Scott or Matan — they get the mandate. They're just like, "This thing is going to be an enterprise diffusion play. So you have to get it to the enterprise."

Anybody who mistakes the mandate right now — you're just going to lose. It's game over. Sorry. There's quite literally trillions to trillions up for grabs at the applied layer, and the companies that know how to build the teams and get to the enterprise will be the ones that win. Obviously guaranteed.

Well said, Aaron. This is a very fun conversation. Thank you so much for joining.

Aaron: Thanks for having me.

[music]

## 一、真正的护城河不是模型，而是"权限拓扑学"
Levie 抛出一个看似普通的观察，却隐藏着一个惊人的悖论：**当研究员想象"个性化模型"时，他们下意识地假设自己就是用户——一个拥有全域访问权限的人**。但真实世界里，一个律师的知识边界是由他今天早上被加入/移除的项目组决定的。
这里有个反直觉的洞察：**企业级 AI 的最大瓶颈不是智能，而是"访问控制的动态拓扑"**。每一秒钟，组织内数以万计的权限关系在重构——某人被加入一个诉讼、某个文档被移入法律保留、某个客户关系需要"中国墙"隔离。这意味着，**未来最有价值的不是"更聪明的模型"，而是"能在毫秒级理解组织权限动态的中间层"**。
这也解释了为什么 Levie 说"研究员想让模型跟他们一样"——因为研究员活在一个**低摩擦的权限世界**里，而企业活在一个**权限每秒都在变化的动态图谱**里。这种认知落差，就是 Neolab（应用层新贵）的全部机会。

item.dc:creator: 邦妮區塊鏈 Bonnie Blockchain
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个被忽略的隐喻：Brian 的人生轨迹本身就是一份"分布式账本"

看完这段访谈，我最意外的发现是：Brian 的成长路径和 Bitcoin 的运行逻辑惊人地同构。他描述自己作为孩子时"晚上 10 点到凌晨 2 点最有活力"——那正是全球异步、去中心化的工作节律。当校园（一个中心化机构）在白天运转时，他却在"另一个时区"里独立挖掘知识区块。他后来发现的 Bitcoin，本质上就是把这种"个体在非同步时间里独立创造价值"的模式，编码成了协议。他没有选择加密货币，是他的神经系统提前选择了它。

阿根廷不是他的间隔年，而是一次"预训练"

大多数人把他 2010 年前后的南美之行解读为"迷茫期的漂泊"。但换一个视角：阿根廷是一个天然的宏观经济实验室——恶性通胀、外汇管制、跨境汇款困难，全都在一个国家里同时发生。他在这里读 Ayn Rand 和 Milton Friedman，然后回国读 Bitcoin 白皮书——这三份材料的化学反应，需要一个"具身的语境"才能被激活。这让我想到一个跨领域的类比：语言模型的能力涌现，往往不是因为参数变多，而是因为训练数据里恰好出现了几个关键的"连接性文本"。阿根廷就是他个人认知里的那份连接性数据集。如果他直接从硅谷跳到 Bitcoin，可能永远无法真正"感受"到货币主权对普通人意味着什么。

最深的洞见藏在"命名哲学"里——它其实是一套认知劫持理论

他谈 Coinbase 命名时说的那段——"Google 其实是个烂名字，Slack 几乎是它自己意思的反义词，但一旦被赋予意义，你就不再想起原义"——表面在讲 marketing，实际在讲神经可塑性和符号劫持。这与银行业的悖论形成惊人对照："Bank"这个词也被劫持了。它早已不意味着"安全的资金保管"，而意味着一套受深度监管、优先服务监管者而非客户、以未经许可的杠杆运转的系统。Brian 说"fractional reserve 是一个奇怪的历史遗留物"——他真正在做的不是发行新货币，而是在替一个已经语义漂移的词做一次品牌重定义。这也解释了为什么银行游说团体如此激烈：他们不是在保护业务，是在保护那个已经被劫持了 300 年的词的语义主导权。

一个反直觉的观察

他 20 岁时的目标是"10 万美元被动收入 = 自由"，但成功后他发现：不工作反而无聊、缺乏意义。这几乎是所有 FIRE 运动追随者不敢承认的真相。但更有意思的层次是——他推翻这个目标的方式，恰恰复用了 Bitcoin 的哲学：价值不来自"存量"（余额），而来自"流量"（交易/贡献）。他的人生结论和他所建帝国的技术哲学，是同一个命题的两种表达。

📝 转录文本

开场：从害羞少年到硬碰硬华府

As a young person, I actually had to call my mom and dad and tell them I was quitting my job to go do this crazy thing that they had never heard of.

— Coinbase. Coinbase is Coinbase. Coinbase.

Coinbase.com was available for \$1,700. So, it was a reasonably priced. I remember thinking, uh, I'm not sure I love it. All right. Temporarily, I'll pick Coinbase and I'll choose a better one later. Did I know if it was going to be a successful company? No.

What was holding you back? Why didn't you go all in?

Self-doubt. Part of me was like afraid of looking stupid. I was very introverted as a kid. I was probably a little on the autism spectrum. It can be a superpower.

You are crawling on the floor crying.

There's some dark days. They were saying, "Shut down Coinbase. It's over. Give the money back." My phone just starts ringing non-stop. I had never had the experience at that time of having thousands of people angry at you at the same time, you know, spewing like the most hateful things you could imagine.

Genius Act has passed and the banks are coming back with Clarity.

Some of the banks still hate it and are trying to kill it. I don't think banks should be lending out people's deposits without their permission. That's like this weird historical artifact that happened a long time ago. Banks have become so heavily regulated. They're like quasi government entities. They become enmeshed with government. There's only a few people who can sustain this such high level of regulation. Then your first priority is to your regulator. Your second is to your customer. And that's why most customers are dissatisfied with the current financial system. People should support a level playing field where everybody can compete.

Very little is going to get done actually in DC without concerted effort and a large constituency. And you have to make it a priority. And it's not their fault. It's just there's a lot of things going on in the world. There's wars. There's trade debates happening. There's AI.

Would you make a prediction?

I think the consensus view is... Great to see you. Thank you for flying in. I appreciate it. Yes.

采访开始：一个像漫画一样的故事

Bonnie：I'm Bonnie Chang and I am with Brian Armstrong, the co-founder and CEO of Coinbase. Brian, good to see you.

Brian：Yeah, thanks for having me.

Bonnie：So, the more I look into your story, the more I feel like I'm reading this comic book. There's this shy kid that created Coinbase and then took on Washington, took on Wall Street. It is a fascinating story.

Brian：I've never heard the superhero idea, but you know, if I had been bit by a spider or something. Anyway, I like the reference.

童年：害羞、Linux、深夜的能量高峰

Bonnie：Yeah, I want to know how shy were you? Let's I want to establish this main character, right? How shy were you? Do you have like a most painfully Brian shy story?

Brian：Well, yeah. I was very introverted as a kid, I would say. And I was never very good at speaking to people and communicating my ideas. I was kind of awkward or shy. And the thing that I found that I liked doing was playing with computers. And so I would usually stay up late most nights learning how to install Linux or read books.

And it was actually kind of a problem because I would feel the most alive and energized at like 10:00 p.m. to like 2 a.m. every day, and then I would be kind of a zombie at school the next day.

And it might seem strange because now I feel pretty comfortable talking to people, but it's like anything — if you practice it a thousand times, you can get better at it. And I don't know what the lesson of that is other than maybe for kids who feel awkward or shy, it doesn't really hold you back. You can learn how to do anything if you want to.

Bonnie：So your parents actually brought back this secondhand computer with German keyboard.

Brian：Yeah, I mean you did your research. Yeah, we would just kind of find used computers and pick them up at garage sales and I think I had like three different computers in my room at one point just kind of building the hardware and learning different operating systems.

So yeah, that was something that I gravitated towards. I mean, yeah, I would say like I was probably a little on the autism spectrum, too. I don't know if that came up in your research, but I never formally got diagnosed, but I've taken these tests where I'm like, "Yep, that's pretty clearly what I had."

And you know, it can be a superpower actually. But it can also hold you back in some ways. I think it's net positive actually to be somewhere on the spectrum. In my case, what it allowed me to do was like I kind of had infinite ability to just concentrate on one thing for a long time if I got interested and excited about it.

Sometimes with people I couldn't read their emotions or how to react and I would have — later I developed all these like coping mechanisms where I would sometimes ask people "well 1 to 10, how happy do you feel about that?" you know, cuz sometimes I'm trying to read somebody and I'm like, they seem really excited, but they wouldn't be that, you know.

So, there's lots of things like that I learned as coping mechanisms over time.

家庭与价值观：来自 IBM 母亲和工程师父亲的底色

Bonnie：So, your parents, I saw them in the documentary. They seem like wonderful people. Your mom used to work at IBM. Your dad was an engineer. What did you pick up from them, each of them?

Brian：Well, growing up in the house, there was a lot of focus on math and science and academia in general. So I did learn from them to study hard, focus on school.

I would say the other thing they really taught me indirectly was my value system, right? Which I probably didn't really appreciate at the time. It came from them about trying to create something useful in the world, trying to give back, trying to contribute. And really just treating others the way you wanted to be treated.

Someone might say these are like Judeo-Christian values. And I also went to like a Jesuit high school that had some of those values as well. So at the time I didn't feel like it was influencing me, but I think later in life it probably did.

宠物、企业家启蒙与"影响力可以规模化"的顿悟

Bonnie：One interesting thing is you had a green iguana.

Brian：Yes.

Bonnie：Dogs and cats. So, a lot of animals in the household. What else did you have?

Brian：Well, the iguana's name was Spike, I believe. And I mean, I was interested in having pets. That was fun. I actually at one point later in life had a pet tarantula, which was fun. I think it'd be cool someday to have like a pet raccoon or something, but it's actually illegal in most jurisdictions, so I haven't found a way to do that yet.

And that's just kind of fun to have like living things around the house that you're taking care of.

I was also interested in business, so I'd read like the business section of the newspaper every day.

Bonnie：When you were a kid.

Brian：Yeah. And I don't know why, but I thought it was fascinating. I remember seeing these folks like Bill Gates and Marc Andreessen and people like that and Steve Jobs — like these were kind of my heroes, you know? I don't know why, but I just thought it was really cool what they were building and they were changing the future and you could build this thing and people all over the world could use it at the same time. That just felt like so exciting to me.

And I remember I learned how to build some of these early websites and I'd put something on the internet and I'd go to sleep and I'd wake up in the morning and there was like a hundred people had clicked this link. And I just for some reason that gave me so much energy and excitement. I was like, this is cool. Like I can build something that helped 100 people while I was sleeping. You know, in real life I'd have to go meet a hundred people in one day and do it every day over and over, but this could scale. This could scale impact.

And so I was just tinkering early on with these little websites and these little businesses. Like a friend of mine in high school, we started reselling computer hardware and we built a little e-commerce site for it. So I didn't really know exactly at that moment that it was going to be a career of doing technology entrepreneurship, but the signs were there in hindsight looking back.

大学：家教网站与"何时坚持、何时放弃"

Bonnie：And you built a tutoring website.

Brian：Yeah, that was when I was in college. I started a tutoring company with one of my roommates at the time. It started because in college I was sort of trying to have like a job to earn a little bit of extra money. And you know, you could work at like the library on campus and maybe earn like \$10 an hour or something. And I realized that if I was to tutor high school kids in the area around the university, I could make like \$60 an hour instead of 10. I mean, it was 6x.

So I started off tutoring high school kids in the area and then — I guess my mind went back to this kind of scalability thing. How do I scale the impact? So I realized at a certain point, okay, instead of me doing the tutoring, why don't I build a website to help match high school students and their parents with tutors — and started just at the university I was at, Rice University. Eventually it scaled to a bunch of other universities. So eventually we had thousands of tutors helping high school kids and we were trying to take a small cut.

It was an interesting business in the sense that I had trouble scaling it beyond that. So I would say it was like a base hit, but it was not scaling and becoming really successful. And at some point I had to learn how to go build a more successful startup.

Entrepreneurship is tough because you always have these moments where it's like, okay, I've been working for years on this thing — is it one or two more fixes away from really taking off in viral growth, or is it never going to do that? And the difficult thing is you — no one can really tell you. And so, you have to know when to double down and when to quit.

Eventually I realized, okay, I don't think I was going to find a way to scale it. I put the project pretty much on autopilot and I decided to go take a job — this was eventually at Airbnb — where I got to learn a little bit of what a fast-growing startup in Silicon Valley actually looked like.

So, in hindsight, I can paint all these pieces and point to how they have a through line, but at the time, I really felt lost. I felt like, oh, my startup is a failure. I really didn't know what I was doing. So it only makes sense in hindsight.

阿根廷之年：一份意外的宏观经济预训练

Bonnie：And you went to Argentina when you felt lost.

Brian：I did. I took kind of a gap year, you could say. I wanted to sort of travel abroad and experience a bunch of different cities and I did fly down to Argentina and lived there for about a year.

Bonnie：Why Argentina?

Brian：Well, I had been to Europe, I had been to Asia. My plan was actually to go to Buenos Aires and then spend like a month in each major country in South America just because I hadn't really been there. But once I had set up things in Buenos Aires and had a bit of a home base, I was like, I don't know, it's going to be a pain to move and try to set that all up again and find another condo or apartment. So I just stayed there. I did a couple trips to other places, but mostly stayed in Argentina.

And again, in hindsight 2020, I saw a country that had gone through hyperinflation. That later helped me understand the power of Bitcoin. I saw some of the challenges that people had of moving money cross-border. So these were all pieces of the puzzle, if you will.

And I ended up reading a lot of books when I was living in Argentina too — some Ayn Rand and some Milton Friedman and sort of libertarian economics — and these things all primed me for when I later read the Bitcoin white paper in December of 2010.

从 BitBank 到 Coinbase：一场关于命名的心理学课程

Bonnie：Let's fast forward Coinbase. Before Coinbase, it was BitBank.

Brian：That's true.

Bonnie：Why did that not work out?

Brian：Well, it's a funny story. So, yeah, I always liked these names for companies that alliterate and have a repeating consonant sound like PayPal or Coca-Cola — you know, they seem to stick in people's minds and they're very memorable.

So when I was first brainstorming the name and I came up with this site BitBank — the double B — and I applied to Y Combinator early on when I had this prototype I had built nights and weekends while I was working at Airbnb. It would eventually become Coinbase, but at the time, BitBank.

So I applied to Y Combinator and I got accepted, and one of the first things that the lawyer they have on staff said was, "All right, about the name — it's actually illegal to have the word 'bank' in your name if you don't have a bank license." And so, "You're going to have to pick a new name." And I was like, "Darn, I really liked that one."

But I ended up doing a quick search. The criteria that I had for the name were:

  • Ideally it would have an alliteration sound, but that wasn't a requirement.
  • Can you say the name in a loud bar and the person can actually hear it and know how to spell it?

Because imagine how annoying it'd be if you start a company and for the rest of your life people are like, "What is that called?" And you're like blah blah blah. And they're like, "How do you spell that?" So it can be something that's not really ambiguous how to spell it. You can hear it in a loud bar and spell it.

  • Something that had like eight letters or less.
  • It had a positive connotation.
  • It hinted at what the thing actually did, but didn't have to be explicit.

So I did a search of these different domain names and Coinbase.com was available for \$1,700. So it was a reasonably priced. I remember thinking, "I'm not sure I love it." Because once you have a name for a company like BitBank, it sticks in your mind and you begin to feel resonance with it. So any other name that you see, it's like, "eh, I don't know, it's not that good."

So eventually I was like, all right, temporarily I'll pick Coinbase and I'll choose a better one later just because I have to keep making forward progress. So here we are 14 years later. And now I like it.

Bonnie：The world loves it.

Brian：It sort of goes to say — I think the first time you hear any name, it doesn't mean anything to you. So a lot of times when people are thinking of naming a company or a product, they're comparing it to something they like Google or something they know really well. But you have to put yourself in the mindset of seeing Google for the first time without knowing what it was.

The word, if you think about it, Google is actually a bad name for a company because — first of all, what is "goo"? It's like slime or something, right? And Google sounds like the word a baby would make, like "goo goo gaga" or something. It doesn't — that's not a serious name for any company. It doesn't really hint at even what it does. And it's actually a bad name. But the thing is, once you imbue it with meaning, it means something else in your mind and you actually never think about it.

Like the product Slack, for instance — it's a workplace productivity tool. Why the heck would you name it Slack? It sounds like "slacker," you're not working. It's literally almost the opposite of what you want. But nobody cares. You think Slack is like a different neuron in my brain firing. It has nothing to do with the word slacker.

So these names can grow on you over time as you imbue them with meaning, which is really the art of marketing.

全职 All-in：自我怀疑与 Paul Graham 那 15 万美金

Bonnie：Wow, beautifully said. Now after Y Combinator, you were still working for Airbnb. Is that correct?

Brian：No. So that was before I got into Y Combinator.

Bonnie：Right? So you were working on Bitcoin product and working for Airbnb.

Brian：Nights and weekends. You have to be careful — if you're ever at an employer and you're thinking about doing a startup, make sure that you don't do it on company time and don't do it on company laptop. So I'm always careful to say — and this is true — I built it on my own computer nights and weekends. And then applied to Y Combinator and they got accepted, and that's when I left Airbnb.

Bonnie：But I want to know why — like what was holding you back? Why didn't you go all in?

Brian：Oh, right. Until the Y Combinator acceptance.

I mean, basically it was self-doubt, you know? I didn't know. I had read the Bitcoin white paper. I had gone to some meetups. I couldn't stop thinking about it. I was like, this seems really powerful. And what if this happened? What if — is the government going to try to shut it down? Or could it get enough traction? Is it going to be for payments or trading? To me, it was like something I couldn't stop thinking about. So I had to try doing something. But did I know if it was going to be a successful company? No. I had no idea.

I mean, part of me was afraid of looking stupid, right? I actually — I remember I told several of my friends this idea in 2011 timeframe and I was like, "I've been reading a lot about Bitcoin. I think it's kind of interesting and what if this could happen." And some of my smartest friends were like, "I don't really get it. It doesn't make sense. Why would anybody use like a currency that's not issued by a government? That doesn't make sense."

So Peter Thiel has this great concept of — startups need to be contrarian but right. If you're doing something that's obviously right, there's probably other people already doing it. You know, it's like cloud computing — yes, okay, Amazon came up with that whatever 15 years ago. So now you can't just be contrarian for being contrarian's sake either. You can do all kinds of contrarian things. But it has to be contrarian and right, which is the sweet spot where you're like, "I think this could be big, and most people don't think that."

That is the sweet spot of maybe something you should go pursue because you could be early and right. And so that's exactly where I was with Bitcoin.

And so I don't think — by the way, if I had not gotten accepted to Y Combinator, which came with a \$150,000 seed check, I'm not sure if I would have had the confidence to quit my job at Airbnb. Because this is going to sound dumb too, but as a young person, the factor that was in my mind was — I actually had to call my mom and dad and tell them I was quitting my job to go do this crazy thing that they had never heard of.

My mother and father were always very supportive, but they were a little more risk-averse. And I think they would have said, "Really? You're gonna quit another job to try another startup? Like, don't you want some more job security and maybe try to save some money for the future and buy a home someday and have children or something like that?"

So I remember getting that Y Combinator check, and Paul Graham was somebody who I really looked up to, and he was willing to take a bet on me and say, "Maybe you're not crazy. Maybe there's something here. I'll give you \$150,000 to check it out."

And so I called my parents and I said, "I'm quitting my job, but this really cool guy, Paul Graham, gave me a check for \$150,000." And I don't know why, but that was enough to get me to go take the leap.

Bonnie：It's important that someone believes in you.

Brian：It is. And I think a lot of people, if you ask them, "What's the most impactful thing someone's ever done for you?" — it's somebody who took a bet on them when they maybe saw something in them they didn't even see in themselves. And that's a powerful moment if you can try to recreate it for the next generation.

崩溃的一夜：一万张未读工单和响个不停的电话

Bonnie：I saw that you were overwhelmed by support tickets once and you were crawling on the floor crying. I'm not sure if it's true. When was the last time you cried like that?

Brian：There is some truth to that. I don't remember if I actually did cry or I just felt like I wanted to cry, but startups have lots of ups and downs. There's some dark days. Sometimes you feel like, oh my gosh, it's going to work — like everything's happening — and the other days you're like, it's over, we're screwed, I can't see any way through it.

So I remember there was a rough day where — this was probably in the first couple years of Coinbase — we had some bug that emerged on the website where people's balances were showing wrong.

Bonnie：Yeah.

Brian：And we started to get lots of angry customers. This was when we had maybe five employees or something. So there was like 10,000 unread support tickets, 20,000. We couldn't get through them fast enough. And it was spilling out onto the internet too, where people on Reddit and forums and X were saying, "Shut down Coinbase. It's over. Give the money back. They're all thieves. They stole our money."

And I had never had the experience at that time of having thousands of people angry at you at the same time on the internet, you know, spewing like the most hateful things you could imagine. And now, you know, I feel like I've developed thick skin, but at the time that was very stressful.

And I remember somebody put my personal cell phone on the internet because they were like, "Well, if you're not getting a response from customer support, call the CEO. Here's his number."

Bonnie：Oh, no.

Brian：So my phone just starts ringing non-stop. We're in the office. We're all sleep-deprived. It's like 2:00 in the morning. We've been working around the clock trying to fix this bug. And I remember I needed to get some food delivered to the office so we could all stay up that night and work. And my phone's just ringing non-stop, but the delivery guy is downstairs. So I'm like, "Oh my gosh, I'm going to have to answer my phone to see if I get the delivery guy."

And so I answer like a random call, and it's like, "This is a reporter in Japan. Is this Brian Armstrong?" I'm like, "No, wrong number." "Okay, you know." And after picking up a couple calls, it was like, "I'm the guy downstairs with your food." I was like, "Okay, cool. I'm coming down."

Anyway, there were moments like that where I was like, "Oh my gosh, we're failing and now everyone's mad at me and why did I even do this?" And then those were the moments where I wanted to like cry on the floor. But then, after a few minutes, I would pick myself up and say, "All right, what's the next step? How do we solve it?"

There's always something you can do to try to make forward progress. And you just have to be relentlessly resourceful and figure out some way to move the ball forward.

GENIUS 法案、银行的悔意与稳定币的奖励

Bonnie：You just said developing thick skin. Now GENIUS has passed and the banks are coming back with Clarity. Now do you feel like at the time they feel like they've given away a little too much? That's why they're fighting now. What is happening?

Brian：Yeah. So the GENIUS Act did create a lot of regulatory clarity for stablecoins, and it included something I think is really good for Americans, which is the ability to earn rewards on their stablecoins. Why shouldn't people be able to earn more money on their money in a free market?

I do think the bank lobby in particular, and a couple of the big banks, had a lot of buyer's remorse about the language that got into the Clarity Act — or sorry, in the GENIUS Act. I'm still not entirely sure why. I think it's basically a competitive pressure thing where they have large payment businesses and they thought stablecoins — especially if they were paying rewards to customers — they would feel more competition from that.

That to me is not a good reason to oppose legislation. People should support a level playing field where everybody can compete. They made other arguments about community banks, about how these companies paying rewards should have a bank license — which doesn't make any sense because, you know, fractional reserve...

Bonnie：Sounds like you've heard it all.

Brian：So I think at the end of the day it was basically an anti-competitive thing that they were doing.

But going forward now to Clarity, they've made an effort to try to put that in a better place for them. We've pushed back and tried to defend our customers' rights. The Senate ultimately did a good job of brokering an agreement there, and it landed in a place where — at least in the draft of Clarity that we've seen that's going to come up for a vote I think next week in the Senate — the ability to pay rewards on stablecoins is preserved.

You can't pay them on idle balances, but as long as the customer has some sort of activity like a trade or a payment in a relatively short period of time (which they'll determine later), then you can still pay rewards. And so that was the compromise. Some of the banks still hate it and are trying to kill it. Other banks have come out and endorsed it — like BNY Mellon and Goldman Sachs and Fidelity.

So I think there's enough momentum. There's also a bunch of reports have come out that have showed that the community banks aren't going to be affected by this. Their deposits have grown along with stablecoin growth. So I think there's a good chance we can get something over the line. And if not, the regulators have said they're going to publish rules to create the clarity anyway.

Bonnie：Would you make a prediction — what's going to happen next week?

Brian：I mean, I'm always cautiously optimistic on this. I think the consensus view is that it's less likely to happen. I actually would take the other side. I think it's more likely to happen, but in politics, nothing is guaranteed. There could be something next week that breaks out that has nothing to do with crypto or the bill at all that just derails something. But I'm always an optimist, and we'll keep showing up and defending our customers' rights to get regulatory clarity in various places around the world. Some will go faster and some will go slower.

银行的历史遗留问题：部分准备金、信贷与"未经许可的借贷"

Bonnie：Let's play devil's advocate. Let's say the fund actually goes from fractional reserve to fully backed stablecoin. And it feels like a safer system, right? But where does the credit come from now?

Brian：Well, first I like that you said "moving to a safer system," because I think actually a lot of people don't understand — they just think, "Oh, banks must be safe because it's regulated." The reason they're so heavily regulated is it's fractional reserve. They don't have all the money there.

As you pointed out, a regulated stablecoin under GENIUS is required to have a 100% reserve in short-term US treasuries — like less than 90 days — which are kind of the lowest-risk asset you can imagine.

So long way of saying: I do think stablecoins are more safe. Now, I don't think that means there's going to be an evaporation of bank deposits. I think the banks have a big role to play in this. I think stablecoins are going to be used for payments, for things online. I think the banks are also going to keep growing and do what they do with bank deposits.

But just to push on this a little bit — I think having credit available in the market is important. Obviously, we need ability for people to borrow to go build things. I don't see why customers need to have their funds lent out without their permission or knowledge. And this is kind of the bank business model, right?

Many of our customers, for instance, on Coinbase, they choose to put their funds into lending products to earn yield. They can do it with DeFi. They can do it in traditional finance methods. I think there would be a market-clearing price of how many people want to earn this amount of yield and how much of their deposits they opt into lending out.

I don't think banks should be lending out people's deposits without their permission. That's like this weird historical artifact that happened a long time ago. They said, "All right, we're going to allow you to lend it out without their permission, and maybe there could be bank runs periodically or these things might fail, but in exchange we're going to give you this high level of regulation."

I think it created some dangerous outcomes — unintended consequences, somebody might say — in the sense that banks have become so heavily regulated, they're like quasi-government entities in some cases. In some countries, they're literally government-owned. In America, I'd say they're like quasi-government entities. And they become enmeshed with government because the bar of regulation is so high.

Then the other thing that happens is innovation slows down. If your primary person you're trying to satisfy is your regulator and put the customer second — because it's almost like an oligopoly, there's only a few people who can sustain this such high level of regulation — then your first priority is to your regulator, your second is to your customer. And that's why most customers are dissatisfied with the current financial system.

华府现实课：政治不是靠"教育"就能推动的

Bonnie：Now you're talking about regulators. You are going to Washington quite often these days. What is it about Washington that surprised you the most?

Brian：Well, wow, lots of things. I think when I first started going to Washington I was really just trying to be like an educational resource. Crypto was a new technology. To me, it was clear we needed legislation to pass, and I assumed that if I could just be a helpful resource when they needed some information, that would all happen.

Turned out that was not the case. Very little is going to get done actually in DC without concerted effort and a large constituency. And you have to make it a priority. And it's not their fault. It's just there's a lot of things going on in the world. There's wars, there's trade debates happening, there's AI data centers or whatever the flavor of the day is that people get excited about. And so they're overwhelmed with priorities. There's people coming in and out of their office all the time trying to convince them that something should be done. And so they're not going to do it unless there are real upsides or downsides in terms of the next election. Is there a real political constituency behind it?

And so anyway, to make a long story short, we had to get organized as a crypto industry. That meant organizing Stand With Crypto and funding that to help organize a grassroots movement with millions of voters who wanted to elect pro-crypto candidates. It meant — for better or worse — money is a factor in American elections with super PACs and hard money donations. It meant doing more of that. It meant writing research papers and sort of the supply chain of research reports and they go through think tanks and judges and everything.

And so we had to build a real political operation along with many other companies in the space to help stand up for our customers' rights. I believe that we have that in place now and it's been a major benefit to getting some rules passed here hopefully.

尾声：如果能回去见 20 岁的 Brian

Bonnie：And you're doing a great job. So before we wrap up, one last question. When you were younger, you said you wanted \$100K passive income and that is, you know, financial freedom for you, and now look at what you've achieved. You know, Coinbase has mega market cap and you're obviously very, very successful. Now, looking back, what would surprise the 20-year-old Brian if you could meet him?

Brian：Yeah. Well, in my mind at that time, work was an obligation, and I felt like with financial freedom, that it would allow me to then choose what I wanted to do every day.

The interesting thing about achieving some level of financial success and not needing to work is that it turns out it's quite boring and unfulfilling to not work. You know, you don't necessarily want to have to do a job that you don't like. But once you feel like you can choose a job — and you can actually do that almost at any stage. I actually recommend people do it sooner.

Like if there's a job that pays 40% less, but it's actually a bunch of really smart people in a field that you are really passionate about — you know, look, it's easy for me to say this here, but even when I didn't have any money, I would say take the job that you're actually passionate about with smart people. You're going to learn, you're going to grow, you're probably going to make more money also, by the way, just because if you're passionate about it, you'll be better at it. You can become the top 1% in your field.

But yeah, I think that's the biggest thing I learned: if you reach a point where you don't have to work, you almost have like an obligation to society to try to keep giving back — and you'll feel a sense of fulfillment if you keep working on something you believe in that you think will help the world.

So that's what I'm trying to do with Coinbase. That's what I'm trying to do with other companies I've incubated and started and invested in. And I hope to keep doing that for as long as I can.

Bonnie：That was beautiful. Thank you, Brian, for having me in your beautiful office.

item.description:
## 一个被忽略的隐喻：Brian 的人生轨迹本身就是一份"分布式账本"
看完这段访谈，我最意外的发现是：Brian 的成长路径和 Bitcoin 的运行逻辑惊人地同构。他描述自己作为孩子时"晚上 10 点到凌晨 2 点最有活力"——那正是**全球异步、去中心化的工作节律**。当校园（一个中心化机构）在白天运转时，他却在"另一个时区"里独立挖掘知识区块。他后来发现的 Bitcoin，本质上就是把这种"个体在非同步时间里独立创造价值"的模式，编码成了协议。**他没有选择加密货币，是他的神经系统提前选择了它。**
## 阿根廷不是他的间隔年，而是一次"预训练"
大多数人把他 2010 年前后的南美之行解读为"迷茫期的漂泊"。但换一个视角：阿根廷是一个**天然的宏观经济实验室**——恶性通胀、外汇管制、跨境汇款困难，全都在一个国家里同时发生。他在这里读 Ayn Rand 和 Milton Friedman，然后回国读 Bitcoin 白皮书——这三份材料的化学反应，需要一个"具身的语境"才能被激活。这让我想到一个跨领域的类比：**语言模型的能力涌现，往往不是因为参数变多，而是因为训练数

item.title: [Bits + Bips] Oil, Bonds and the AI Slowdown in One Week

item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、这场"AI减速"论战的真正主角不是安全，而是资产负债表

表面上，Jacob Coxin辞职、Dario"我们必须给前沿踩刹车"、Sam Altman附和——像是一场关于人类命运的道德觉醒。但如果你把时间戳叠加在Anthropic的S-1准备窗口上，画面立刻转为另一种叙事：这是一次典型的"从收入增长不惜代价"切换到"现金流开始有意义"的姿态调整。

Jordy的观察极其锋利：Anthropic正处于IPO静默期，一位在职六周的"前员工"发声，公司不但不撇清，反而附和——这不是失误，而是一次被授权的信号泄露。对照Meta的沉默（因为它有自造血能力去支撑capex），你会看到一个反直觉的规律：在AI这场军备竞赛中，谁最先呼吁"放慢速度"，往往就是那个最需要用监管护城河来保护估值倍数的人。这几乎是2010年后大银行剧本的AI版——用合规成本挤死小玩家，把冠军位置制度化。

二、一个被所有人忽略的跨领域连接：AI capex正在挤压加密和债券市场，但源头是同一根管道

节目里三个话题看似互不相干——AI放缓、俄乌与中东搅动油价、10年期逼近5%——但它们其实是同一台机器的三个仪表盘。

先看链条：AI capex需要天量资本→前沿实验室发债+超算数据中心项目融资涌入投资级市场→投资者被迫在"僵尸国债"和"最好资产负债表的公司债"之间做选择→长端利率被推高→油价+柴油因中东路由中断继续上行→通胀预期粘住→中期选举压力下Trump必须压通胀→Kushner和Witkoff飞去俄罗斯。

惊喜观察在这里：Jordy说"利率对AI公司毫无影响，因为他们的毛利足以吸收"，这句话的暗面是——AI公司实际上正在成为长端利率的边际做市商。它们的融资需求大到足以扭曲整条曲线的形状。这意味着：宏观分析师如果仍然把AI当作科技板块的股票问题，他们已经落后一个时代——AI capex现在是债券市场的定价因子。而这也是为什么crypto作为无息资产在这个环境下反而有隐性优势：当"最优质公司债"被AI建构者占满，边际储蓄开始溢出到别处。

三、真正的"啊哈时刻"：AI监管、去中心化、tokenization合规问题共享同一个哲学基因

节目一开始讨论Robinhood offshore synthetics时，Chris提出一个几乎没人接得住的观点：如果AI责任无法在中心化架构下被清晰界定，市场可能被迫转向去中心化——因为在去中心化系统中，责任天然落回用户，就像"车会杀人，但我们不告丰田"。

这个观察连接了三个看似不相关的战场： - 代币化股票的争论（合成还是发行方赞助？谁承担投票和股息的KYC责任？） - AI前沿模型的责任问题（模型被伊朗用来分析美军军舰，Anthropic承担什么？）
- 中本聪的原初洞见（"人类控制货币系统一定会腐败，所以把规则写进数学"）

三者共享一个哲学结构：当一个系统的能力增长超过人类问责机制的承载力时，去中心化不是意识形态选择，而是唯一的责任分配解。这就是为什么Chris"这也许把AI推向去中心化栈"的直觉是深刻的——它复现了比特币的存在论论证，只是把"货币"换成了"智能"。

最反常识的预测：三年内，你会看到"链上AI推理"从边缘玩具变成合规刚需，不是因为技术优越，而是因为它是唯一能让Anthropic式的产品责任风险外部化的架构。Kleros、Gensyn、以及节目里那个用"1500个AI节点达成共识"来做主观事实裁决的系统——这些今天听起来像玩具的东西，是在为一个即将出现的巨大真空提供答案。

四、一个被节目主持人本人露出而无人捕捉的信号

Austin在节目里几乎无意间说了一句极重要的话："revealed behavior of many people is that they say they care about privacy and then the moment you ask them to be inconvenienced, even 1%, they reveal they do not."

这是行为经济学里被称为"隐私悖论"的现象，但在AI时代它有一个新含义：如果隐私不能通过用户行为定价，那它只能通过监管定价。而AI公司恰恰是最反对隐私监管的主体。所以一个奇特的三方博弈正在形成——AI实验室要监管来抑制竞争但不要隐私监管；用户嘴上要隐私但行为出卖自己；只有加密行业既有技术又有意识形态动力去把"不便利的隐私"变成"默认的隐私"。这可能是crypto在未来五年最被低估的产品市场契合点：不是"隐私币"，而是为AI agents提供的默认加密执行层。

📝 转录文本

一、代币化股票、投票权与合成品的隐忧

...mandate that it includes full security entitlements including votings and dividends and corporate actions and the like offshore. Um, do I think that they should? I think that yes, I think that we should aspire to making sure that the securities that are offered in the market are wholesome and offer all of the entitlements. So, I think it makes sense to go in that direction, and you probably heard like Broadridge is out there trying to offer services to different people tokenizing to facilitate a voting process.

But like that also connects to the non-KYC, right? So, like you have to ask yourself if you're issuing synthetics and they're going to non-KYC wallets, right? All of a sudden the question is like — I don't know, is this Al Qaeda and Hamas who are voting my shares, or is this just, you know, some individual in another country who's voting the shares? So I think for voting and even for dividends, like in the United States, you have to know who they are before you issue them a dividend.

Though I think issuer-sponsored tokens are better than synthetics, or custodial tokens that have full pass-through of entitlements are better again than synthetics that aren't necessarily passing through all of the entitlements that go to investors.

But what's interesting in this particular case is you have a synthetic, and then you have meme coins and other things that are even being built off of that. So there's like another derivative. And so in my view, like when I think about what concerns me the most, it's not even necessarily the synthetic product that's been offered offshore — it's all of these other things that are being spun up that are then paired to that.

And the fact is that these are trading in markets that are completely unregulated, that are happening over the weekend when there's no underlying market liquidity, where people are running trading strategies. And look, there's some people who are probably making a lot of money, and there's some people who are getting their faces ripped off in the process, right? And so how that is unfolding is a concern of mine. And I think that that sort of pairing and those sorts of dynamics concern me even more than the simple synthetic product, for example, that Robinhood has issued offshore.

二、Coinbase的perp vs. 实股背书代币：两种截然不同的市场效应

I get why they would be arguing here, but you really need to descend into what's going on to make some of these critiques. And I think they largely reveal somebody who does not understand how markets work — which, hypothetically, maybe some other things have also revealed in this case in the past.

But a good example is this. If we look at what Coinbase is doing, Chris, you alluded to this earlier, which is perpetual futures for tokenized US stocks versus, call it, an actual stock-backed like deposit token that doesn't pass on governance rights or maybe even not dividends, and can be traded by people. Those have two different effects on markets, right? The futures are a funding trade. Maybe they can be used for hedging, but without a party to stand between the futures and the actual price token, right? Or use them in a hedging way — to Rahm's point, this is largely speculation. And what it's revealing to me is unfulfilled demand for US stocks by non-US investors.

On the other hand, doing the reverse of an ADR is actual demand for capital. You need the underlying AMC shares to do the lock — the shares in a box — and create a thing off the box. So in that case, the critiques of "hey, we lose control of our fundraising" is like — no, that's strictly wrong. This actually gives you more people to fundraise from, not less, and expands the audience of people who want to buy your stock.

三、柴油、油价与中期选举的宏观压力

Couple things that I'm watching is diesel. Diesel is hitting records, shattering prices — I think averaging like $5.85 a gallon. That hits, you know, real America, that hits the truck drivers. And so it's no surprise, off goes Kushner and Witkoff to Russia-Ukraine, because a lot of that's hurting supply.

And so if you're Trump right now, your eye is on midterm elections. You don't want to go through impeachment after impeachment if the Congress turns. So you need to keep as many seats as possible. How do you do that? You got to attack inflation. There are some things hopefully he can do to help control that vis-à-vis the Middle East. He's been trying to do that. It's been difficult. Bessent needs rates down, which is another challenge. And so to me, I don't think anyone's in a position to raise rates under this environment, whether they're independent or not.

四、加密黑客伦理：赎金不是白帽

I just wanted to wrap this up by saying — I just want to emphasize, like, when you steal the money, period, like, you're not — it's not a white hat situation. Even if the team is a piece of [expletive] and they're arrogant as hell and there's no bounty program, you still shouldn't take the money. Okay? You're stealing people's money. It's generally a bad thing to do. If you insist on doing it, I also, you know, I recommend returning all the money immediately, and definitely don't extort people. Like, you are now in a double position of power.

And so to all the people — there's just been a lot of people on Twitter, and I guess, like, you know, Kane, you and I have done this for years. I guess in Bitcoin it's not as prevalent of a situation, but it's just odd to see people being [expletive] because they're basically playing in the hacker's hands, right? When you anchor the hack value at, say, $320 million, then you're like — for whatever. Yeah. 4,000 Bitcoin, right?

$50 million. But the reality is, taking $50 million or getting a $50 million bounty, that's freaking — it's insane. Like, we can't — that's not how the world works. I'm sorry.

五、Satoshi的启示与AI的"人机在环"弱点

Think about like the origins of crypto and like Bitcoin itself and Satoshi. One of the brilliant parts of Bitcoin was a recognition that humans controlling a monetary system is always going to be corrupted. It's always going to be an issue. And so one of the brilliant parts was, well, what if we put all those rules into math, and the humans don't control the system? They all have access, they can all use it, but they can't change it.

And I think on the AI side, there is this belief that they can really create this thing, and that they as humans will somehow be able to resist, you know, this power — that absolute power is somehow not going to corrupt them, and that they will be able to just morally, you know, dish out everything that the world needs. And it's not recognizing that you are relying on this human in the loop of this incredibly powerful system you're creating to not basically be the weakness point that falls over the ability.

六、多AI共识作为主观事实的裁决层

...really, like you get an answer in something like 3 to 5 minutes. Then you have the first window of finality — would be 30 minutes — and then if you appeal, all of them would be something like 3 hours, right? These are the timeframes that we're talking about. If you appeal everything, it would be like the cost of a transaction would be like $100. If you just do the first round, let's say, would be, you know, will be something like 50 cents to a dollar, right?

So that's the current cost of compute and current cost of AI, that's how much it is. So it depends on what the actual monetary value is, right? If we're just doing, for example, a transaction where I'm doing some clipping, for example, you can get paid whatever — a dollar, $5, whatever it is — then, you know, that's maybe okay, but you just want to go to the first round, right? So whatever, 30 cents. Now, if you're actually moving thousands of dollars, maybe yes, maybe you want to go to the thousands of them, but in reality, it depends on the question.

What we're missing right now is that both humans, right — for example, you have a prediction market like Polymarket. Polymarket uses UMA for the resolution, right? That means that it's a bunch of humans that are voting on whether Zelensky is wearing a suit or not, right? Well, you're getting an answer from, let's say, one person, maybe five or 20 people essentially, you know, deciding — that they even have a stake. They have, you know, a few days to even think about it. They need to pay gas, like dollars and dollars, to be able to vote. It's very inefficient, right?

So what we're proposing is a similar system, but it's essentially a blockchain where each validator is connected to a different AI model at the consensus level. So the network itself is that different AIs reaching an agreement on subjective things — and so it allows you to make something reproducible. You would be — if you ask a hundred times the same question to the network with the same nodes, let's say, you will get the same answer, right? Because you're basically escalating it up to like 1,000, 1,500 different AIs, and they all need to reach an agreement on that.

So it's a different type of problem. Like, we're very used to having blockchains that are deterministic, right? Like an input is giving the same output, and you repeat that, right? 2 plus 2 is 4, and it doesn't matter how many times I ask you. These AIs are not like that — they're not deterministic.

七、赞助商与频道公告

$540 million. That's how much concentrated liquidity sat idle in a given week in the first half of this year. About 30% of the DeFi TVL, if you're wondering. That's according to Dune Research commissioned by 1inch. But there's a solution. 1inch Aqua is the new shared liquidity platform. It lets LPs back multiple positions with the same token balance and keep their tokens in their wallet till a swap comes. Why does that help? Because the LPs don't have to split their tokens across positions — they can cover more market conditions and pairs with their full balance. That means more activity across deeper liquidity. See how it works at 1inch.com/aqua. Remember that providing liquidity carries risk and fees aren't guaranteed.

OpenAI的Navier-Stokes声明：OpenAI said on September 8th that a group of its agents solved the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize problem using OpenAI's next-generation models, significantly more capable than GPT-6 Astra. Anthropic的辞职风波：At the same time that was happening, Jacob Coxin, who spent three years in pre-training research at OpenAI and Anthropic, quit Anthropic on September 9th, saying, "Neither company is acting responsibly. He said the Navier-Stokes result is the start of a feedback loop of further acceleration, and said warning shots like Hugging Face attacks have made pacing agreements between US labs more viable.

Dario与Sam的响应：Dario Amodei then published "We Must Pace the Frontier" on September 12th, saying we must slow the pace at which we improve the capability of AI models. Step one of that is Anthropic unilaterally committing to third-party evaluators with permanent employee-level access.
