item.description:
## 一、被忽视的"意外时刻"：AGI 不是里程碑，而是命名权的政治
Greg 说 "AGI 已经到来" 时，其实在悄悄完成一个语言学操作——**把 AGI 从一个"点"重新定义成"光谱"**。这是极其精妙的一步：过去十年，整个行业把 AGI 悬在天上作为终局奖赏，任何未达到的东西都可以被贬低为"只是工具"。而现在 OpenAI 把定义权从"能通过图灵测试/自我改进/替代所有人类劳动"悄然滑向"能连续运行 24 小时完成任务"。
这不是技术判断，而是**叙事主权的转移**。谁掌握"AGI 是什么"的定义，谁就掌握了监管框架、投资叙事、和公众预期的锚点。有意思的是——这个操作跟 20 世纪初"现代艺术"运动如出一辙：当学院派掌握"什么是艺术"的定义时，杜尚就用小便池重新定义了艺术本身。Greg 正在用 Astra 做同样的事。
## 二、跨领域连接：网络安全的"防御者窗口"其实是热力学窗口
Greg 反复强调的 "defender window"（防御者窗口）——攻击能力尚未广泛扩散、而前沿实验室有差异化访问权的这段时期——本质上是一个**熵增窗口**。
请注意他讲的一件出人意

item.title: [Flirting with Models] Lucas Schuermann - Swapping Out Perpetual Futures (S7E34)
item.dc:creator: Flirting with Models
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、永续合约作为「过渡性物种」——被自己的成功谋杀的金融创新

Lucas 表面上在推销一个新产品（swap），但他实际上在宣告一个时代的终结。永续合约本身是一次加密世界因缺乏结算基础设施而被迫发明的黑客式产品——因为没有中央清算、没有到期日管理、没有滚动机制的市场基础，工程师们发明了"funding rate"这个反馈回路，把利率、基差、市场情绪、投机需求全部塞进一个变量里。它优雅得像热力学中的熵——用一个混沌的数字掩盖了所有底层复杂性。

而现在讽刺的是：当 Variational 用 RFQ + Tier-1 dealer 网络把 TradFi 的结算和信用基础设施拉进链上后，永续合约存在的第一性理由就消失了。这是生物学上的"过渡性物种"——它的成功来自填补了一个真空，而它的消亡将来自那个真空被真正的基础设施填满。对交易者的隐含警示是：那些看似定义了一个品类的产品，往往其实只是等待被替代的"占位符"。

二、Flow Segmentation 的隐藏跨域连接——它其实是「信息经济学的价格歧视」

Lucas 反复强调"flow segmentation"是他们能给出更紧价差的核心。他把这解释成 Wintermute、Jump 等做市商的经济学逻辑。但让我意外的是：这个机制其实是保险精算和 AI 广告拍卖背后的同一套逻辑，甚至更古老——它源于 Akerlof 1970 年"柠檬市场"的论文。

在保险业，如果你不能区分健康人和病人，你必须按最坏情况定价，健康人就会退出市场，市场崩溃。在 Google 广告拍卖里，如果不能区分用户意图，广告主必须为所有点击出低价。Variational 做的事情本质上是把"信息不对称的税"从零售用户身上退还给他们——因为它知道你不是 Citadel，它就可以不给你"防备 Citadel 的价格"。

这里有个反直觉的推论：一个"歧视性"平台（对不同 flow 报不同价）在福利经济学上可能比"公平"的中央限价簿更有效。集中订单簿的"平等对待"其实是一种伪装的平等——它把散户当作潜在的 HFT 来防备。这也解释了为什么散户券商模型（Robinhood 那种 PFOF）在全球范围内战胜了直接交易所接入。Variational 只是把这个模式带到了链上。

三、Lucas 最后那个「他自己都没意识到的」核心信号

他被问到「工作外痴迷什么」，给出两个答案：电力/算力市场 和 机器人。看似跳跃，但如果你把三件事放在一起——链上衍生品、电力市场证券化、通用机器人——它们指向同一个宏大主题：过去因为摩擦成本而无法金融化的物理/信息资产，正在被批量证券化。

他用了一个惊人的词——"recommodification of a new type of commodity"（一种新商品的再商品化）。这几乎是列宁式的表述。电力从来都是商品，但现在因为 AI 训练的时空非弹性需求，电力被重新发现为一种可以被切片、打包、期货化、swap 化的资产。机器人代表劳动的商品化——把人类工时切成可交易的 API 调用。

这里的跨域联结令人心惊：Variational 的 swap 产品不是加密的终点，而是一个更大的"万物金融化"浪潮的早期实验场。当 Lucas 说他想上"tens of thousands of listings"时，他真正想上的可能不是纳斯达克的股票——而是每一度电、每一小时机器人算力、每一个数据中心 GPU 时段的远期。而 RFQ + 单一 dealer 中介模型，恰恰是这些长尾、非流动、需要信用担保资产的天然结构。

意外洞察：一个做加密永续合约替代品的公司，实际上正在为"后 AI 经济基础设施"搭建结算层。他自己在采访里都没有明说这一点——他只是在痴迷里泄露了它。

四、一个容易被忽视的策略性弱点

我要打破一下他的叙事：他反复说 flow segmentation 是护城河，但这个模型有一个内在的自反悖论——当他们成功到聚集了 99% 的散户 flow，剩下的公共订单簿会变得极度 toxic，届时他们的对冲成本会飙升。他给出的回答（"我们有议价权"）在逻辑上正确，但忽略了博弈论上的一个死角：如果所有主要 broker 都做同样的事情，公共订单簿会退化到只剩 HFT 对打 HFT，价格发现本身会开始失灵，进而反噬所有依赖那个订单簿作为 index price 的产品——包括他自己的永续合约。

这是一个跨越 20 年才在美股 PFOF 争议中浮现的问题。加密世界如果沿着这条路走，会以几倍的速度撞上它。

📝 转录文本

Cold Open

Corey: All right, Lucas, are you ready? Lucas: Yep. Corey: All good. Let's do it. All right. Three, two, one, let's jam.

Introduction

Hello and welcome everyone. I'm Corey Hoffstein and this is Flirting with Models, the podcast that pulls back the curtain to discover the human factor behind the quantitative strategy.

Cory Hoffstein is the co-founder and chief investment officer of Newfound Research. Due to industry regulations, he will not discuss any of Newfound Research's funds on this podcast. All opinions expressed by podcast participants are solely their own opinion and do not reflect the opinion of Newfound Research. This podcast is for informational purposes only and should not be relied upon as a basis for investment decisions. Clients of Newfound Research may maintain positions and securities discussed in this podcast. For more information, visit thinknewfound.com.

My guest in this episode is Lucas Sherman, co-founder of Variational, which seeks to bring the trillion-dollar OTC derivatives market on-chain. This is my second episode on Variational. A little over a year ago, I spoke with Lucas's co-founder, Edward U. In that time, the mission hasn't changed, but a lot else has.

We begin with a reintroduction to the business and its retail-facing platform, Omni. Unlike a central limit order book where a crowd of competing market makers quote against unknown flow, every trade on Omni is quoted by a single internal liquidity provider — the OOLP — through a request-for-quote model that segregates flow. Because OOLP knows who it's trading with, it can price retail flow as non-toxic, netting offsetting positions against each other, warehousing what it chooses to keep, and hedging only the residual risk externally. It's a model that lets Variational list a long tail of crypto-native assets at competitive spreads even where on-platform interest remains thin.

The surge in demand for real-world asset exposure on-chain has pushed that model in two directions. The first is widening where those hedges can go. Rather than trying to rebuild 40 years of traditional market depth on a crypto order book, Variational has built a global network of dealer relationships to tap into it directly. The second is questioning whether the perpetual future is even the right instrument to begin with. Perp funding is driven by where the contract trades relative to its index, which can make it volatile and hard to forecast. Variational's answer is a swap — a price return leg plus an explicit financing leg priced off short rates — a far more predictable cost of carry for anyone who wants to hold levered exposure for the long haul. And there's currently over a billion dollars of dealer capacity behind it.

I hope you enjoy my conversation with Lucas Sherman.

Reintroducing Variational

Corey: Lucas, welcome to the show. Excited to have you here talking to you from across the world — late night here, early morning there. I know you are super busy. It's been an extremely busy summer for you, so I appreciate you carving out the time.

This is going to be a fun one because it's in many ways a follow-up to a conversation I had with your partner Ed over a year ago. So this is kind of a part two. For listeners who are just seeing this episode that haven't heard of Variational before, or didn't hear my episode with Ed — please go back and listen to that one. Hit pause here, go back, give it a listen. It's going to give you some great background as to what's going on with the platform. But for those who aren't going to go back, Lucas, maybe you can give a brief reintroduction as to what the Variational platform is and who you're trying to serve.

Lucas: Yeah, brief reintroduction. I'll squeak in about myself as well. I like to joke sometimes I'm the discount version of Edward — the other co-founder. Ed is a quant by background. We've been working together for the better part of a decade in hedge funds, in market making and HFT, and in crypto. I sit more on the engineering side by background, but these days more on the business side of the protocol as well.

Skipping forward to a very brief introduction about Variational: our main goal is to bring derivatives trading on-chain, and that takes two main forms.

One is retail derivatives trading. We're building a broker-like model — as opposed to an order book or an exchange — using RFQ to match versus our users, and offering, because of this different model, some very interesting benefits in terms of liquidity aggregation for RWAs direct from TradFi, zero-fee trading, hundreds of different pairs, some of the best liquidity you can find, and a one-click interface where you can trade all of this from a single account, single USDC balance. We can get into that more, and that's been very exciting and growing incredibly rapidly since your last conversation with Ed. So we've been very happy about that.

Our longer-term vision is not just stopping with retail, though — it's pro and the institutional side. We come from this background in OTC trading in crypto and beyond, and OTC options and structured products. That's a very interesting segment to us, asking the question: how do we bring institutional trading, settlement, and clearing on-chain as well? I liken that to kind of the ambition of stablecoins for FX settlement and remittances. We're the other side of the coin. We're saying, hey, that's working really well for fiat — moving that on-chain. How do we move the derivative trading piece broadly on-chain? That's kind of our mission.

Omni: How Zero-Fee RFQ Beats the Spread

Corey: As you mentioned, you've seen incredible growth in that retail side, the part of the platform that you call Omni. So we'll focus most of our attention there. Maybe we can turn to the institutional side a little bit at the end.

With Omni, this is a platform where you are charging zero maker and taker fee. As you mentioned, it is an RFQ-based platform, which is very different than sort of the central limit order book platforms that we have traditionally seen both in the centralized exchange and the decentralized perp exchanges that have come to market.

Now, what's interesting here is it means that the revenue that you're going to generate — because you're not generating maker or taker fees — is entirely in the spread. But your pitch is that that spread is going to be a tighter all-in cost compared to other venues that are going to charge fees on top of their spread. Can you walk us through how these things can coexist? How can you charge a tighter spread than a venue that is going to have those fees?

Lucas: So I think there's two questions really to answer here. One is the economy of scale of market makers and why that's an amazing flywheel. And the second is walking through the life cycle of the trade.

Maybe a common misconception that you're asking about that we can blast through to start with: because we aggregate liquidity, because we hedge (which we do — we don't counter-trade users, we don't B-book) — that our execution quality on kind of these venues must mean always crossing the spread and the taker fees, and therefore that our net execution cost should be, you know, super-set etc. higher than that. That's not the case. For the same reason that if I trade against Jump or Jane or Hudson River Trading, or in crypto Wintermute or Selini and beyond — you can imagine that if I do a large order with them, they might be aggressing to offlay the risk. They might be trading on a variety of different exchanges to build those hedging positions on the other side.

Let's say I sold $100 million of BTC to Wintermute. Does that preclude them from quoting me very, very, very tight on that order — tighter than the taker fees on Binance, tighter than we could possibly walk the book at that size on any of these exchanges? No, it doesn't preclude them at all. I mean, that's very much their core business.

So when I think about how does OOLP aggregate liquidity — we use "aggregation" as one way to describe our model, this intermediation of the flow, this principal-brokerage-style model. But another way to think about it is: we act like a market maker. Our goal is to build a large economy of scale through internalization of flow, through broad connectivity to hedging venues, through economies of scale that we have at the hedging venues and beyond, such that just like a large market maker would, we're quoting better than the sum of our parts, both in terms of fees and in terms of spreads externally.

So the short answer to your secondary question — how can we provide a better price than one could get executing that whole size immediate-loan to a Binance or immediate-loan to a Hyperliquid or whatever — it's for the exact same reasons as any market maker. We can unpack that in a bit, but that's very much the economy of scale and the whole point of this intermediation that we're doing.

The Market-Making Flywheel

On the former side, on the flywheel, I actually just wanted to briefly contemplate: what are the drivers that allow market makers at scale, or our system at scale, to offer such tight spreads but still generate quite a lot of revenue?

Again, I'll liken this to our comparables in traditional finance — let's talk about the Janes or the Jumps, etc. They generate billions of dollars of profit every quarter, maybe even every month depending on where you're at in the market. So these are amazing businesses. But does that mean that these spreads that these guys are providing onto, say, retail brokerages like Robinhood, or onto the actual liquidity that exists on NASDAQ or NYSE or CME — does that mean the spreads are wide? No. No, not at all.

The bigger the economy of scale, the cheaper they can be, because the lower their fee tiers are, the better connectivity they have, the more internalization they have, the better short-term alpha they have, etc. So this is our broad mental model, and it's why I'll make an even stronger statement than your original question:

Our execution costs are some of the best anywhere on Omni because we have zero fees plus very tight spreads — but we expect those to actually improve over time, mostly due to the economy of scale. As the system gets bigger, just like any other market-making system, we're able to drive a larger economy of scale, higher internalization rates, etc. We can actually simultaneously expand our margins (which is good for the protocol) and reduce our spreads, offer better size to our users.

Flow Segmentation: The Real Structural Edge

Corey: So let me continue to push on the first point you made a little bit — because any other market maker at scale is also going to be implementing cross-venue hedging, right? If I go to put an order on at Hyperliquid or Binance, large sophisticated market makers are going to take that order and hedge it across a multitude of venues, as well as internalize the risk as they see fit, the same way in theory that you can. What is actually structurally different about the RFQ model that allows you to potentially create tighter spreads than a market maker could in a CLOB model?

Lucas: There are a few nuances here, and I'll unpack probably three of them, but let's start with the big one, which is called flow segmentation.

The idea here is that there is a huge difference between us taking the other side of a trade on the Omni platform — more like, in your example, someone trading on a single-dealer platform or with a known counterparty and an OTC block trade — quoting via RFQ. RFQ is just kind of the matching primitive. Of course we like to talk about RFQ as a clear differentiator versus limit order books; it's easy to understand. But really the biggest difference in our model is having this single system, this principal brokerage on the other side, and being a broker-like aggregator as opposed to having an order book for price discovery.

So the point being: RFQ versus order book is a bit of a semantic way in which we do that matching. The bigger difference is actually — again — we're on the other side of the trade. We have full information about who's facing us. We're getting the quantity and the size all up front. What this information allows is essentially safety in information leakage, or let's call it adverse selection on the flow.

A Concrete Example

Let me unpack that in a more specific case. In my $100 million example, let's make it a little bit more reasonable — 10 or 50 million. No one in their right mind is walking the book on an order book. Firstly, these businesses like Jump and Jane and everyone else who's posting liquidity there — they're not charities. They will very quickly see that someone's walking the book, or even if you're trying to TWAP it on a public exchange, they're very quickly going to be moving the market price, right? Because their goal is to maximize profits per dollar traded. So that's number one.

Number two: as they generate more risk on a public order book, you don't know who the other participant is. I could be sweeping the book as a taker with a lot of risk because I have short-term alpha and I'm sitting at Tower or HRT — and Jump and everyone else is going to be scared of that.

So the idea of providing a good all-in price depends a lot on the segmentation of flow — or in other words, what you would assume is the toxicity of the flow. Because taking on this size, this amount of inventory, and then going and hedging it — a lot of the game is in understanding: how long are we okay holding that inventory? How much will we be able to internalize it versus other participants that are coming in? And then indeed, what is our connectivity and our view on the hedging venues, and where those are going, and how much we can size up?

So the short answer to your question: pillar one is flow segmentation. And this is the biggest mechanical difference between trading via RFQ, or more particularly via what our system looks more like — a single-dealer platform in many ways — and again, like trading on an order book. We don't have to be taking down floor or posting quotes that can be sniped by anyone, that can be front-run by high-frequency takers that might be trading into the public void of who knows how smart the guys are at the top of the book on Binance. And I'll give you a cheat code: they're very, very, very smart. So you have to be very defensive on that.

Whereas for us — we don't have an API yet, it's on the roadmap, we can come back to that question later — but we're optimizing for: what's the best possible price we can show to retail order flow when we know that it's retail order flow? When we can see who's on the other side of the trade, and when we can get comfortable with quoting very big size because this isn't adversarial or front-running or arbitraging. These are guys just trying to get the best all-in price for their block trade or their entry into a mid-frequency day-trading position. And that's a completely different ballpark in terms of how you can quote it.

To put this all in a summation form: our liquidity quality does look like — if you're looking for an RFQ from, say, a tier-one desk (I pick on again, a Jump or Wintermute or something like that) — I would expect it to be in the same ballpark. But the difference is that's not at all what's happening when you're matching on a public order book. But that is what's happening if you are, say, a $10 billion institution onboarded onto an OTC trading relationship with one of these guys.

So one of the ways I like thinking about what we're doing in Variational is democratizing access to that quality of execution and that style of trading, which is massively usually better for the end client than having to trade directly on an order book. There's a few more mechanical things, but in the interest of time let me pause there on your question. I think that's one of the big lion's-share reasons.

What Happens as Non-Toxic Flow Migrates?

Corey: And maybe my next question will get you to continue to extrapolate. Lucas: I agree in part with the last part of that statement, which is actually asking the question: over time, will we have as many venues for hedging crypto, and is that necessary, especially in a world where most retail trading — which we is called soft non-toxic flow — moves to broker-like platforms, namely ours? If we think through it a bit from first principles: let's say Variational is soaking up more and more retail flow (which is what's happening right now and is very much our goal), and this is moving from other platforms where it might be currently trading directly onto order books — indeed making them more toxic in some sense — and moving more and more towards Variational. This is the absolute dream scenario for us.

We have soft flow to monetize. We have some cases of short-term alpha or some information signal that's coming from the flow. Retail flow drives a huge portion of notional nominal activity these days. We have the ability to internalize it — in other words, I like to joke about squeezing the lemon. We don't counter-trade our users, and we're quite clear about wanting to always be more of an aggregator, more tilted towards just providing the best all-in price than necessarily juicing the spread. That's very different from a market maker. That's why it's a lossy comparison where I'll pick on maybe Jane G — like, their goal is absolutely to maximize their profit on the desk. They're not a charity. They're not trying to say, "how can we make these spreads tighter to build a better retail-facing brokerage product?" No, they're like, "how can we possibly juice the spreads as wide as possible and still get people to transact?"

The point is: in a world where we have all the — call it — soft flow, the non-toxic flow, this is a dream scenario for monetization. It's a dream scenario for pricing, because we know our flow is non-toxic and therefore we can quote it really, really tight while still monetizing nicely. And it's a dream scenario for hedging. We have all the negotiating power in the world. If everyone else's flow is toxic and ours is not, that's the good thing. That's the best thing. Because even our aggregated hedging flow is still highly non-toxic and would be very desirable to these venues — in this toy example where you assume the books are getting more and more toxic.

But even one layer up, it gives us a huge amount of negotiating power just at that size and scale. Again, if you assume non-toxic order flow is somewhat scarce (which it is, even in traditional markets), that equilibrium gives a lot of negotiating power to the guys who are the ones orbiting where that goes. Do we hedge it OTC just to a small set of counterparties? Do we hedge it on what I think will eventually exist in crypto, like ECN-style platforms, dark pools, one-level-lit pools? Or does it go directly onto exchange? It'll be an interesting question to see how it evolves.

I do agree with the premise that it will lead to a thinning of the herd. You do need those quote-unquote toxic — those price-discovery high-frequency venues. The NASDAQs and NYSEs and CMEs are those in the traditional markets. But absolutely, I think it makes sense that those will eventually look a little bit different.

And it brings me to a final point here, which is: I like to say we're not a direct competitor to Hyperliquid or a Lighter, and we really respect their businesses. I think many of those will succeed both in crypto and beyond. We're similarly not a competitor — and in many ways like a downstream client or beneficiary — of CME and NASDAQ and NYSE and so on, in the same way that traditional market brokerages are.

But I do think that we have to ask the question: exchanges are infrastructure. They are for order matching. They are for price discovery. They are for institutions hedging against each other in HFT. I do think eventually retail flow will move to a broker-like model like ours.

The API Question

Corey: You mentioned the potential introduction of APIs. How does that change your thinking about toxic versus non-toxic flow that you'll be facing on the platform?

Lucas: I'll give you a surface-level and then I'll give you a nuanced answer.

The surface-level answer is: beauty of RFQ, beauty of our model, broker-like platform. We have perfect information, perfect flow segmentation. A quick sub-question of what you're asking is: how do you avoid getting run over? What if you do have an adversarial counterparty connect to this API? Isn't the whole idea that we're able to quote really tight because we have the soft flow on the UI, etc.?

Yes. But the reality is, to put it incredibly reductively, it's quite trivial to protect ourselves. We want to service real retail, and that includes guys who might be using cloud and building API strategies and so on. What we don't want is truly high-frequency takers — indeed the tier-one HFTs we were just describing — to be trying to arbitrage our prices. And that goes back to your earlier point on the order books. By definition, if we allow that to happen, we have to widen out prices for everyone. That's not what we want to occur.

So instead, what we'll be building is ways to detect and monitor that, and essentially on an individual-by-individual basis, let's just say protect ourselves as necessary. And that allows us to still service the 99.999% of the world both on the UI and even on the API that will be on that high-frequency basis highly non-toxic — likely very normal — because that's an incredibly small number of firms that would really be looking to arbitrage or cause issues there.

The slightly more nuanced answer: this is the exact same problem set as, indeed — again returning to my example — what we'd be facing if we're building a single-dealer platform. I have, at parts of my career at a market maker like a Wintermute, or in traditional markets a Jump or an HRT and so on — you want to figure out the toxicity, information leakage on every single venue, and that includes the cross-connectivity you have to direct retail clients or API clients. There's a lot of theory that goes into how to measure it, what to do about it when you do identify that there's some toxic flow, and indeed how to balance that such that you can still win the flow.

We like to service API clients essentially up to that ultra layer, because again — we're a brokerage. Jump doesn't trade on Robinhood. That's just a silly premise. From a first-principles perspective, it's not our core business. And as you can imagine, there's a lot of tools once you've identified [toxic flow] short of shutting it off. You can widen, you can add speed bumps, all sorts of stuff to stop the abuse.

The RWA Explosion

Corey: One of the biggest evolutions that's happened over the last year since I had my interview with Ed has been the growth of real-world asset perps — RWAs. They were around for years with like gold perps and were largely a niche product, but in the last 12 months they have really exploded in depth and volume and open interest, and just seem to be attracting a lot of attention. A lot of platforms are figuring out ways on how to list them.

What we've seen is a lot of venues have gone to list them the same way they listed crypto — they have external market makers who are quoting an on-chain order book, but now those external market makers have to go figure out how to hedge in markets that live entirely off-chain predominantly, and sometimes aren't even open.

You guys, in your Series A announcement, made the point that you can't rebuild — and this is a quote from you, I believe — "40 years of traditional market depth from scratch on a crypto order book." Talk to me a little bit about why you think that the way other venues might be going about this is overly inefficient, overly expensive, and how you're looking to solve this problem differently.

Lucas: Let me unpack that, because I think it's a great question. It's something that we think best illustrates why our model works incredibly well, and I'd argue absolutely the best for solving RWA trading on-chain.

The Sheer Magnitude of TradFi Liquidity

A couple observations here, quite a few. Number one is that the amount of liquidity in traditional markets, and this is perhaps the most obvious statement in the world, is incredible. We're talking over decades and decades — global networks of participants, dozens and hundreds of different HFT firms, banks, non-bank dealers, broker-dealers, so many layers. We can get into even what it looks like in the US versus abroad. But just incredible amounts of capital, structure, liquidity, sophistication.

When we're comparing even the grand success — and we have all the respect in the world for say Hyperliquid and the trade.xyz team — when we're comparing the depth of like an oil order book there, which is one of the most tradable things on-chain right now (let's say CL on xyz), it just pales — and I mean pales — on its face in comparison to the depth on just one venue like CME in this case. But this goes across the whole board.

When we think about the aggregate depth in traditional markets, there's so many orders of magnitude greater that it becomes silly to compare them at a certain point. We're talking about markets that trade single-digit and sometimes even double-digit trillions a day, versus markets that trade a few hundred million. These are exponential. These are orders of magnitude. So there's huge differences.

We're also talking about, at the end of the day, a subset — and again with all the power to them and all the respect for defining this category first — a subset of 30, 50, maybe a little bit more than that, things that are actually tradable in terms of decent depth, even at retail size, on-chain. And outside of that set, either they're not listed because they haven't found ways to build good liquidity yet, or they're listed but the spreads are laughably wide.

The Retail Analogy

Maybe another mental model here, for the more retail folks in our audience: if I go trade Nvidia on Robinhood, or Schwab or traditional brokerage, Interactive Brokers — not even just that, which is one of the most liquid markets, but anything of the hundreds if not thousands of different global securities and FX markets and so on that we can list — I barely even think about execution.

I won't use the word "I" too heavily here, but let's say I'm a prop shop and I have a 10, 20 million book and I'm executing. I can truly get incredible size on a top 300, 500 asset by volume in the US. I can trade a liquid options chain, etc. I won't belabor the point, but just to say — when we think about what's tradable, meaning the liquidity is good enough to not have just absurd execution costs, in TradFi the menu is thousands if not tens of thousands of global markets, and so liquid that we barely think — I barely think — you know, maybe I'm betraying myself as not the best day-trader, but I rarely think about market ordering a million or 10 million of, say, some of these especially more liquid names like Nvidia. And I think a lot of people would join me in that sentiment.

That's a better user experience. I don't want to have to be worrying all the time about what's the depth, the liquidity — can it really support my trade? If I enter, can I get out? Maybe it's really thin over the weekends, or gets volatile — am I gonna get liquidated? These are just not things that cross the mind in the depth of liquidity in traditional markets. And that's why it's so important, because it's not expensive. It lets users forget about this and just place their trade, know they're going to get a good fill, know they can always get out.

The Crypto-Native Puddle

Now let's look at crypto-native liquidity. It's kind of like starting up a new version of, I don't know, CME or CBOE — let's say offshore, to make the point even more poignant. At the time when I'm starting a competing exchange, I have no liquidity in the books. It's like a social network with no users. There's nothing there. And I'm going to have to incentivize and beg and claw and give subsidies my way to getting that first little puddle of liquidity into the books, and move up from there.

And again, this is why we say all the power and respect to Hyperliquid and others who are innovating in this — that was a real zero-to-one moment. It's amazing that any of these things are tradable at all. But they're tradable by virtue or by nature of assembling what went from a puddle to a little bit of a pond of liquidity, and maybe even similar to like oil has moved closer to a lake — but there's an ocean of liquidity out there in TradFi. And that difference is just too huge in magnitude to ignore.

Variational's Answer: Skip the Queue

So to return to your question — I've spent a lot of time essentially just really hammering home the point that there's just a massive gap between on-chain order books and TradFi. I think this is probably quite intuitive. But the question is: how do you bridge that gap? How do you solve that problem?

The solution right now that everyone who's building order-book-based exchanges is — as you said — full frontal, right? It's just saying, well, we're just going to compete. We're just going to incentivize and claw and beg and commercial-agreement our way to get more and more guys on-chain, more and more of this little puddle to a pool, to a pond, to a lake, and eventually we'll do that across the board.

And the reality is that's a really uphill battle. It genuinely is. Because we see global markets also moving towards 24/7, including in the US and abroad. We see thousands and tens of thousands of global symbols that we'll have to do this for, right, if we're using this mental model. And I just worry, or I question the premise of, does it make sense to be rebuilding all of global liquidity step by step, brick by brick — something that I think is going to take decades to really reach par? People have tried this even in traditional venues, and it has taken decades to build up new exchanges in even other Asian countries and beyond.

Returning back to what does Variational do differently — we just skip the queue. It's that simple. We're not rebuilding liquidity. We're aggregating. We talked about that a little bit at the beginning of the conversation. We uniquely have this aggregation model where our liquidity, as I said at the beginning, is more than the sum of the parts. It's our hedging venues, and then we add our own market-making system on top of it. But you can think of it as: our liquidity is a superset of what we're connected to.

The unique major innovation in Variational as it relates to RWAs is we connected directly to TradFi. And when I say directly to TradFi, I don't mean crypto-native dealers that are sitting on a little bit of TradFi liquidity through a retail broker. I mean directly to the largest dealers, and hopefully in many cases non-bank and even future bank prime brokerages, that underpin these in the traditional markets. That is the structural difference — because our liquidity is approximately equivalent to TradFi through that.

And there's a lot to do there. I'll pause because this has been a lengthy answer so far, but that's just the start for us. That's the biggest systemic difference: we're not rebuilding the order books, we're just going straight to where they're most liquid — which is on TradFi — and we're bringing them on-chain by nature of this broker-like model.

When Does On-Chain Hedging Still Make Sense?

Corey: One of the biggest differences I think about here is when there's a crypto order that flows through, you can hedge on the venues where price discovery is actually happening. Arguably that's Binance maybe 99% of the time. With real-world assets, that price discovery lives on ICE and COMEX, or is in the traditional finance world. But as you mentioned, there is liquidity on-chain now.
